Besides, Apple already used iBook for a previous laptop line, and then reused it for its digital books app, before renaming it to Apple Books. iFold, iPhold, iPhone Fold. Not a chance. I can’t see Apple using a name that’s so synonymous with Android foldables, like Samsung’s Galaxy Fold series. So, what then will Apple call the foldable iPhone? I’m going to just throw this out there. I see two paths Apple could take. The first is to just call it iPhone Plus or iPhone Max. Apple has ascribed both descriptors to iPhones before to emphasize a larger screen size. Apple first used Plus for the iPhone 6 Plus through the iPhone 8 Plus. Then, switched over to iPhone Max to describe the bigger model with the iPhone XS Max. When Apple introduced the first “Pro” iPhone, the iPhone 11 Pro, the bigger screen model was christened iPhone 11 Pro Max. Since then, the larger Pro iPhone has always been called “Pro Max.” Apple also brought back “Plus” for the iPhone 14 through iPhone 16 series. The iPhone 16 Plus was replaced with an iPhone Air last year. What if foldable iPhone is called: iPhone Max It’s not a “Pro” because it doesn’t have telephoto or the longest battery or Face ID or action button Just the biggest iPhone screen ever Just iPhone Max — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 8, 2026 Which brings me to the next possibility: what if the foldable iPhone is actually viewed as part of the iPhone Air family? It’s supposed to measure around 4mm when open, which would make it thinner than the 5.6mm iPhone Air. It’d definitely qualify to be an “Air” device. If that’s how Apple sees it—as an iPhone Air with a huge screen—then I think it could be called the iPhone Air Max, iPhone Air Pro, or iPhone Air Plus. Nike would probably not be okay with Apple using “Air Max” branding. As some of my followers have astutely pointed out, Tim Cook may be on the Nike board and use every chance to wear Nike sneakers in public, but that may be a line too far. That leaves us with iPhone Air Pro or iPhone Air Plus. Or iPhone Air Duo, even. So here are my final name bets: - iPhone Max - iPhone Plus - iPhone Air Pro - iPhone Air Duo Who wants to take bets? Fight me in the comments 😛

item.title: Silicon Valley’s AI Agent Push Has Been Paying Off—for Cybercriminals
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.44
AI companies have made a lot of noise about the technology supercharging healthcare, scientific discovery, education, productivity, and just about everything else worth caring about. But so far, probably the most dramatic change wrought by the AI race has been the sudden appearance of dangerous new cybersecurity threats. The most infamous of these are the autonomous hacks launched by swarms of AI agents, the most recent of which was first reported last week (even though OpenAI, the company behind the agents, had reportedly been aware of the incident for quite a while longer). But it’d be a mistake to think that new cyber threats in the age of AI are only coming from mindless, reward-hacking bots; there are still plenty of good ol’ fashioned human hackers, for whom new AI tools have been a godsend. A new report from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG)—a research team within Google monitoring emerging cyberthreats—found that threat actors, many of them with direct ties to the United States’ geopolitical foes, have been leveling-up the sophistication of their AI usage, transitioning from basic chatbots to more agentic, autonomous systems. “Over the past quarter, threat actors have moved beyond simple prompt-based LLM interactions to integrate AI capabilities into multiple stages of an attack lifecycle,” GTIG wrote in its report, which was published online Tuesday morning. “While traditional script-based automation has long been a staple of threat actor operations, groups are increasingly upgrading these workflows, creating highly autonomous systems capable of reasoning through complex tasks and making dynamic decisions without the need for human oversight.” In plain English: the technology that leading AI companies (including Google) have been building into their AI systems, giving them the ability to handle complex tasks without constant hand-holding, is also making hackers’ dirty work a whole lot easier. Some of the “adversaries” that GTIC identified in its new report appear to be backed by China, Russia, and Iran. One group, which GTIC first reported earlier this year and identified only as “UNC6508,” has been targeting American academic, medical, and military research institutions in a manner “aligned with the strategic interests of the People’s Republic of China.” According to Tuesday’s report, UNC6508 has been observed using an open source AI model within its targets’ cloud environments to steal compute without leaving the kind of trail that would be left if they’d been using a commercial, publicly available AI model. “[UNC6508] continues to research how to set up and use AI tools, including using open models locally, and researching vulnerabilities in AI models themselves,” GTIC wrote in its new report. In another case reported by GTIC, threat actors traced to Iran used Gemini to generate realistic deepfakes to be used in social engineering campaigns. Rather than entering one prompt after another to fine-tune the deepfakes’ appearance, they deployed the AI model to autonomously define “granular technical parameters—including camera angles, studio lighting, and realistic facial textures—to achieve photorealistic visual outputs.” GTIC also reported “coordinated campaigns” being carried out “on a regular basis” to distill its proprietary AI systems, which it said is a violation of Google’s terms of service and could be subject to legal action. Though distillation has long been a widely used practice within the AI industry to develop new models, it’s recently become a political flashpoint. Leading American developers including OpenAI and Anthropic have accused their Chinese rivals of distilling their AI systems in an effort to gain a competitive edge, and the White House has vowed to crack down on what it’s described as “deliberate, industrial-scale campaigns to distill U.S. frontier AI systems.”

item.title: This Photon Survived an ‘Impossible’ Journey to Earth. To Explain it, Physicists Had to Break Einstein
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.00
In 2022, astronomers detected an absurdly bright and long-lasting gamma ray burst, GRB 221009A—nicknamed “BOAT,” for “Brightest of All Time” (seriously). The shower of photons was so old and powerful that, theoretically, it shouldn’t have reached Earth. And yet, it clearly has. But how? In a paper published yesterday in Physical Review Letters, a pair of physicists offer a puzzling solution to a puzzling problem: hypothetical particles from the cosmic dawn. Specifically, the researchers propose that photons could temporarily transform into axion-like particles, which are extremely light, paired with a separate tweak to account for photon behavior at extreme energies. It’s this second piece that technically violates something called Lorentz invariance, a key tenant of Einstein’s special relativity. But here’s the thing—using this model, the pair predicted a secondary effect that would arise from the photon’s journey. And, it turns out, a completely unrelated observatory actually had observed exactly this. In other words, there’s actually empirical support for this theory. “We started from a very simple question: how did this photon survive a journey that, according to known physics, should have destroyed it?” Giorgio Galanti, the study’s co-author and an astrophysicist at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics, said in a statement. “We therefore looked for a theoretical scenario capable of consistently describing what we observe, without resorting to arbitrary corrections to the equations.” ‘B.O.A.T.’ Because GRB 221009A was so powerful, it “temporarily blinded most space-based gamma-ray instruments,” according to a NASA explainer—hence the nickname, “BOAT.” But the signal was also exceptionally long, at about 10 minutes. The flash remained detectable for the next 10 hours, and soon astronomers were able to lock down some key statistics of the BOAT. Originating roughly two billion light-years from Earth, it exerted energies around 300 teraelectronvolts (TeV). For context, 1 electronvolt is the kinetic energy of 1 electron in a 1-volt vacuum; 1 teraelectronvolt is equivalent to 1 trillion electronvolts. At the time, experts with NASA surmised that the burst of light came from the birth of a new black hole, and subsequent investigations of the signal deemed that such luminous events would occur once in every 10,000 years. A broken signal? Then, astronomers had to reckon with the elephant in the room: the logistics of GRB 221009A’s journey to Earth. In the paper, Galanti and co-author Marco Roncadelli, of the Italian National Institute for Nuclear Physics, explained that GRB 221009A was “in tension” with conventional physics. According to the physics rulebook, photons at similar energy levels should have collided with the cosmic microwave background—traces of radiation from the universe’s earliest days—and been annihilated in the process. In the statement, the team likened this to “shooting an arrow through an extremely dense forest stretching for two billion light-years and expecting it not to hit a single tree.” So, if the signal got here—and we know it did—the photons must have found a way either to dodge all of these trees or disregard them altogether. The pair believes the answer is the latter. Some models of quantum gravity allow for slight flexibility in one of the fundamental rules of Einstein’s special relativity for matter at the highest energy levels. The pair coupled this mechanism with axion-like particles. As a result, what you get are what the researchers call the universe’s “fast lane,” through which super light, very powerful particles zip through obstacles as if they didn’t exist. Cheat code Understandably, this might sound like an ad hoc solution to the problem; after all, it’s not like we have concrete proof that axion-like particles exist. The team recognized this in the paper, explaining that its proposal is just one out of many ideas to probe this unexplained signal. That said, the latest calculations predicted a one-hour gap between a shower of lower-energy photons and the 300 TeV photon’s arrival on Earth. And, remarkably, this was precisely what one Chinese observatory caught at the time. “The most interesting aspect of our work is that, for the first time, it brings together two ideas that until now had been developed separately,” Roncadelli said in the statement. “If future observations confirmed this scenario, the universe would become a natural laboratory for studying quantum gravity at energies enormously higher than those achievable by any accelerator built on Earth.”

item.title: That Free MyChart ‘Medicare Kit’ Is a Scam
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.88
Have you received an email about a free MyChart Medicare Kit recently? Don’t click on anything in that email because it’s definitely a phishing scam. Gizmodo obtained consumer complaints filed with the FTC, and it appears the scam has gotten much more popular in the past two months. Dozens of hospital systems across the country have issued warnings about the scam in the past two weeks, which is made to look like it’s coming from MyChart. The software is made by Epic Systems and is the most popular patient portal in the U.S. Gizmodo filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with the Federal Trade Commission to obtain consumer complaints about MyChart-related scams. A total of 166 complaints over the past five years are on file with the FTC related to MyChart, though not all of them relate to phishing scams. The subject lines to the current wave of scams often carry messages like, “Your MyChart Medicare Kit Awaits!” or refer to a “Senior Health Package.” The complaints include the text of one scam email, which reads: Dear Member, Our records show that your account [redacted email] is currently eligible to receive the official MyChart Medicare Home Health Kit at no added cost to you. This comprehensive package is distributed as part of your annual wellness benefits to support daily home health monitoring. Because allocated inventory for your zip code is limited, unclaimed kits will be reassigned to the next member on the waiting list. Notice: Unclaimed packages will expire within 48 hours of notice. This administrative notice was transmitted to [redacted].com regarding Medicare Advantage wellness allocations. To adjust your email communication preferences, you may unsubscribe here. It’s the kind of thing that many people will immediately clock as a scam. But if you don’t have your guard up, anyone can get swindled into clicking on the links just out of curiosity. Especially since Medicare does actually send out a “Welcome to Medicare” package that includes a letter, booklet, and Medicare card when people sign up for benefits. It’s not something that anyone has to pay for and isn’t like a “kit” as in the screenshot below. Reached for comment, Epic directed Gizmodo to online guidance it published about MyChart scams. Among its most important tips: If you entered credit card information, contact your bank and have the card replaced. If you downloaded or ran a program from a phishing site—or entered sensitive information into one—disconnect the computer from the internet and have it inspected by a professional before using it to access personal, financial, or work accounts. We’re publishing some of the complaints below to help users understand the different kinds of emails that may be advertising a “free” Medicare health kit. They hopefully provide some additional context for what people should be looking out for. “I paid it with my Mastercard.” - Illinois - July 2026 - Age: 70-79 I received an email purporting to represent mychart and offering a free ‘Medicare kit.’ Unfortunately, I failed to notice until later that the email address used had nothing to do with mychart. I answered a questionnaire about my use of mychart, and moved on to the point where I was asked to pay shipping. I paid it with my Mastercard. After I realized that this was not legitimate, I received another email for the same thing from a different email address, as follows: [redacted].com. This is an obvious scam if they are trying to sell me the same thing twice. Now they have information about my card, so I will have to change that, along with my passwords for the card and email. “I am extremely upset and concerned that I am going to be a victim of medical/personal identity theft…” - Minnesota - July 2026 - Age: 70-79 Less than 1 hr ago, I received an email claiming to be from MyChart, my medical records, appointment scheduling app used by my health provider, Welia Health in Mora, MN. It was offering a free Medicare Kit if I took a survey regarding my experience with MyChart. I took the survey. It was then stated all I needed to do was pay for shipping. I completed the form, entered my CC info and hit send. A few minutes later, I checked my CC app to see it the item had been processed and saw that the transaction was listed as an animal/pet service. I immediately did a web search and read about all the scams pertaining to just what I had thought was a legit offer from MyChart. I am extremely upset and concerned that I am going to be a victim of medical/personal identity theft and am reaching out here immediately to get protection and assistance with how this horrific incident can be quickly and effectively resolved. Please contact me ASAP with help and what I need to do next. I am so grateful for your attention and all information you can provide me to protect myself. “I know now it was a scam…” - Oklahoma - July 2026 - Age: 60-64 It was a give away for a free medicare kit. You did a survey of about 6 questions about the usefulness of My Chart Portal and then provided your info for shippiing and then you pay for shipping. I recieved a second email today saying i needed to provide my address and it went through the same questions and wanted me to pay for a kit. (again) I know now it was a scam, should have known from the begining. “They then charge you the 9.95 and immediately try charging your card another 29.95 for another scam company.” - Indiana - August 2026 - Age: 50-59 The email was supposedly from My Chart, an app that gives you access to your medical information. The email stated that you will receive Medicare first aid kit for submitting a survey about My Chart then says you only pay for shipping of 9.95. They then charge you the 9.95 and immediately try charging your card another 29.95 for another scam company. “It looked real, with the MyChart logo, offering me a free and ‘completely new’ Medicare Kit.” - August 2026 I received an email, which I immediately suspected as fraudulent because the subject title was ‘Congratulations b(6)’ so I reported it as junk before opening it in my junkmail folder, just to make sure it wasn’t a legitimate email from MyChart. The email came to my regular inbox, not my junkmail, but my suspicions were confirmed since 1) it was from a gmail address, not a MyChart address, and there were 2 email addresses on the ‘To:’ line that weren’t me, but rather 2 email addresses I didn’t know [redacted] @comcast.net, [redcacted]@comcast.net). The email itself was an image, so I cannot copy and paste the text here, but it looked real, with the MyChart logo, offering me a free and ‘completely new’ Medicare Kit. I am a MyChart user, but not yet a Medicare user, so this was obviously a phishing email trying to get me to click on their link/image to claim a kit that doesn’t apply to me and inviting me to take a survey as a valued customer. This so called Medicare Kit, however, is shown and later described in the email as a ‘premium first aid and medical-grade preparation kit’ not a kit about Medicare to be received upon filling out the survey. I didn’t click on anything, including the unsubscribe link, already reported it as junk to Juno and will delete it after submitting this report. Also, I will note that while perhaps unrelated, I received this fraudulent email after my Juno email account was behaving strangely, not pulling up my emails or other folders in Juno and mostly unresponsive, even after I closed it and updated my browser and reopened it once. It wasn’t until I reopened Juno again this morning that my Juno was working again and I received this sent yesterday, so technically I first encountered (opened) it today, 8/1/26 rather than yesterday 7/31/26. “The emails come from various senders” - Illinois - August 2026 - Age: 70-79 I have received several emails pretending to be the MyChart health company asking me for personal information so they can send me a MyChart Medicare Home Health Kit ant no cost. The emails come from various senders which I assume are fraudulent. I included the latest sender info in the question above.

item.title: Anthropic Builds Model to Predict Economy in 2030, Leaves Off the ‘Everybody Dies’ Outcome
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.67
Life as a member of the communications team for frontier AI labs must be fascinating. Imagine you’ve got this big report ready to go out on the extremely elaborate model your economics team built that you want to position as a tool for policymakers and academics to understand how AI is going to impact the workforce, and the night before it publishes, your colleagues just casually (and publicly) declare that there’s a greater than 10% chance that your technology kills everyone within the next decade. Is that in the model? Do you address that? Anthropic went with no to both of those questions, but it did, in fact, release its Economic Index growth model, which is designed to project what the economy could look like by the end of the decade, based on different levels of AI functionality and adoption. You’ll be shocked to learn that the big takeaway from the model is that everything is going to be a-okay in most cases—though the outcomes that aren’t on the chart are probably as noteworthy as the ones that are. Per Anthropic, as long as we stay within the parameters of somewhere between “business as usual” and an economy where “AI increases growth to about twice the normal rate,” we can expect unemployment to stay within historically normal ranges and wages to “remain flat or rise depending on the industry.” However, if we reach growth that is “faster than anything in economic history,” then there will be “adverse impacts on wages and job prospects for knowledge workers.” But don’t worry, because even when it’s bad, it’s good! “In those scenarios, society is far wealthier, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are broadly shared.” And since we’ve historically been so great at wealth distribution, there are certainly no red flags to raise there. The model is interesting, at least. As the AI lab explained it, it sought to effectively break down jobs into bundles of tasks, then determine how the availability of AI might impact those tasks—what can be automated, what new work will be created because of AI, and what will likely remain human labor. Then it scales AI adoption levels to each job to determine how different industries and the economy as a whole will be affected by the technology. It ultimately spits out a model that, at the extreme end of the spectrum, projects an economy that is 50% larger than it is today and has a nearly 30% unemployment rate. For what it’s worth, the furthest you can push the model the other way is zero AI adoption, which amounts to the economy functioning as usual. It doesn’t account for a potential AI bubble and how its popping may impact workers and the economy, which is currently wildly overleveraged on the idea that the AI boom is for real. Even the model’s most extreme edges also don’t account for everyone dying, which is apparently within the internal parameters for possible outcomes. Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s alignment science lead, posted on Twitter yesterday that, “We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” and put the odds at greater than 10% over the next decade while admitting, “we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” Feels like that’d probably result in some economic shrinkage, but maybe eliminating humans would just get rid of inefficiencies. Guess we’ll just plow forward unimpeded until we find out!

item.title: Nope, Anthropic Won’t Be Buying That Un-Anthropic-Like Company: Report
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.45
Decart would have been kind of a funny company for Anthropic to buy, which is why it was newsworthy when Bloomberg reported that Anthropic was looking to do so. Last month, I wrote that Bloomberg’s initial reporting on this story was “one of those anonymously-sourced Bloomberg articles you can’t help but suspect might exist solely to help out one or another side in an ongoing negotiation,” and I finished by saying, “the deal could still crumble.” So what have we learned now that, according to Bloomberg, it has? To remind you, this is Anthropic’s vibe: And here is Decart’s vibe: Decart is an intriguing company. Its marquee products are the flashy “world models” Lucy and Oasis. Both make for eye-popping demos. Its Lucy model allows for real-time replacement and editing of major details—like entire faces—in high quality video, allowing one to, say, replace themself on a Twitch stream with a high-resolution facsimile of an anime character. Oasis, meanwhile, can accept images as inputs and generate playable “worlds” in the form of what are essentially first-person-shooter video games (minus the shooting). Anthropic’s interest in this would almost certainly have been the underlying tech powering Lucy and Oasis: DOS or the Decart Optimization Stack, which purportedly optimizes the interactions between AI hardware and software, cutting down on compute cost. Anthropic spends a lot on compute, and is planning what may soon be the world’s largest IPO, now rumored to be coming around Halloween. According to Bloomberg’s anonymous sources, Anthropic “performed due diligence on Decart, but ultimately walked away.” But one of them added that, in Bloomberg’s words, Anthropic and Decart, “may still pursue other opportunities to collaborate.”

item.title: Google-Backed Nuclear Plant Gets Nearly $2 Billion Loan From the Energy Department
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.34
The AI boom is driving up electricity demand, helping fuel a revival of nuclear power. And the Trump administration is fully on board. The U.S. Department of Energy announced Tuesday that it closed a loan of up to $1.9 billion to help finance NextEra Energy’s plans to restart the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa. The nuclear plant operated for more than 45 years before shutting down in 2020. NextEra had already planned to close the plant later that year, but a storm damaged parts of the facility and forced it offline several months early. Google announced last October that it was working with NextEra to restart Duane Arnold and explore deploying more nuclear power around the country. Under the deal, Google signed a multi-year agreement to buy power from the plant, helping make the investment needed to restart it financially viable and cover the cost of energy production. “We expect Duane Arnold to be back online in early 2029, and the plant will provide more than 600 MW of clean, safe, “always-on” nuclear energy to the regional grid,” Google said in a blog post at the time. The electricity will help support Google’s growing cloud and AI infrastructure in Iowa. The company also announced last year that it was investing an additional $7 billion in the state over two years, including in new and expanded cloud and AI infrastructure. Once restarted, the Energy Department says Duane Arnold will add 615 megawatts of power to the grid, enough to power nearly 500,000 homes. The department also says the project will help drive down electricity costs. Google isn’t the only tech company turning to nuclear power to fuel its AI ambitions. A Microsoft-backed project to restart Constellation Energy’s Crane Clean Energy Center in Pennsylvania, formerly known as Three Mile Island Unit 1, received a $1 billion Energy Department loan last year. Meanwhile, Meta announced earlier this year that it had reached agreements with several companies to support up to 6.6 gigawatts of new and existing nuclear power by 2035. Major tech companies like Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and Google are all pouring billions of dollars into data centers and other infrastructure needed to train and run increasingly powerful AI models. All of that infrastructure requires a lot of electricity. The Trump administration has also gone all-in on expanding nuclear power to help meet growing electricity demand. President Donald Trump signed several executive orders last year aimed at speeding up nuclear development. One of them directed the Energy Department to stop most of its previous plans to dilute and dispose of surplus plutonium and instead establish a program to process the material and make it available to private companies. Even Trump Media, the parent company of Truth Social, has gotten in on the action, announcing last year that it would merge with private nuclear fusion company TAE Technologies in an effort to help “America win the A.I. revolution.” NextEra Energy and Google did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: The Fight Over OpenAI’s Math Breakthrough Is a New Kind of Scientific Arms Race
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.92
In the past 24 hours, Silicon Valley has erupted in bitter debate over what may seem from the outside to be an esoteric, trivial issue: the solution to a longstanding math problem which, despite its importance among academics, doesn’t have any clear practical applications. And yet it raises urgent new questions about the nature of competition—not only between humans, but also between humans and machines—in the age of AI. On Tuesday morning, OpenAI published a blog post claiming it had used an unreleased AI model “significantly more capable than GPT-6 Astra” to solve the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, which is related to the physics of water and other fluids. It’s one of seven “Millennium Problems” laid out by the Clay Mathematics Institute in the year 2000, each of which offers a $1 million prize for the first correct solution. OpenAI wrote in its blog post that it doesn’t intend to accept the prize for its result, which it said was discovered by human researchers collaborating with around 10,000 AI agents working for a little under ninety hours. The company’s announcement has largely been overshadowed by controversy around how its result was reached. OpenAI said in its blog post that its work on the Navier-Stokes problem started Tuesday of last week, “after hearing a rumour” that two independent mathematicians, Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge, had achieved a breakthrough in another area, called forced Euler, related to Navier-Stokes. The company says it then reached out to the duo “to offer a concurrent release of our result and to recognize their priority in a joint announcement.” The previous evening, Buckmaster, a mathematics professor at NYU, published a statement confirming he and Alpöge had been contacted by OpenAI after the company learned of their work on forced Euler, but that the company had played hardball to make sure it wasn’t scooped. Buckmaster said that he first learned about OpenAI’s approach during a Friday call with OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck, which he said sounded suspiciously familiar to the approach he and Alpöge had taken with forced Euler, for which they had used multiple AI models, including OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude. (Alpöge was not on the call.) Buckmaster says he asked Bubeck if the model OpenAI had used to solve the problem had access to his and Alpöge’s Codex logs. “I was told the model did not look up user data,” Buckmaster wrote. “I asked again, about training, and I did not get an answer.” OpenAI wrote in its blog post that neither its researchers nor its AI agents saw the two researchers’ work before it was published, but also that it “cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models.” Buckmaster claims Bubeck offered him two potential paths forward to ensure he shared the credit with OpenAI for the pathway that led to the Navier-Stokes solution, both of which involved completely removing Alpöge’s name from the solution; Alpöge has been employed with Anthropic, OpenAI’s biggest competitor, since 2024. Buckmaster says he declined both offers and told Bubeck that if OpenAI opted to move forward with its announcement, he would publish an account of the conversation. According to Buckmaster, Bubeck replied: “Why would you ruin your career?” In a reply posted Tuesday on X, Bubeck said he “could not consider Levent to be an independent academic” after he learned that Anthropic’s AI models had been used as part of his work with Buckmaster. He also apologized for the threatening-sounding question he posed to Buckmaster, calling it an “extremely poor choice of words” and “the opposite of what I was trying to convey.” A new era for competition Historically, the formalizing of a new mathematical proof—even one that doesn’t have any obvious practical application—was a cause for celebration. Science is a collaborative enterprise, and friendly competition is a vital engine for fresh discoveries. There has, of course, been controversy and infighting over the matter of who reached a breakthrough first. But at the end of the day, it was humans bickering among one another, all operating within human limits. Until now. With the Navier-Stokes solution controversy, we’ve entered a strange new era of scientific competition: one where humans compete not only with one another, but also with deep-pocketed tech companies wielding powerful AI models, hell-bent on being the first to tout major technical breakthroughs, and operating under the assumption that anything published on the open internet—and perhaps shared with their proprietary AI tools—is fair game. Money isn’t the issue here. Even if OpenAI were to accept the Millennium Prize for its Navier-Stokes solution, it has no need for the $1 million reward. The computing power required by the agents working on the problem cost millions of dollars, according to OpenAI researcher Noam Brown. “[OpenAI] didn’t do this for the bounty,” one X user wrote on Tuesday. “They needed a headline that says ‘our AI solved one of the hardest problems in mathematics’ and they needed it before someone else got credit.” Terence Tao, a Fields Medal recipient who’s widely regarded as the greatest living mathematician, had a similar response to the controversy. If humanity’s collective endeavor to understand the universe—which relies not only on friendly competition, but on the free and open exchange of ideas—is subsumed by competition between jealous and power-hungry tech titans, the total store of shared human knowledge is doomed to shrink, rather than expand, contrary to what the AI companies themselves have promised over and over again their technology would deliver. “We have now seen that even the rumor of someone working on a problem can trigger a massive amount of AI-powered effort to flatten it before the original research project has time to reach its full potential,” Tao wrote in a Tuesday post on Mastodon, responding to the Navier-Stokes controversy. “The incentives may now be pointing in the direction of no longer sharing any promising research directions with the broader community, which would reverse centuries of traditions of open science and do serious long-term damage to the future of the field.”

item.title: This one Linux setting is capping your Wi-Fi speed far below your router's rating
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.83
A Wi-Fi router can advertise hundreds of MBs, yet your Linux laptop may deliver a fraction of that speed. Before replacing the router, changing channels, or blaming the wireless adapter, there is one Linux setting worth checking. Linux puts a wireless interface into power-saving mode to optimize battery life. On a laptop, that can make sense when battery life matters more than maximum network performance. The problem is that power-saving behavior can also introduce latency, reduce responsiveness, and, with some wireless hardware and drivers, interfere with achieving the best possible throughput. Check your actual Wi-Fi configuration first Do not confuse router ratings with negotiated link speed Before changing anything, inspect the connection itself. It can be done using: iw dev Then check the negotiated connection: iw dev wlp3s0 link The output provides details such as signal strength, frequency, channel width, and negotiated RX and TX rates. For example, a connection might report: Frequency: 5200 MHz Channel: 36 Width: 80 MHz Signal: -35 dBm RX bitrate: 866.7 Mbit/s TX bitrate: 390.0 Mbit/s That number is the PHY link rate, not the speed you will necessarily see in a browser download or speed test. This is important because Wi-Fi introduces protocol overhead, retransmissions, encryption overhead, and other inefficiencies. A connection reporting a PHY rate of 866.7 Mbit/s cannot normally deliver that exact figure as usable application throughput. The same command also shows the channel width and frequency being used, which helps establish how the wireless connection is actually configured. In my case, the Intel Wireless-AC 8265 is connected to the fiber network on the 5GHz band at 5200MHz, using an 80MHz channel. The signal is strong at -35 dBm, while the negotiated RX and TX rates are 866.7 Mbit/s and 390.0 Mbit/s respectively. These figures give us a much clearer picture of the actual Wi-Fi connection before investigating whether another configuration is responsible for slower real-world speeds. See whether Wi-Fi power saving is enabled iw gives you the answer immediately
To find if Wi-Fi power saving is on, the command is very simple: iw dev wlp3s0 get power_save An enabled configuration reports: Power save: on To perform a quick test, disable it temporarily: sudo iw dev wlp3s0 set power_save off Then verify: iw dev wlp3s0 get power_save You should now see: Power save: off You do not need to reboot to perform this test. Once power saving is disabled, run the same speed test you used before. Ideally, perform several tests against the same server or service and compare the results rather than relying on a single measurement. I used iperf3 for benchmarking: In my test, enabling Wi-Fi power saving reduced sustained throughput from about 159Mbps to 138Mbps, a drop of roughly 13%, which is entirely plausible on an 802.11ac connection, although the exact impact varies considerably between adapters, drivers, access points, and traffic patterns. The 159 Mbps result with power saving disabled is also reasonable for a 2x2 Wi-Fi 5 connection operating under real-world conditions, where application throughput is well below the theoretical PHY rate. More interestingly, the enabled test recorded 283 TCP retransmissions, while the disabled test recorded none, suggesting that power-saving behavior was contributing to additional buffering or delayed transmission in this particular setup. That does not mean every Linux system will behave the same way, however. Some laptops may see almost no throughput difference, while others can experience noticeable changes in latency, retransmissions, or sustained transfer performance. In practice, the biggest benefit of disabling power saving may therefore be more consistent network behavior and lower latency, rather than a dramatic increase in peak download speed. Make the change persistent with NetworkManager Update the connection profile The iw command changes the current wireless interface state. If NetworkManager later reconnects the interface, that setting may be restored according to the connection profile or global defaults. NetworkManager provides its own Wi-Fi power-saving property: 802-11-wireless.powersave First find the connection name: nmcli connection show Then disable power saving for that profile: nmcli connection modify "Your UUID" 802-11-wireless.powersave 2 Reconnect: nmcli connection down "Your UUID" nmcli connection up "Your UUID" Finally, verify: iw dev wlp3s0 get power_save The interface should report: Power save: off Test before you change hardware Before spending money on a new wireless card or router, it is worth checking whether the problem is actually coming from the software stack. Linux gives you enough visibility into the wireless interface to investigate these issues yourself. For many, that also makes this kind of troubleshooting a worthwhile first step. A setting buried in the operating system can be changed in seconds, tested under normal workloads, and reverted just as easily. That is considerably easier than replacing hardware only to discover that the original problem was somewhere else.

item.title: The invisible PC killer from the '90s is still around—and most people don't know it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.82
The early days of people having internet in their homes were pretty wild. Viruses were pretty much everywhere, and unlike now, many users had no clue what to do with them. I was a tween in the early '00s, but I remember intervening when my mom's PC had what felt like hundreds of them, with pop-ups and ads covering up the entire desktop, impossible to remove. Annoying and potentially hazardous as those viruses were in the '90s and the '00s, there was a much bigger PC killer in town, and it's one that's still around to this day. I'm talking about static electricity. You could carry thousands of volts without realizing it Your PC could feel a shock that you couldn't I'm one of those people who get zapped by static electricity each time I touch a doorknob, so I'm no stranger to the concept. Even then, static electricity is easy to underestimate, because you mostly just notice these tiny little zaps, if anything at all. But under the right conditions, your body can build up thousands, even tens of thousands, of volts. This is especially easy in a dry climate, or in a moderate climate during the winter when the heaters are running. That was a particularly nasty combo in the '90s, when beige PCs were often sitting in carpeted bedrooms and offices. (Did you know that you shouldn't keep your PC on carpet? No? Well, you do now.) Weather conditions aside, the important part is that this doesn't make static electricity dangerous to you (phew), because the amount of energy involved is tiny, and each zap lasts a split second. Your PC's components are a different story. Sensitive electronics can get damaged by electrostatic discharge (ESD), at voltages that are nowhere near what you can actually feel. You might not notice static discharge, but your PC can be affected at a tiny fraction of what it takes for you to experience that sensation. The TL;DR is you could touch a part of your PC and discharge static into it without knowing. This makes static a super-stealthy ninja PC killer that was a big threat back in those days, arguably bigger than most viruses. Static didn't have to kill a component immediately Sometimes the PC kept working At the risk of making a blanket statement, most modern viruses can be pretty stealthy compared to the stuff we dealt with in the '90s and '00s. Back then, many were up in your face, just the way I described above. Some still are, too, but most scams involve trying to fool the user into thinking they're on a legitimate platform, or working in the background without being detected. So, viruses kind of announced themselves back then. If you had one, you probably knew. But static damage can be much sneakier. A sufficiently strong ESD event might kill a component outright, and with component prices as they are right now, that can quickly turn into a $2,000+ mistake. It's not always so dramatic, though. Your PC or your components may sustain some damage, but not enough to stop working outright. They might throw errors or fail earlier than they otherwise would've, though. The PC upgrade boom gave static plenty of opportunities Every new RAM stick meant touching exposed electronics The other reason static was such a perfect '90s PC killer is that people were opening their PCs up quite a lot. Not everyone, of course. But there was just more to be done inside a PC compared to now; you could add a sound card, add a modem, replace drives ... Still doable now, but much less necessary. Every such upgrade meant handling exposed parts, circuit boards, and contacts. Often in that carpeted environment I talked about above. Viruses needed infected files or disks to get in, but static discharge only needed you to touch the wrong thing without grounding yourself. That's why manufacturers and repair pros took anti-static precautions so seriously. RAM sticks, expansion cards, and motherboards were all supposed to be handled by the edges, kept in anti-static bags, and installed while you were grounded to the chassis. Those rules still apply to this day. The invisible PC killer never actually went away Ground yourself before reaching inside You'll often find me going on and on about how cleaning your PC is the best $0 upgrade you can give it. That was true in the '90s when PCs were beige and loud, and it's true now when they're filled with RGB lighting and cooled with AIOs. The problem is that doing this the wrong way can still very much damage your PC. It's not like magically, over the years, static became a non-issue. It's just that most people who actually open up their PCs are more aware of it now than they may have been back then. I'll say it again: Please, do clean your PC. Just ground yourself properly first. The scariest PC threat was 100% invisible At a time when viruses were less than sneaky, static electricity was the cause of death for many a PC. These days, the tables have somewhat turned; many viruses are far from obvious, and static is the same way, as ever. In both cases, exercise caution and you'll never have to worry about either one of those two, vastly different, issues.

item.title: 7 ways to repurpose an old or broken smart doorbell
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.80
Smart video doorbells can be incredibly useful, but they don't last forever. If you have an old or even broken video doorbell, you don't need to throw it away. There are plenty of ways you can put it to good use. Use your smart doorbell as a security camera A battery-powered doorbell can be placed almost anywhere If your video doorbell is still in full working order, but you've replaced it with a different model, then there are plenty of things you can do with it. A video doorbell is effectively a security camera with a button, so if you stop using it as a doorbell, you can use it just like any other security camera. If your video doorbell is battery-powered, this is even better. It means you can place your security camera almost anywhere you want. Turn it into a smart button You can still use it even if the camera doesn't work If your video doorbell is broken, you may still be able to put it to good use. If the camera is no longer working, it may still be the case that the doorbell ringer is functional. If this is the case, then you can repurpose your video doorbell as a smart button. Many smart home systems allow you to use doorbell rings as a trigger for automations. This means that when you press the doorbell ringer, you can run whatever automations you want. Set up a dedicated wildlife camera See what critters visit your backyard If you don't need your video doorbell to work as a doorbell anymore, it can make a great way to track local wildlife. Most video doorbells can detect motion, and many can record motion-triggered video and offer night vision features. You can set up your old doorbell in the backyard and have it record video whenever motion is detected. You can then watch back the recordings of all the animals that have snuck into your yard at night. Use it as a 3D printer monitor Keep tabs on your print remotely One of the biggest benefits of a smart video doorbell is that it allows you to see who is at your door even when you're not at home. You can access the live doorbell feed remotely to see who just rang your bell. This feature makes an old video doorbell a great fit as a 3D printer monitor. When you start a print, you can walk away and leave your doorbell focused on your printer. You can then use your phone at any time to see how your print is getting on. Leave it mounted somewhere as a deterrent Even a broken doorbell can give you protection If your doorbell is completely broken and no longer functions at all, you might think that all you can do is dispose of it. However, it could still serve a useful purpose. Security cameras only have limited views, so a single camera is never enough to cover the entire exterior of your home. The more cameras you have, the fewer blind spots you have. If you mount your broken video doorbell outside your home in a prominent position, it's hard to tell at a glance that it's not a working device. This may be enough to deter people who might otherwise see your home as an easy mark. Repurpose it as a dedicated pet camera Keep tabs on your pet inside your home If you have pets, an old video doorbell can make a great dedicated pet camera. Most video doorbells have motion detection, and some have pet or animal detection too, so that you can receive alerts when your pet is spotted by the doorbell. You might place the doorbell pointing at your pet's food or water bowls. You can then track when they eat or drink and monitor the bowls remotely to see when they need refilling or if there's been a spillage. You could also monitor a cat flap, or place the doorbell externally to track when your pet has gone outside. Use the housing to hold your own smart doorbell Keep an ESP32 doorbell protected If the internals of your smart video doorbell are completely dead, that doesn't mean it's useless. Many video doorbells have high-quality weather-resistant housings to protect the electronics from the elements. You can use these housings for your own projects. For example, you can build your own video doorbell using an ESP32-CAM board that combines an ESP32 with a camera module. The problem is that you can't stick an exposed circuit board to your front door. By using the housing from your old doorbell, you can keep your DIY doorbell protected, and it will look smart, too. Video doorbells don't have to become e-waste There are plenty of reasons why you might want to upgrade or replace a video doorbell, but you don't need to throw your old ones away. Repurposing old tech can save you money and help to reduce unnecessary e-waste.

item.title: These Bash shortcuts save me hours of terminal typing every month
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.70
If you type a lot of commands in Bash, it can be time-consuming to navigate, correct, and add strings to achieve the desired output. I've found my fair share of typing errors, multi-instruction commands, and complex interpreters. There are ways to speed up the typing process without wearing you out or giving you headaches, from short codes and hotkeys to cool shortcuts and hidden features. Navigate Bash commands fast without reaching for your mouse Clever cursor movement by page, word, or even section using your keyboard When dealing with the terminal, there are certainly some Linux commands you should never use. If you know what you are doing and have a couple of simple mistakes in your instructions, navigational hotkeys can save you time, such as pressing Alt + B to move backward word by word, or Alt + F to move forward. It's much quicker than repeatedly pressing the arrow keys to get where you need in your commands. For an even faster approach, try pressing Ctrl + A to jump to the beginning or Ctrl + E to go to the end. I've also used Ctrl + XX to jump to the beginning of a command line, and I repeat it to return to the previous cursor position. Let's say you're typing a sudo command and forgot to add "sudo" at the beginning; you can use this shortcut to jump to the start, add the short code, then return to where you were and finish your command. Forget speed reading; try speed typing in Bash Auto-finish, multiply, repeat, and append commands quickly If you need to reuse the last typed word (often a filename or path) in your previous command, you can type !$ in the Bash console to use it again in your new command before pressing Enter — you won't see it until you execute it, but it's fast and simple. To insert it visually, type Alt + . to paste it into your command, then continue typing before pressing Enter. If you enclose the path, filename, or group of words in double quotes ("example of using quotes"), both options will consider it all to be the last word. This little trick allows you to run different commands for a specific path or filename by auto-pasting it into the new command, as long as it was at the end of the previous one. This is handy for copying code that contains spaces and switches. Some more really cool shortcuts you may not know include an actual undo function (pressing Ctrl + _), yank — pasting back (Ctrl + Y), and Ctrl + R to autocomplete from history — you can press again to cycle through your history matches. You can also command multiple items using brace expansion, such as sudo apt upgrade {Upwork,Timeshift,Inkscape} or mkdir ~/Documents/"New Folder"{1..3}, , which creates three new folders in the Documents folder named New Folder1, New Folder2, and New Folder3. When using sudo, I've had times when I copied a command from somewhere and executed it, but it failed because it required admin privileges. To correct it quickly and efficiently, I'd type sudo !! so it starts the new command with "sudo" and pastes the last command I entered. You can also use !! to copy the last command, and then type whatever you need along with it. This little trick can save you 10–30 seconds per command. Autocomplete is also a nifty shortcut in Bash, and it only takes one key to launch it. If you press the Tab key while typing your command, folder path, or filename, Bash tries to autocomplete it based on previous command history. When there is more than one possible match, press it again to view the next option—you can repeat as needed to get what you want. This makes typing commands twice as fast because it auto-populates based on your history, and it helps prevent mistyping incidents that cause you headaches and consume time rather than save it. If you want to go bigger and better, and prevent accidental Enter presses or command errors on long strings, a full text editor has you covered. Whenever I have complex or long-winded commands to type, I press Ctrl + X then Ctrl + E to open my command in Nano. I make changes or add to it, then I press Ctrl + O, then Enter to save it, followed by Ctrl + X to exit, and it magically executes the command in the terminal. Don't worry, Nano saves to a temp folder and deletes the contents after rebooting, unless you intentionally load a specific file to edit. Using Nano is also a safe and secure way to prevent auto-execution. Sometimes, I copy code from a website that would otherwise execute when pasted into the terminal — it does happen. Launching a temp Nano session allows me to paste it and review it before transferring it to the terminal. It's also a simple option to prevent command errors in the terminal, especially for long lines of code or advanced command sessions that include pipes, multiple actions, loops, or more. You wouldn't want to execute an advanced command with errors or have to go back to fix something it performed that was not correct. You may also need it to create an actual file — you can load the editor with a new filename like nano myscriptname.sh and create your new file with the necessary code or script, then write it out. Correct typos, delete segments, and fix long strings efficiently Quick Linux Terminal editing at its best When typing away in the terminal, I easily make mistakes and have to correct them as I go, from misspellings or wrong directories to forgotten switches or case-sensitive issues. I speed up the editing process by using hotkeys rather than arrows, backspaces, or delete. A quick way to erase a whole section of your command or code is to press Ctrl + U to delete everything from your cursor to the start of the command line (moving left). Ctrl + K does the same but deletes from the cursor to the end (moving right). This also comes in handy if you copy your previous command into your new line using !!. Place the cursor where you want to erase everything to the right, use Ctrl + K, then type the new characters at the end. It's a quick way to use the beginning of a command and create the rest. Another fabulous editing shortcut is to delete the word or segment before or after the cursor's position. If you catch an issue with your command that is one word before the current cursor location, press Ctrl + W to cut the word. You can also press Alt + D to cut the one after the cursor position. Don't forget you also have the Ctrl + Y (the yank feature) mentioned earlier to paste back what you cut. Become a multitasking pro in Bash without losing anything Suspend, switch, move to the background, and repeat or append previous commands easily Bash terminal operations can get rather complex at times, leading to multiple processes like archiving and downloading, numerous command sessions, or Nano editing within one terminal. Sometimes, I need to switch between directory locations to use commands, which is where I use the pushd and popd short codes. It's not like using cd where you can only reside in one directory, although there are great replacements for Linux cd commands these days. These two commands help manage a list of directory locations (a directory stack), where you pick which location you want as the active directory. The "pushd" command adds your current directory to the stack, so to speak. The "popd" removes it from the stack and returns you to the previous directory. If your current CLI directory is set to "~/Documents" and you type pushd in the command line, it will add that location to the temporary folder stack and go to it — you can repeat for each new directory location or insert pushd before a location to not only add it but go to it. When I have more than two directory locations, I add "+0" or "-0" to the command to select the current directory — counting starts at 0 from the left for "+" and 0 from the right for "-" of the stack. I'll type pushd +1 , and it goes to the second folder from the left in the stack, whereas pushd -1 goes to the second one from the right in the stack. When typing popd in the command line, it removes the current location from the library. Numbers work the same, so typing popd +1 means it will remove the second folder from the current stack. If no more exist, it ignores the command and stays in the current directory. Another task-efficient trick is to multitask in the same terminal. To save time, I use Ctrl + Z to suspend the running process and bg to let it run in the background while working on another task. I also use the fg short code when I need to bring it back to the front of the terminal. All these shortcuts and commands are tied to one terminal session — just avoiding confusion here. You can also use the "&" operator to launch an app while keeping the terminal active and usable, such as typing & brave-browser in your active session. Without the operator, your terminal freezes up, and that is not a lovely experience. Create shorthand aliases for command strings you commonly use Abbreviate complete lines of code, parts of commands, or shorthand common words Aliases are excellent time-savers, enabling you to use your own short codes to create partial or full commands. I like to open ".bashrc" using Nano to add my aliases so they are usable in any terminal, but you can also type them in your current session for temporary use. I type sudo nano ~/.bashrc and then add my aliases at the bottom. I press Ctrl + O to save it, then Ctrl + X to exit and return to the terminal. This feature can save hours of typing, allowing you to use short code in the terminal for long or specific commands or scripts. Yes, you can make Bash easier to use and spend less time in agony Linux is better than Windows for scripts and coding in many ways, but it can be tedious at times. Using short codes and hotkeys can cut your typing time in half, but there are so many shortcuts to learn that I suggest practicing a few first, then branching out to others as they become second nature. From quick typing and editing shortcuts to navigating and multitasking, Linux will be easier to use — less headaches and more free time for other projects or activities. You may want to bookmark this page so you can return later as you master each skill or shortcut like a pro.

item.title: 16 years later, the iPhone 4 remains Apple’s most important smartphone design
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.46
Let’s face it — iPhone announcements have become a bit boring. We don’t need leaks and rumors to know what to expect anymore. In 2010, however, things were wildly different. It started with a police raid and ended with historic memes. This is the story of the iPhone 4. Step into the Wayback Machine The mother of all phone leaks The iPhone 4 was officially unveiled by Steve Jobs on June 7th, 2010, but the story starts much earlier. At this point in time, Apple had released three very similar iPhone models: the original, a 3G version, and a faster “3GS” model. But it didn’t matter — everyone wanted an iPhone. The hype for the next one was unprecedented, and it began a solid five months before Steve Jobs walked on stage. On January 27th, 2010, the world got its first look at the iPhone 4 — it just didn’t know it yet. Engadget received leaked images of the original iPad, but it wasn’t until three months later that people realized the iPhone 4 had also been present in the images. That information came from perhaps the most infamous leak in technology history. On April 19th, 2010, Gizmodo published an article titled “This Is Apple’s Next iPhone.” It revealed the iPhone 4 and its brand-new design in full glory. Now, it’s important to understand that the secrecy surrounding Apple products was on another level at this time. When Steve Jobs showed off the original iPhone on stage in 2007, it was largely a genuine surprise. The company went to great lengths to ensure that no one saw products before they were officially unveiled, and it was ruthless about leaks. So, how did Gizmodo get its hands on an actual iPhone 4 two months before it was announced? The story goes that Gray Powell, an Apple Software Engineer, accidentally left an iPhone 4 prototype at a bar in Redwood City, California. Someone else at the bar ended up with the phone, thinking it was an iPhone 3GS with weird stickers on it. The next morning, the phone had been remotely wiped, and the person realized it was actually an unreleased iPhone in a disguise. Weeks later, after having no luck contacting Apple, Gizmodo acquired the device for $5,000, confirmed it to be real, and introduced the world to the iPhone 4. Later that month, the California REACT task force raided the home of the Gizmodo editor. Apple was accused of making this happen, but it denied any involvement. Regardless, the damage had already been done. The iPhone 4 set the standard for phone design A new era of Apple design After months of drama, Steve Jobs finally stood on stage and held up the iPhone 4 on June 7th, 2010. It marked a brand new hardware design for the iPhone — a design that has aged extremely well. Tell me if this sounds familiar: glass front panel, flat glass back panel, and a flat-edged metal frame. 16 years later, this exact style can be seen in countless smartphones. - Galaxy S26 series: glass front panel, flat glass back panel, and a flat-edged metal frame. - Pixel 11 series: glass front panel, flat glass back panel, and a flat-edged metal frame. Apple eventually switched it up with a rounded-edge profile and metal back cover, but for the last several generations, it’s been back with the tried and true glass front panel, flat glass back panel, and a flat-edged metal frame. It’s a timeless design. Reviews praised the iPhone 4’s design. Previous models were certainly not ugly, but this was a significant visual upgrade. Smartphones of the time typically were plastic and utilitarian, but the iPhone 4 looked and felt every bit like a piece of jewelry. Apple was so proud of the design that it released a “bumper” case that left the back of the phone fully naked. This case would end up being more important than Apple intended. The iPhone 4 kicks off “antenna-gate” “You’re holding it wrong” The flat-edged metal frame was not only an aesthetic choice, but it also doubled as the iPhone 4’s antenna. As sophisticated as it looked, this design ended up causing a lot of trouble for Apple. Not long after the iPhone 4 launched, people began reporting signal strength issues when holding the phone in a specific way. If you touched the lower left edge of the phone, it would interfere with the antennas enough to drop calls in areas with poor reception. It affected so many people that Apple was forced to address it. Apple’s first statement only made the situation worse. It took no responsibility for the issue, claiming it was a “fact of life for every wireless phone.” Even more egregiously, Apple advised people to “avoid gripping it in the lower left corner…” or use a case. This is when the infamous “you’re holding it wrong " meme was born. Apple put all the blame on its customers and hoped the problem would go away. It did not go away. In July, only a month after the iPhone 4 launched, a class action lawsuit was filed against Apple and AT&T (the exclusive carrier of iPhones in the U.S.). The lawsuit alleged that Apple knew about the manufacturing defects that caused connection issues before the phone was released. Apple quickly issued another statement, saying it had discovered the issue causing the "dramatic drop in bars". Good timing. It explained that the issue was in the formula it used to determine the number of signal bars to display, but not in the actual ability of the phone to hold a signal when gripped a certain way. Once again, people did not appreciate Apple’s response. The situation continued to escalate to the point where Apple held a special press conference and gave journalists a private tour of the company’s antenna design lab. Steve Jobs announced that Apple would give all iPhone 4 owners a free bumper case — or refund those who already purchased one — to help with the antenna issue. Technical issues couldn’t stop the iPhone Renaissance The iPhone 4 was a hit The iPhone 4’s launch was marred by negative publicity. It was even pulled from several publications’ “Top Phones” and recommendation lists due to the reception issues. Despite all of that, the iPhone 4 was a massive success. In early 2011, the iPhone lineup finally broke free from AT&T’s grasp when the iPhone 4 launched on Verizon. Apple took this opportunity to include a brand new antenna array. The iPhone 4 ended up sitting as Apple’s flagship iPhone model for 15 months, and the company continued to manufacturer it for nearly four years. The iPhone 4 has gone down in history as a complicated device. It showcased the best and worse of Apple. A ground-breaking design that has stood the test of time, and a condescending attitude toward customer complaints. Ultimately, it’s clear that the iPhone 4 marked a turning point for the iPhone.

item.title: 3 physical Home Assistant projects to try this weekend (Sep 11-13)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.92
We live in an increasingly digital world, but as Olivia Newton-John said, sometimes you just need to get physical. Here are three projects that let you interact with Home Assistant in a physical way. Scan empty grocery packaging straight to your shopping list An ESP32 barcode scanner makes life easier Home Assistant is not just able to help you control your smart home. It can be useful in many different aspects of your life. I use Home Assistant to help with everything from reminding me to take my medication to gamifying chores for my kids. Home Assistant can also help make the mundane things a little easier, such as grocery shopping. Having to figure out what to buy each week feels like a never-ending nightmare, but there's a clever Home Assistant project that can make things a little easier. The BeepBasket project lets you build a system for scanning the barcodes from real products and automatically adding those products to your Home Assistant shopping list. It uses an R35C-B barcode scanner hooked up to an ESP32 that can transfer the data to Home Assistant. BeepBasket then looks up the product using the Open Food Facts API and adds the item to your shopping list. If the product isn't found, the barcode itself is added to your list instead. There's even a dedicated BeepBasket card for keeping track of products through a Home Assistant dashboard. The idea is that you place your scanner next to your trash can. When you finish a product and throw away the wrapper, you scan the barcode and the product is automatically added to your shopping list. It's one less thing to think about. Let Home Assistant press the buttons on your car keys An ESP32 can control a car that wouldn't otherwise integrate with Home Assistant Many modern cars offer smart features that let you control things remotely via an app, such as unlocking the doors and turning on the heated seats. Home Assistant offers integrations such as the Tesla Fleet integration that allow you to perform these actions through Home Assistant. Not every car has these smart features, and not every car that does can integrate with Home Assistant. One user came up with an alternative solution for giving Home Assistant some measure of remote control over their car without the need for apps or APIs. The user took a spare key fob for the car, opened it up, and wired its button contacts to an ESP32. Home Assistant is then able to send commands to the ESP32 that activate the different buttons on the key fob. The battery was removed, so that the fob is only powered by the ESP32 when a command is received, reducing the risk of a relay attack. Obviously, you're limited to what your key fob can do, but the user was able to set up an automation that automatically locked their car at 9:30 PM. If anyone is detected in their driveway between 12:30 AM and 5:30 AM, Home Assistant triggers a different button, which causes the lights to flash and the horn to beep. This project comes with significant risks, since an error in your automation or a problem with Home Assistant could leave your car unlocked and vulnerable. It's worth taking precautions to ensure that any similar projects consider these risks. Turn Home Assistant data into a moving analog needle See your data the old-school way Home Assistant can display data on dashboards in a wide range of different ways, from simple numbers to dials or charts. The data is usually displayed on a digital screen such as a wall-mounted tablet, but one Home Assistant user wanted to create something more physical. The project involved creating a physical needle display built around an ESP32 and an X27.168 stepper motor. The ESP32 retrieves the data from Home Assistant, and the stepper motor moves a physical needle to a specific position related to the value it is trying to display. There are even addressable LEDs built in to show different colors depending on the values. One example of the gauge in action shows the user turning down their heating. The needle turns counterclockwise to a lower position, and the LEDs change from red to blue. The whole thing is built into a laser-cut acrylic enclosure, which looks awesome. The user shared a prototype on Reddit and got some very useful feedback from the community. They are now selling ready-made gauges that are hand-built by the user. There's nothing to stop you from building something of your own using a similar concept. Sometimes we all need to get physical While Home Assistant is highly digital, there are plenty of ways you can make it more analog, from using physical knobs to turning your lights on by snapping your fingers. It's worth exploring what's possible beyond the same old dashboards.

item.title: I upgraded my Excel PivotTable with these 3 simple features
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.49
I'm probably guilty of making Excel spreadsheets more complicated than they need to be, but I have one rule I keep coming back to: if I'm going to build a PivotTable, I want to actually enjoy using it. The basic summary is useful, but a few small additions can make a surprisingly big difference. After converting my data into a table with Ctrl+T, creating a PivotTable in a new worksheet via Insert > PivotTable, and dragging fields into the different areas of the PivotTable Fields pane, it's easy to stop there. But that's only the start. I usually add three simple features—slicers, timelines, and PivotCharts—to make the results easier to filter, explore, and understand. For the examples in this article, I'm using a fictional 500-row sales ledger. You can download a free copy of this worksheet to try the three features yourself. When you click the link, you'll find the download button in the top-right corner. Slicers make my PivotTables much easier to control I like being able to see my filters The first thing I tend to add to a PivotTable is a slicer. I like being able to see exactly how I've filtered my data, rather than opening a small drop-down menu and trying to remember which options I've selected. I also like that I can use a slicer to filter by a field that isn't actually visible in the PivotTable, giving me another way to explore the same summary. For my sales ledger, I started with a PivotTable showing Revenue by Category. I clicked inside the PivotTable, went to PivotTable Analyze > Insert Slicer, and selected Salesperson. Excel added a set of buttons for the eight salespeople in my dataset, and clicking Ava Patel, for example, immediately filtered the PivotTable to show only her sales. I can select multiple salespeople by holding Ctrl while clicking, or clear my selection using the Clear Filter button in the top-right corner of the slicer. Slicers aren't exclusive to PivotTables—you can add them to a regular Excel table—but I find them particularly useful with PivotTables because one slicer can control multiple PivotTables based on the same source data. In my case, I created a second PivotTable showing Revenue by Region. I then right-clicked my Salesperson slicer, selected Report Connections, checked the box for my Region PivotTable, and clicked OK. Now, whenever I click a salesperson, both PivotTables update at the same time. That's the part I really like. Instead of opening separate filter menus for each PivotTable, I have one set of visible buttons that lets me control the summaries I'm looking at. A timeline makes date filtering much less fiddly It gives me a better way to explore a year's worth of sales Dates are one of the first things I often want to filter when I'm looking at my data, but the standard PivotTable date filter isn't my favorite way to do it. When I have a whole year's worth of records, scrolling through individual dates feels cumbersome. That's why I usually add a timeline. I went back to my first PivotTable and clicked PivotTable Analyze > Insert Timeline. I then selected Date, clicked OK, and Excel added a timeline showing the 2025 sales data. Because I had two linked PivotTables, I also right-clicked the timeline, selected Report Connections, and checked the box for my Revenue-by-Region PivotTable. Timelines let you filter the PivotTable by Years, Quarters, Months, or Days. I usually stick with Months for a dataset like this. Then, instead of opening a filter menu and selecting individual dates, I can simply click a month or drag across several months to create a date range. For example, I can drag from April through July and immediately see how my PivotTables change to reflect those four months. The timeline also works alongside my slicer. If I select Ava Patel in the Salesperson slicer and then drag across a few months in the timeline, I can quickly narrow both connected PivotTables down to Ava's sales during that particular period. I find that much easier to work with than repeatedly opening filter menus. The timeline also makes it obvious which period I'm looking at, which is particularly useful when I come back to the spreadsheet later. PivotCharts show me what my numbers are actually doing Sometimes a table of numbers needs a picture I like being able to see the actual figures in my PivotTable, but sometimes I want to spot a trend without having to study a column of numbers. That's when I add a PivotChart. For this example, I wanted to see how my sales changed throughout 2025, so I went back to my Revenue-by-Category PivotTable, clicked PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart, and chose a Line chart. I then removed Category from the Rows area and used Date instead, while keeping Revenue in the Values area. This gave me a single line showing total sales for each month of 2025. Keep an eye on the Rows area of the PivotTable Fields pane when adding a Date field. Excel can add things like Days (Date) to your PivotTable. If you don't want them included, drag them out of the Rows area. The useful thing about a PivotChart is that it stays connected to the PivotTable. I can use the field buttons around the chart to change what I'm viewing, and those changes are reflected in the PivotTable too. My Salesperson slicer and timeline are connected as well. If I select Ava Patel in the slicer, the chart immediately changes to show only her sales. I can also use the timeline to narrow it down to a few months. That means I don't have to create a separate chart every time I want to look at a different slice of the data. I can use the chart controls, slicer, or timeline to change what I'm looking at, while the PivotChart gives me an immediate visual representation of the result. A few small additions can make a big difference A basic PivotTable is only the starting point. Slicers make filtering easier, timelines make date ranges easier to explore, and PivotCharts help me spot trends at a glance. Once everything is set up, I can use PivotTable conditional formatting to highlight the numbers that matter. I also make use of a few little-known PivotTable tricks to take them to the next level, like generating separate worksheets for each category, using distinct counts to track unique values, and calculating month-over-month growth without using any formulas.

item.title: These are the 7 greatest Kindle mods of all time
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.25
Like most of its products, Amazon has locked down its Kindle devices so that you can't easily make changes. Thankfully, some clever people have figured out ways to hack Kindles over the years. These are some of the very best mods of the past and present. KOReader The document viewer that puts the stock Kindle firmware to shame This is perhaps the most significant Kindle mod there is, because it's essential to the core purpose of a Kindle: reading books. KOReader turns a standard Kindle into a much more capable eReader that can coexist with Amazon's normal software without replacing it. With KOReader, you can read a huge number of formats that a standard Kindle doesn't support, including comic formats such as CBZ and even Word documents. The PDF support is particularly impressive; the Reflow feature can effectively transform a messy PDF into an eBook format that's a breeze to read. There's so much more too, with OPDS support, Calibre integration, progress sync, and a wide range of plugins. I can't imagine using a Kindle without KOReader now. Duokan EPUB support and comics, while it lasted Duokan was one of the most impressive early Kindle mods. Instead of just another reading app, it was an entire alternative OS for a Kindle. Duokan enabled you to do things that a standard Kindle couldn't, such as reading EPUB files and ZIP-based comics, and it offered strong support for Chinese-language books. Sadly, Duokan abandoned the Kindle some years back, but not before it showed just what was possible to do on the Kindle hardware. KUAL The launcher that lets you run almost anything on your Kindle The Kindle Unified Application Launcher (KUAL) is an important component of the Kindle hacking ecosystem. It's not as exciting as other hacks, but it's arguably more useful. KUAL gives your Kindle a graphical interface that you can use to launch various applications. Instead of running a single mod on your Kindle, KUAL lets you access multiple different packages and use the interface to launch or control them. The best part is that developers can create their own extensions, which means that you can build your own Kindle mods that you can run through KUAL.
