If there's something you wish your jailbroken Kindle could do, even with no coding experience, you can ask an AI chatbot to build it for you and have your very own Kindle mod running in KUAL. The original KUAL no longer works on Kindle firmware 5.19.4 or later. You'll need to use an updated version called KUALA for newer firmware. USBNetwork Bringing networking and SSH to the Kindle This is another mod that doesn't sound all that exciting, but it makes doing almost anything to your jailbroken Kindle so much easier. USBNetwork creates a network connection between your Kindle and computer and, most importantly, allows you to connect to the Kindle over SSH. This means you can connect your Kindle to your computer and get a root shell, allowing you to browse and edit the filesystem, run commands, and much more. USBNetwork became an invaluable tool for developing mods for the Kindle. It's a lifesaver on older Kindles, where trying to type anything is a horrific nightmare, because you can make all the changes from your computer. Custom screensavers Making the most of the E-Ink display This was one of the popular early Kindle hacks. A Kindle spends far more time sleeping than it does awake, but in its wisdom, Amazon didn't let owners use their own images as the sleep screen. The community created screensaver hacks that allowed you to replace the stock Kindle images with user-selected images instead. This may sound like a minor change, but it allowed users to take advantage of the Kindle's E-Ink display. Since an E-Ink display doesn't need power to maintain a static image, it makes a Kindle a great way to show off images and artwork when it's not being used for reading. These mods have developed over time, with KOReader now having screensaver options of its own. Some screensaver hacks can also be configured through KUAL. Collections Manager Giving the Kindle the nested collections it lacked This is another classic mod that was first designed for the original Kindle Touch and Paperwhite models. It was intended to give users far more control over how they could organize large libraries of books on their Kindles. The key feature was the ability to create nested collections. A stock Kindle let you create collections, but you couldn't place one collection inside another, making larger libraries an organizational nightmare. Using the Collections Manager mod, you could set up a collection for a specific author, which contained other collections of their different book series, with each of those collections containing the relevant books. It was then far easier to navigate to the book you needed. Sadly, firmware updates broke the nesting mechanism that Collections Manager used. More than a decade after the Collections Manager mod appeared, you still can't create proper nested collections on a standard Kindle. Custom fonts A classic hack that made reading on a Kindle better This is another mod that sounds fairly trivial, but it's one of the most important because it directly improves the Kindle's main purpose: displaying text. Older Kindles offered very little control over fonts, so community hacks soon appeared to try to fix this problem. Some of these hacks didn't even need a full jailbreak; the "Font Hack Lite" for the Kindle 3 and Kindle 4 models let you use hidden features already in the Kindle firmware. Modern Kindles allow you to install custom fonts, so this is something that is far less of an issue. However, even today, options such as KOReader give you far more control over exactly how your text is displayed than is possible on the stock firmware. The best Kindle mods solve genuine restrictions There are plenty of weird and wonderful Kindle mods that let you do everything from running Doom to working as an external monitor. The best mods, however, are those that make it easier to do what the Kindle was intended for: reading books.

item.title: 3 easy Windows 11 commands every PC user should know
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.13
I consider myself a Windows power user these days, but I wasn't always. I can remember when the command line seemed like something programmers used, and I stayed out of it unless I absolutely had to. Even now, opening Windows Terminal and seeing a blinking cursor can make what you're about to do feel more complicated than it really is. You don't need to know PowerShell or understand a bunch of command-line syntax to get something useful out of it. There are a few simple commands that handle things I regularly do in Windows faster than clicking through menus and settings. You type or paste them into Windows Terminal, press Enter, and Windows handles the rest. Update almost all of your installed apps with WinGet One command saves me from chasing down updates Keeping apps updated on Windows used to mean opening them one at a time, looking for an update option, or heading to the developer's website to download a new installer. WinGet makes that process much faster. It checks the apps it recognizes on your PC, finds available updates, and lets you install them from one place at the same time. I also prefer this to searching the web for installers. WinGet pulls package information from configured sources, so I'm not clicking through search results and hoping I've found the right download page. You should still pay attention to what you're installing, but it removes a lot of unnecessary searching. To see which apps have updates available, open Windows Terminal or PowerShell and run: winget upgrade WinGet will scan your installed apps and show the ones it knows how to update. I like doing this first because I can see exactly what it found before making any changes. If everything looks good, run: winget upgrade --all WinGet will work through the available updates for you. Some installers still open their own prompts, so the process isn't always completely automatic. If WinGet tells you that one or more package versions can't be determined, you can include those packages with: winget upgrade --all --include-unknown I wouldn't use that option automatically. I prefer to run the normal upgrade command first and only add --include-unknown when WinGet tells me it's leaving something out. Remove the Windows apps I don't want PowerShell lets me remove things that are hidden from Settings I first used PowerShell to remove the Xbox Game Bar from my work PC by removing Microsoft.XboxGamingOverlay. I don't game on this machine, so keeping Xbox-related components around didn't make much sense. That was useful, but the better example was the Windows Web Experience package, which powers the Widgets/Discover flyout. I've always thought this was a distracting component in Windows 11, and I've never used it on purpose. I have, however, opened it by mistake many times. Windows lets me hide the Widgets button from the taskbar, but that doesn't actually remove the board. I decided to remove the package instead. First, I checked that the package was installed using this command: Get-AppxPackage *WebExperience* That returned the Windows Web Experience package information. Once I confirmed I had the right package, I removed it with this command: Get-AppxPackage *WebExperience* | Remove-AppxPackage This is where PowerShell has an advantage over the normal uninstall process. I can search for the exact packaged app I want and remove only that one, even when Windows doesn't expose it like a regular program in Settings. I wouldn't remove a package just because its name looks unfamiliar. I check what it does first and only remove it when I'm sure I don't need it. Check and repair corrupted system files SFC is one of the first things I try when Windows starts acting strange I don't run System File Checker as part of regular maintenance, but it's useful when Windows starts doing something it shouldn't. Maybe a built-in feature stops working, Windows throws unexplained errors, or something just doesn't seem right after an update. Before I start changing settings or installing a third-party repair utility, I can have Windows check its own protected system files. That's what makes sfc /scannow so useful. There's no extra software to download and no troubleshooting wizard to work through. Windows scans its protected system files, looks for damaged or incorrect versions, and attempts to replace them with the correct copies. Open Windows Terminal or PowerShell as an administrator and run this command: sfc /scannow The scan takes a little while, and you'll see its progress in the terminal. When it finishes, Windows will tell you whether it found any integrity problems and whether it was able to repair them. I just ran it, and it found and fixed some corrupted system files. I wouldn't treat SFC as a tool that speeds up your PC. If Windows is running normally, there's no reason to run it just for the sake of it. I keep it in mind for those times when something isn't working correctly and I want a quick way to rule out damaged Windows files before digging any deeper. A few commands are worth keeping around I still use Settings for plenty of things, but these are three cases where opening Terminal is quicker. They're simple enough that I've stopped thinking of them as command-line tricks and started treating them like any other Windows shortcut.

item.title: An $8 ESP32 beats Raspberry Pi for these 4 DIY smart home projects
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.65
Raspberry Pis have been popular devices for DIY projects for years. They're ideal for many tech projects, but they're not always the perfect choice. There are many projects where a cheap ESP32 board is a better option, and the benefits go beyond the much lower price. Building battery-powered door or window sensors A Pi can't match the deep sleep of an ESP32 ESP32 boards are great for building your own sensors. You can often create working smart home sensors for a fraction of the price of buying a ready-made sensor. You can build sensors using Raspberry Pi models too, but there's one area where the ESP32 is the clear winner. Some sensors aren't ideal for connecting to power. Window and door sensors, for example, need to be placed on the windows or doors, and it's not always practical to use power cables in these locations. Using batteries is often a more sensible solution. These sensors spend most of their time doing nothing. It's only when a door or window is opened or closed that they need to report home. An ESP32 can enter deep sleep when nothing is happening, significantly reducing how much power it uses. When the reed switch changes state, the GPIO event can wake the ESP32 so that it can report the change and then go back to sleep. In comparison, a sensor built using a Raspberry Pi can be configured to halt and wake through GPIO, but it's not the same as the ESP32's deep sleep. When the Pi wakes up, it has to go through the boot process, load the operating system, reconnect to the network, and start the appropriate software. This results in a significant delay before the event is reported. You can keep Linux running to reduce this delay, but this requires the Pi to maintain continuous power. Even a Raspberry Pi Zero will draw a reasonable amount of power when idling, making battery power far less practical. Extending Bluetooth coverage ESPHome makes an ESP32 an ideal Bluetooth proxy One of the simplest ways to use an ESP32 is as a Bluetooth proxy. Placing a Bluetooth proxy within range allows your smart home to communicate with Bluetooth devices that are too far away from the main smart home hub to talk directly. Instead, the signals are passed back and forth over Wi-Fi to the Bluetooth proxy, which then communicates with the Bluetooth device over a shorter distance. You don't need any additional hardware to use an ESP32 as a Bluetooth proxy, since many ESP32 boards come with built-in Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. Setting one up is also easy to do; ESPHome has ready-made Bluetooth proxy firmware that you can flash to your ESP32 without having to write a single line of YAML. You can use a Raspberry Pi as a Bluetooth proxy, but it's likely to be overkill if that's all the device is doing. In addition, there are some potential issues with using Bluetooth on Linux that ESP32 boards don't have. Home Assistant's documentation mentions that Linux kernel updates have previously broken Bluetooth functionality, and that Linux Bluetooth driver support can often lag behind other operating systems for newer hardware. The documentation states that in many cases, a better approach is to use an ESP32. There is a list of ESP32 devices that work well as Bluetooth proxies. Controlling addressable LED strips using WLED Linux makes control more complicated Addressable LED strips are a common choice for smart-home lighting projects. These strips contain multiple LEDs which can be controlled independently to produce impressive lighting effects. The strips don't work on their own; you need something to control them. Running WLED on an ESP32 turns the cheap board into a network-accessible LED controller that can display different lighting scenes and effects and is controllable via Home Assistant or a web interface. You can control addressable LED strips using Raspberry Pi models, but there are several issues that you don't get with an ESP32. These LED strips require precisely timed control signals, which a Raspberry Pi running ordinary software on Linux can't do all that well. It often requires the use of specialized libraries or hardware-assisted methods to ensure that Linux doesn’t get in the way of accurate timing. There are often secondary issues. For example, some methods of controlling LEDs via a Pi can interfere with the Pi's onboard audio. An ESP32 is much better at handling precisely timed hardware tasks in a predictable way. Making capacitive-touch smart buttons Touch is built into many ESP32 chips Automation is great, but sometimes you need a way to control smart home devices manually. Smart buttons make an excellent choice, and you can build a physical smart button using an ESP32 or a Raspberry Pi. One thing a Raspberry Pi can't do is let you easily make a capacitive-touch-controlled smart button. Some ESP32 chips have capacitive-touch sensing built in. All you need to do is connect a conductive surface such as copper tape to a touch-capable pin on the ESP32, and the board can detect the change in capacitance when your finger touches or nears the surface. You don't even need to physically touch the surface. Capacitive touch sensing can work through thin non-conductive materials such as glass, plastic, or wood. You can hide the smart button under a surface and control your smart home just by placing your finger in the right location. Raspberry Pis don't have the same capacitive-touch sensing hardware. If you want to achieve the same goal with a Pi, you need to add additional components to detect the touch and pass the information to the Raspberry Pi. The benefits of an ESP32 aren't just the price An ESP32 board can cost just a few dollars, while many Raspberry Pi models have become increasingly expensive in recent months. The benefits of using an ESP32 aren't simply the price; there are plenty of situations where it's the better hardware for the task.

item.title: There's a problem with DLSS 5, and it's not even the AI slop
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.33
When Nvidia first announced DLSS 5 neural rendering, many were quick to label it "AI slop." And I get it. We're definitely getting some uncanny valley vibes. Now that it's here, the AI slop allegations persist, but I'd say we're all focusing on the wrong thing entirely. The problem with DLSS has nothing to do with the all-too-realistic-but-also-not-realistic faces in games. The problem lies entirely elsewhere, and it's arguably bigger than just liking the aesthetic. The frame rate hit is real And it hurts a lot I'm not here to debate whether Nvidia's DLSS 5 looks good. For some people, it's great. For others, it's awful. Some say they can barely see a difference. No matter where you land in that particular conversation, there's one downside to DLSS 5 that's undeniable: the performance hit. It's real. It's too real, even. I personally own an RTX 4080 Super, so the only way I can test it is with DLSS Swapper, and yes, I've noticed the performance difference—but that makes sense. Nvidia didn't officially release DLSS 5 for the RTX 40-series, after all, so forcefully injecting it into a game that was never meant to have it on my GPU should result in performance issues. Naturally. Only, it's not just me. Some of my colleagues here at How-To Geek have tried it on RTX 50-series cards, including the ever-overpriced RTX 5090, and we're all united with the same opinion: DLSS 5 results in a massive performance hit across the board. No, it's not just us. Nvidia itself has said that turning DLSS 5 on will result in a 50-60% performance reduction. But some reviewers notice it doing even worse: TechSpot saw the RTX 5080 falling from 185 fps to 53 fps at 4K, which is a 71% drop. Even the RTX 5090 ran 60% slower at 4K, matching Nvidia's worst-case scenario. So, is it playable? It depends. You can't tune your way out of it Nothing can save you from an fps drop In the last few years, or should I say, last few generations, Nvidia's gotten really good (and shall I say, really reliant) at letting you optimize your GPU with the help of AI. Upscaling helps you "cheat" a little. Frame gen helps you "cheat" a lot. We're all allowed to believe that our GPUs are better than they actually are, while also offsetting for the fact that these days, frame gen and AI come baked into the software and the hardware. Performance expectations are built around the idea that you'll be using these features, and you'll be using them a lot. So, we've all gotten used to the idea that the DLSS section is the place to go when your game isn't running as smoothly as you'd like. But with DLSS 5, that's no longer true. Although DLSS 5 lives in the same menu, it won't up your frame rates; it'll drastically reduce them. Moreover, lowering the other settings to make up for those precious AI-generated faces isn't going to help you much. TechSpot found that on an RTX 5090 at 4K, dropping from max settings all the way down to low gives you a measly 9 fps back. There's no universe where that's ever going to be worth it. That's because DLSS 5 is largely tied to your output resolution, and it runs on the finished frame after upscaling rather than before it. Enabling upscaling doesn't help either; the gains are negligible. You can't cheat your way out of the performance tax on this one. Nvidia's own launch benchmark hides the real problem 'Fake frames' to the rescue Nvidia's own launch benchmarks are super encouraging. The RTX 5090 scores 370 fps with DLSS 5 on, ray tracing on, on the ultra preset. This is in NBA 2K27, which is the only game that currently officially supports DLSS 5. The RTX 5080 pulls off an impressive effort, too, hitting 233 fps on average. You know what I'm getting at, right? These figures have been captured with 6x multi-frame generation and DLSS Super Resolution set to Performance. So, the game was being upscaled from 1080p, and five out of six frames have been interpolated. I've learned to embrace the "fake frames" to the point of believing this type of tech is the future of GPUs. Even then, we can't treat these numbers as absolute, as the GPUs are getting a lot of AI-powered help here. If we strip the frame gen away, the RTX 5090 is rendering at around 62 fps, and the RTX 5080's 233 result works out to roughly 39 fps. You might say that fps is fps, and if it works, it works. Sure, but frame gen multiplies frames, not responsiveness, and a 39 fps base fps still feels like 39 fps. Input latency makes games feel sluggish when played with DLSS 5 on, and that's something that doesn't show up on benchmarks. Whether it's unplayable depends on your resolution And your GPU, of course In all fairness, DLSS 5 is very much playable. At 4K, sure, TechSpot's testing shows the DLSS 5 pass alone takes longer than 16.7ms. That's on every GPU in the RTX 50 lineup, by the way. Dropping down to 1440p, or better yet, 1080p, makes things much less grim, obviously. Even an RTX 5060 can do some type of successful work with DLSS 5 if you play at 1080p. Meanwhile, the RTX 5090, when propped up by all the fancy stuff Nvidia has to offer, will still do a good job. Is DLSS 5 worth it right now? The problem is that this "good job" isn't anywhere close to being an across-the-board type of experience. You should try it, because why not, but will it feel good to actually game with DLSS 5 on? Probably not. But it's still early days—I expect the tech to improve over time.

item.title: This is the only podcast app that makes any sense in Android Auto
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.97
I always find that Android Auto is at its best when you keep it as stripped back as possible. It's great for navigation and music, but throw a podcast app into the mix, and it can quickly start to complicate things again. You don't want to be browsing through hundreds of episodes or fiddling with complicated menus while driving. Pocket Casts is the podcast app that gets the balance right. It's got a powerful phone app that you can use for organizing and queuing up your podcasts, but the Android Auto interface is focused purely on the essentials. In my experience, it's comfortably the best podcast app for Android Auto. Pocket Casts does the organizing before you get in the car Android Auto isn't the place for a complicated podcast app Pocket Casts maintains a clear distinction between Android Auto and phone, or between driving and not driving, that isn't replicated in other podcast apps like Spotify. The phone is where Pocket Casts really shines. The discovery features are excellent. You get top charts, curated lists, and assorted recommendations alongside the regular search function. This alone helped to make it my podcast app of choice some time ago. But what makes it especially useful for the car is its playlist features. It goes way beyond the normal Up Next queue, although you get that as well if you want to do it manually. What Pocket Casts offers is the Smart Playlist function that automatically updates with podcast episodes based on various criteria that you set. You can choose which podcasts you want to add them from, and narrow down the choices based on things like when the episodes were released, how long they are, and so on. It stops you from having to search through all your subscriptions to find things to listen to. As well as a dog-walking smart playlist that queues up the latest shorter episodes from my podcasts, I've got a "long drive" one that finds longer episodes. I queue it up when I get in the car, and I won't have to touch it again. Its Android Auto UI gets out of the way Simplicity is the key In the car, Pocket Casts becomes much simpler and is one of the best Android Auto apps. It isn't designed for browsing huge libraries, and that's a good thing. The features are still there if you really need them — you can discover new podcasts, for example — but that isn't the intended use. Pocket Casts notes that the Android Auto interface uses the standard Google UI templates, with a focus on simple navigation and a distraction-free experience. The buttons are big and obvious, and highly visible in case you ever need to press them. But this simplicity doesn't come at the expense of functionality. Smaller but no less important things like playback speed controls are still accessible, you just don't have to scroll your way through a huge app to find them. Other podcast apps that I've tested on Android Auto, like AntennaPod or Podcast Republic, often either lack the optimization you need when driving, or are stripped back but have a more limited Up Next feature that takes a lot more work to get sorted. For me, Pocket Casts' Smart Playlists make the app feel more like a personal radio station, serving up content for as long as I need it. Pocket Casts finds the right balance. It's very powerful and capable when you use it on the phone, but you interact with it as little as possible when driving. It stays in sync with your other devices Pick up exactly where you left off The other thing I like about Pocket Casts that's relevant when you're on the go is how seamlessly it moves between devices. It syncs your podcast list, playback status, and position within individual episodes so that it's accessible wherever you're listening (and the app works on pretty much any device or platform). So, I can start listening on my phone, continue in the car, and then pick up again later on a desktop without missing a word. It means that Android Auto doesn't feel like a separate part of my podcast setup. It's something more akin to a streaming app like Spotify than an app that's based around local files. Pocket Casts handles the Android Auto compromise well Finding the right balance in an Android Auto app must be quite difficult. You want it to be as simple and distraction-free as possible, but it still needs to be useful. Pocket Casts manages this by making intelligent choices about what you should do on your phone and what you should do on the big screen. Its automation means you can prepare everything in advance, then cut back on how much you ever have to touch the app while you're driving. But your listening remains completely seamless. That's what makes it Android Auto's best podcast app for me.

item.title: No tracker tag? Gemini can now store item locations right in Find Hub
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.68
What you need to know - Gemini can now remember where you left important items, even without a tracker. - You can tell Gemini where you stashed an item or snap a quick photo, and it logs the detail directly to Find Hub. - Then, ask Gemini where your item is later, or view all saved locations in Find Hub's new memory tab. Google’s September Android Drop is introducing a handy upgrade to Find Hub that allows Gemini to remember where you left important items, even if those items don’t have a tracker attached. With the latest change, you can tell Gemini where you put an item instead of using a Bluetooth tracker to find it later. For example, you could say, “Hey Google, remember in Find Hub that I put my passport in my bedroom drawer” and optionally attach a photo for additional context. Gemini then saves that information in a dedicated “remembered items” tab in Find Hub so you can easily get back to it again by just asking where it is. This feature plugs a hole in Google’s current tracking setup. While Find Hub is ideal for tagged belongings, there are plenty of things you routinely misplace — such as passports, spare keys, documents, or other small essentials — that aren’t worth attaching a tracker to. This new feature essentially provides a lightweight memory layer for those items. The feature will be rolled out to Android 16 and newer devices in countries where Gemini and Find Hub are supported. Google says it will be available soon. This is just one part of the September Android Drop, which also includes enhancements such as Motion Assist to help alleviate motion sickness and new upgrades to Google Messages. However, for those of us who spend far too much time looking for lost items, this new Gemini feature may be the most impactful update of them all. item.title: Android Drop: Google's Motion Assist and Guided Vision are two features I'm ready for on Android
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.40
What you need to know - For September's Android Drop, Google is introducing "Motion Assist," a feature to help users suffering from motion sickness while using their phone in a vehicle. - On the Accessibility front, Gemini Live can help users find items or read fine print with "Guided Vision," delivering audio descriptions to guide users. - Google states Motion Assist will rollout on Android 17 devices, while Guided Vision prepares a debut on Android 9 and newer. It's September, and right on time is Google with the latest Android Drop. This month, the company is focusing on the accessibility and comfort of Android with two major updates. Google's press release details a laundry list of new features for September; however, we're focusing on two items: Motion Sickness and Guided Vision. If you've ever tried using your phone while riding shotgun in a car, you might've put it down. Motion Sickness could affect anyone, but Google is rolling out "Motion Assist" this month to help. According to Google, Motion Assist "adds a subtle bubble overlay to your screen that moves with the vehicle." The post states these bubbles will bridge the gap between "what your eyes see and the movement of your ride." Users can start it via the Quick Settings tile, or they can set it to automatically turn on when you're in a moving vehicle. These moving bubbles will appear on the sides of your phone to help reduce motion sickness. The automatic option states Motion Assist will activate if it detects the user in a car, bus, or train. What's more, users will find a few customization options to make Motion Assist theirs. A point to Accessibility Google states Motion Assist will roll out on phones running Android 17. The second major update is Guided Vision. The post states this feature relies on Gemini Live, meaning users will have to share their camera with the AI. After sharing, Gemini Live will provide audio descriptions of what's in front of you. Google says the AI can help with "reading fine print on a food label, ordering from a menu in a low-lit restaurant, or locating household objects." In one example, Gemini Live guides a user to a seasoning they're looking for on a shelf. If the subject leaves your frame, Gemini Live will guide you back so it can help you appropriately. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Guided Vision is rolling out "soon" to phones running Android 9 or newer where Gemini is available. Once it arrives, users can add Guided Vision to their Accessibility shortcuts or launch it via the TalkBack menu. Android Central's Take I will always prefer updates like this over some "new thing" for AI. While one of these features relies on Google's AI, this is the direction I like seeing it go. A direction where it's incredibly helpful to people who may have trouble seeing or what have you. Tech should make life easier. We've got enough to worry about as it is. Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. Writing for him can vary from delivering the latest tech story to scribbling in his journal. When Nickolas isn't hitting a story, he's often grinding away at a game or chilling with a book in his hand. item.title: Google adds shared Keep notes and custom themes to Messages
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.17
What you need to know - Google Messages gets two standout updates, including Custom Chat themes and Google Keep integration as part of the September Android Drop. - You can tap the plus button to add a Keep note, letting everyone view, edit, and contribute without leaving the conversation. - Personalize individual chats using curated wallpaper collections (like Animals, Landscapes, or Space) or your own gallery photos. Google's September Android Drop is here, and while there’s a lot to go over, two features for Google Messages are stealing the spotlight: custom chat themes and seamless Google Keep integration. Beginning today, you will be able to bring a Keep note directly into a Google Messages conversation by tapping the plus button. This lets everyone in the chat view, edit, and add to shared notes, whether you're building a grocery list or planning a vacation. The idea appears to be to turn your Messages conversations into the place where plans are actually made. This might be particularly handy for group chats, where information can get lost in the flood of messages. Google is also rolling out Chat theme, which lets you set different backgrounds and color treatments for individual conversations. Google has curated collections of wallpapers to choose from — including Animals, Landscapes, Space, and more — or you can upload your own photo from your gallery. Google recommends everything from a latte theme for a coffee buddy to a beach photo for a vacation group chat. Messages automatically matches the chat bubble colors. This is much more than the simple “Change colors” option we saw back in 2024. It’s rolling out now in Google Messages. Remember, these customizations are just for you, so that beach photo you set for the vacation chat isn’t going to show up on anyone else’s phone. Google actually announced these custom backgrounds and themes a few days ago, in a post to the Google Messages Community, so the September Android Drop is another confirmation that the feature is coming. item.title: You can now test Nothing’s upcoming devices before launch
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.14
What you need to know - Nothing’s Community Review Program is back, giving selected fans early access to upcoming products before public launches. - Participants must sign an NDA, respect embargoes, share first impressions, and publish detailed reviews and additional content. - Applications close September 10, but spots aren’t guaranteed, and the program isn’t available to fans in India. Nothing is giving its community another chance to test its upcoming products before anyone else. The company has reopened its Community Review Program, allowing select fans to get hands-on time with Nothing hardware and software before public launches. The program offers select members early access to Nothing products, a direct line to the company, and an opportunity to help shape what it builds next, per the company's announcement. Nothing is particularly interested in applicants with experience in 3D animation, graphic design, music and sound production, and product reviews, but no skills are needed to apply. If you love technology, it's enough. There are some strings attached, though. Because participants may handle unreleased products, they'll need to sign an NDA, follow Nothing's embargo dates, and maintain strict information security. They are also required to give their first impressions of the Nothing Community and social media, publish a full review after launch, and create additional content such as unboxings or product use cases. It’s important to note that being chosen once does not place you on a permanent VIP list. Nothing's previous program terms made clear that participation for one product doesn't guarantee selection for future reviews, so every round is effectively another chance to get in. Review devices are issued under the terms of the current program, so applicants should verify the latest conditions before applying. Nothing will also cover the associated shipping costs. Applications are open until September 10, though selection isn't guaranteed. The program is also unavailable to fans in India. Judging by past instances of this initiative, the brand does indeed implement user feedback. Earlier in 2024, Nothing had a public campaign called “The Community Edition Project” for the Nothing Phone 2a. Over several months, the company asked its community to submit designs for the phone's hardware, wallpapers, packaging, and marketing. item.title: Google raises prices on the TV Streamer and Nest cameras effective today
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.78
What you need to know - The Google TV Streamer has jumped from $100 to $150 at the Google Store and Best Buy. - Retailers including Amazon may still have older stock at the original price, but supplies could disappear quickly. - The Nest lineup also gets across-the-board markups, with all five Nest cameras and doorbells seeing price increases of $20 to $50. If you've been holding off on picking up Google’s smart home hardware, your hesitation just got a lot more expensive. The tech giant has quietly increased prices across its streaming and security hardware lineup. The Google TV Streamer arrived in 2024 for $100, replacing Chromecast as Google’s flagship streaming box. It was also pretty easy to find below that price, with holiday discounts knocking a few bucks off. Now, Google has quietly bumped up the device’s price by $50 to $150, as spotted by 9to5Google. The new price is already appearing at Google Store and Best Buy, though some retailers are still selling remaining stock for $100. For example, not all listings have been refreshed by Amazon yet. If you are fast enough, you may be able to pick up older stock at launch prices before it is cycled out. Google mentions increased component costs, with the Streamer’s 4GB of RAM and 32GB of storage making memory costs a likely factor behind the increase. Other recent Google hardware has already been under the same broader cost pressures. The Nest lineup is taking a hit, too. Google has increased the price of all five of its currently available cameras and doorbells by $20 to $50. The battery-powered Nest Cam is now $200, up from $180, while the second-generation wired Nest Cam Outdoor jumps from $150 to $200. The third-generation wired Nest Cam Indoor rises to $130 from $100. Both the wired and battery Nest Doorbells now cost $200, up from $180. Interestingly, the Nest Cam with Floodlight bundle is still priced at $280, and the Nest Hub, thermostats, and the new Google Home Speaker remain unchanged for now. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android These changes went into effect August 31, Google says, and with component costs still a big part of hardware pricing, it may be a lot harder to find these older launch prices. item.title: These popular Samsung phones just received their final software update
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.60
What you need to know - Samsung has officially ended software support for the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 after five years. - Both foldables received four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates, as Samsung originally promised. - Samsung has removed both phones from its security update page, meaning they won't receive regular security patches anymore. Samsung's foldable phones that launched in the summer of 2021 have officially reached the end of their software support cycle. Most Samsung flagship smartphones today, including the Galaxy S26 Ultra and even 2024's Galaxy S24 Ultra, come with seven years of software support. But Samsung hasn't always offered updates for this long. Older flagships came with shorter support promises, and now the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have officially reached the end of theirs. As spotted by Android Authority, the Galaxy Z Fold 3 and Galaxy Z Flip 3 have received their final software updates. At launch, Samsung promised four years of OS upgrades and five years of security updates for both foldables, and the company has now fulfilled that promise. Samsung has also removed both devices from its security updates page. This means Samsung won't be releasing any further regular software or security updates for these devices. The oldest foldables officially supported by the company are now the Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Galaxy Z Flip 4. Even those devices have moved to a quarterly update schedule, unlike newer Samsung phones that continue to receive monthly updates. So, if you're still using a Galaxy Z Fold 3 or Galaxy Z Flip 3, your phone won't receive any new regular security patches from Samsung going forward. That means any new security vulnerabilities discovered from here on may remain unpatched on these devices. If you're still holding onto one of these foldables, this might finally be the time to start thinking about an upgrade. Samsung recently introduced a completely new form factor with the Galaxy Z Fold 8, while its latest foldables also come with a much longer software support promise. If you've managed to keep your Fold 3 or Flip 3 running for five years, one of Samsung's newer foldables should last you considerably longer. item.title: Lumus, Quanta reach licensing agreement for next-gen waveguides for AR glasses that may turn the tide
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.46
What you need to know - Lumus is expanding its partnership with Quanta this week, which brings a licensing agreement between the two companies for next-gen waveguides. - Lumus states Quanta will manufacture its next-gen waveguides: the Z-30 2.0, A-Lens 30 (30-degree FOV), and A-Lens 50 (50-degree FOV). - The company was at CES 2026 where it stated it's future for waveguides for AR glasses will be "thinner, lighter, and easier to produce." This morning (Sept 1), Lumus, a developer of waveguides for several big-name brands, announced a major partnership expansion. In a press release, Lumus announced that it has expanded its partnership with Quanta Computing. This expansion sees the two companies reaching a licensing agreement "to manufacture three new geometric waveguides for AR glasses." The post states Lumus is developing three new waveguides: the Z-30 2.0, A-Lens 30 (30-degree FOV), and A-Lens 50 (50-degree FOV). Thanks to the new licensing agreement, Quanta will handle manufacturing. What we can expect from the Z-30 2.0 is a 30-degree FOV "in a thinner, lighter optical engine." Lumus adds that its latest technology increases the display's brightness, alongside direct prescription lens bonding. The two new A-Lens waveguides (30 and 50) are Lumus' "lower-cost" production solutions. The next-gen A-Lens waveguides are reportedly cutting down the weight and thickness by 50%. However, Lumus states it maintained its image quality and efficiency with this upgrade. This is an ongoing trend that Lumus is trying to introduce into this advancing world of AR glasses. Trimming down waveguide weight and thickness is key, but so is image quality, brightness, and cost. Earlier today, Lumus' CEO, Ari Grobman, said, "Our relationship with Quanta has always been built around solving the practical challenges of bringing advanced AR optics into mass production. This agreement allows us to bring our next generation of lower-cost waveguides into manufacturing with a partner that understands both the technology and the production requirements behind it." Here comes the future, and Lumus is leading it As mentioned before, Lumus creates waveguides for several brands, even for Meta and its Ray-Ban Display Glasses. Earlier this year, Meta announced that it was doubling the production of its Ray-Ban glasses to meet demand. This was something Lumus echoed in its press release this morning. The demand for smart glasses continues to rise, but there's room for improvement. Its work to reduce the weight and thickness of its waveguides for AR glasses is one such upgrade. Additionally, the lower-production-cost A-Lenses are designed to help bring more products to consumers. We'll have to see how things pan out going forward. item.title: Qualcomm's Adreno 'Neural Fusion' GPU will lean on AI to upgrade phone gaming
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.42
What you need to know - Qualcomm continues to tease its next Snapdragon debut with the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. - The company says this chip utilizes AI-drive rendering tech, placing stronger resolution and frame generation directly into the graphics pipeline. - What's more, the GPU adds the Adreno HPM, which helps move larger chunks of data for rendering at a time, effectively saving more battery power. - Snapdragon Summit 2026 takes place from September 22-24 Qualcomm's Snapdragon Summit is coming up later this month, and the company is teasing its graphical improvements. Qualcomm sent a press release this morning (Sept 2) detailing the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. If you thought this wouldn't involve AI, think again. Qualcomm says Neural Fusion is an "AI-driven rendering technology that combines neural processing, AI super resolution, and frame generation into a unified graphics pipeline." For context, Qualcomm says it's looking to deliver what consumers want from mobile gaming: console-like graphics, strong frame rates, and better battery life. This is important because Qualcomm states its Adreno Neural Fusion GPU nails all three of these desires, and consistently, too. The post credits this GPU power to the chip's new Adreno Matrix Cores. This reportedly brings its AI rendering engine into the graphics pipeline, giving developers the exact tools they need to bump up the graphics for your phone. Lower latency is another positive in this change. Helping that lower latency is the Adreno HPM (High Performance Memory), which feeds more data to the GPU for rendering, thanks to a "dedicated optimized cache of 18MB." Many of these changes help Qualcomm hit that last point: better gaming battery life. With the Neural Fusion GPU capable of moving more data at a time, it's effectively moving a lot less, which doesn't eat up your battery. Then, you have its AI models playing more closely to the graphical unit. Qualcomm will undoubtedly show off the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips in greater detail during its Summit from September 22-24. What we've been waiting on? Qualcomm's teasers will likely continue until its Summit in a few weeks. The latest major teaser we got spurred excitement. Qualcomm highlighted "Dual 8 Elites" on approach for 2026. Our eyes are looking at that long-rumored Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 "Pro." Qualcomm hasn't said anything yet, so do with that information what you will (it is rumored, after all). What the company has said is that its Dual 8 Elites will bring "better connectivity, camera functionality, and graphics for games." Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android What's interesting about those "Pro" rumors is that not everyone's phone could see it. While yes, these Snapdragon chips are reserved for flagships, the Pro could only seek out Ultra devices—the Galaxy S27 Ultra would fit that bill. We still have a while until Snapdragon Summit 2026 in Maui, Hawaii. Android Central's Take I believe it was Android Authority's coverage that likens what Qualcomm's doing with the Neural Fusion to Nvidia's DLSS 5. If you're a gamer or you've kept up with gaming in general, this hasn't sat well with people. DLSS 5 "enhances" your graphics through AI, but from the examples out there, people aren't convinced the original artists' intent remains. I hope Qualcomm's AI doesn't do that. And if it does, can I turn it off? I'm all for incredible gaming performance on phones, but not if the game doesn't look as intended. item.title: What's next from Google Translate will upgrade Android in all the right ways
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.19
What you need to know - Google rolls out two major updates for the Translate app to end the week, beginning with multitasking capabilities for Android. - Android users can now continue translating speech in the background, giving them the freedom of opening other apps or locking their device. - For iPhone users, Google says they now have support for real-time translations via earbuds or by holding their phone to their ears. Google wants to end the week with an update for its Translate app across its supported devices. The company says Android users will find capabilities flexible enough for their day-to-day. This morning (Sept 4), Google says its latest features rolling out for Android and iOS will assist users with translating over 70 languages in "near real-time." Users on Android reportedly hold live translation sessions that last "longer than five minutes." Google states the Translate app can now continue translating even while in the background. This lets users hop into other apps and multitask or lock their phone. Google Translate will continue working, ready to reveal its translated content for you when you're ready. This is rolling out for Android users today. Google says it's preparing an update for Apple iOS users, but that is "coming soon." If you have an iOS device, this late-week update brings translation capabilities through a connected earpiece. Android users received it in a previous update. Google Translate will deliver audio translation directly through your earbuds. However, if such a device isn't connected, Google says iOS users can hold their phone to their ear, as if on a call. Like the update for Android, iPhone users can expect this to begin appearing today (Sept 4). The work continues Google Translate isn't among the apps that always get major updates, but the company has been improving it little by little. In a similar vein to Duolingo, the Translate app added "streaks" for users practicing new languages. What's more, this earlier patch expanded the beta for Android's real-time translation support while wearing headphones. Gemini's been brought into the fold heavily for the translation app. It's the AI's speech-to-speech capabilities that get the job done. Earlier this year, Google rolled out a huge Translate app update for iOS users for headphone support. The feature offers a few different modes: Listening, Conversation, and Text-only. "Listening" is for real-time translations. "Conversation" lets you speak in English and lets the person you're talking to hear it in their native tongue. Android Central's Take The usefulness of Google Translate has shot up considerably over the past few updates. They've been strung out, so there's quite a bit of time in between each one. Nevertheless, what Google's brought has been useful. It feels like the days of carrying around a Spanish-to-English dictionary are gone. You can rely on your phone; whether you're learning the language with guided practice or listening to its translations. Just take it with a grain of salt, sometimes. Not every translation is as accurate as I'd like it to be. item.title: The rumored folding iPhone Ultra looks sick, but Android foldables offer something more: choice
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.76
Rumor has it that Apple will announce the iPhone Ultra at its upcoming September 9 event, making it the first iPhone to sport an "ultra" moniker. We're not expecting it to push the boundaries of battery technology or camera prowess, but it is slated to do one big thing that no other iPhone has (intentionally) done: fold in half. This is going to drive a huge boost in sales for foldable phones, a category that has consistently grown since the first models arrived in 2019, but hasn't seen a particularly massive tentpole release like this one yet. Of course, as with anything Apple makes, you'll only get what Apple gives you, and rumor has it that Apple is announcing only one size and shape this time around. But Android foldables, which have been around for eight years now, have had time to develop and branch out. Android offers a substantial choice of manufacturers, shapes, sizes, and capabilities that Apple simply can't offer. If foldable phones are looking like your next big purchase, here are many reasons you should choose an Android-powered one. What is a folding phone and how do they work? Folding phones usually come with two displays: an inner display and an outer display. The inner display is made of special ultrathin glass that can bend (unlike normal glass) and is reinforced with a preinstalled screen protector. The phone's frame is split into two halves connected by a specialized hinge, allowing you to open and close the phone. The foldable inner display is a special type of flexible OLED panel that's built to bend, too. A specialized hinge holds everything together, keeping dust and water out of the phone. It's a true marvel of engineering, and some foldables are even extremely durable, as proven by my Honor Magic V6 torture test. Both the inner and outer displays work the same way a regular smartphone touchscreen does. You can open apps on either of them, allowing you to choose the size of the "canvas" you want to view them on. What types of folding phones exist (and why would someone want one)? The leaked image of the iPhone Ultra above shows what's known as a book-style foldable. When a book-style phone is closed, its size and shape are similar to those of a standard smartphone, so all your favorite apps look and feel nearly identical to those on your existing smartphone. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Opening a book-style phone doubles its size, turning it into a small tablet that lets you get more done without switching to a laptop or other computer. I work on the go quite a bit, and a folding phone makes it easy to get most of my work done efficiently. I rarely watch videos on my phone, but when I do, the extra-large inner display is a real treat. Because of the large size, multitasking is one of the best features of a book-style foldable. You can run two or three apps side by side on these phones, and even put apps in floating windows, like on a laptop OS. Plus, the taskbar on the inner display makes it feel even more like a multitasking beast, similar to a laptop OS (like Windows or macOS). Book-style foldables come in many sizes and shapes, though most are slightly taller and narrower than your average smartphone when closed. Google began its foldable journey with a shorter, wider model, but made the next three entries a bit taller. Meanwhile, Samsung just introduced its first shorter, wider model (the Galaxy Z Fold 8), and Apple's iPhone Ultra is rumored to use this same size and shape. Shorter, wider models are best for video content and feel a lot like holding a small TV when unfolded. Apple's iPhone Ultra is said to come in just one shape and size, while Android foldables offer tons of different sizes, shapes, and form factors. You can even get tri-fold foldables! While book-style foldables get the bulk of the attention, flip-style foldables were better sellers for a few years. Phones like the Motorola Razr 2026 series look like a slightly taller normal smartphone when opened, then fold into a perfectly pocketable half-sized phone when closed. These phones solve the issue of overly large phones while still giving you the flexibility to use a small screen for things like notifications and messaging, then a larger screen when you need it. We generally recommend Motorola's Razr flip phones over Samsung's Z Flip line because Motorola's outer screen is more capable, and the company's designs are far more interesting. Flip phones are also wonderful for photos and videos thanks to their shape. It's easy to bend a flip phone at a 90-degree angle and use it as a "tripod" to take group photos. You can also use this same shape and hold it sideways to take video like a classic camcorder. Do folding phones have any downsides? Folding phones offer unique form factors and ways to interact with your favorite apps, but not everything is a win-win. When shopping for a book-style folding phone, the first thing you'll probably notice is the price. Yeah, there's quite a bit of sticker shock here, and that's mainly because this is a two-in-one device. Think of it as buying a phone and a tablet at the same time, and you'll understand. Flip-style phones are typically priced the same as traditional flagship phones but tend to have one fewer rear camera. Even Motorola's Razr Ultra line doesn't have a third camera on the back, despite the higher price. Both flip and book-style foldables are often a bit less powerful than top-tier traditional flagship smartphones. The problem is that there's not as much space in these phones for cooling, since they have to be thinner than a traditional phone to avoid feeling like a brick when closed. Lastly, durability. Folding phones got a bad rap pretty early on when the original Galaxy Z Fold's inner display would spontaneously break, but those problems have generally been solved. There's always a chance the folding glass could break, but these phones have undergone so many years of evolution and hardening that such a failure is almost unheard of. Stores like uBreakiFix readily have parts to repair them, and phone companies offer warranties and other insurance programs that help cover any potential issues. As someone who has reviewed dozens and dozens of folding phones over the past seven years, I've never seen a phone break in person. My wife has also been using flip phones for the past four years, and the only time one of hers broke was after being dropped with the phone unfolded. Considering how many traditional smartphones break every day from drops, there's no reason to suggest that these phones are any less durable with regular use. Nick started with DOS and NES and uses those fond memories of floppy disks and cartridges to fuel his opinions on modern tech. Whether it's VR, smart home gadgets, or something else that beeps and boops, he's been writing about it since 2011. item.title: The iPhone Duo is here, and it will convince you to buy a foldable
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.73
The iPhone Duo is finally official, and there's plenty of cool features in the wider-style foldable. Apple says it combined a "thoughtful design with breakthrough engineering," and that the name signifies how the foldable is basically two products in one — a phone and a tablet. The naming makes that patently clear, but it isn't the most original — Microsoft may have something to say about that. Anyway, the iPhone Duo isn't like the usual book-style foldables, instead following a wider and shorter design that Apple says is intuitive to use. This is essentially identical to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and the Xiaomi 18 Fold, and now that the iPhone Duo is official, I'd wager we get a lot of similar Android-based foldables that follow a similar style. There's a 5.4-inch outer panel and a 7.6-inch inner panel, and the chassis is made out of titanium. At 5.3mm unfolded and a weight of 254g, it isn't quite as thin or light as the latest generation of Android foldables — even the Pixel 11 Pro Fold is lighter by 15g — but the iPhone Duo has IP68 dust and water resistance, and that in itself is a big deal. What's unique with the inner panel is that Apple is using two layers of glass sandwiched together, and this ensures that the panel doesn't deform with long-term use. This is a big enough problem on foldables, and it's good to see Apple coming up with a novel solution immediately; we should see a similar system used by at least Google on the Pixel 12 Pro Fold next year. There's also a nano-texture coating on the inner panel to reduce glare, and this is bound to make a difference. The iPhone Duo will be available in Star White and Night Sky colors, with the latter delivering a blue hue that looks great. The hinge itself is touted to have a smooth articulation and a custom torque profile, and it is designed to fold fully flat — something that took Samsung six years to get right. The hinge stays open at various angles, and that's good to see as well as it unlocks new use cases while taking photos or viewing content on the go. You can even use the iPhone Duo as a glorified bedside clock, and I like that it has a new StandBy mode that's usable even when it isn't being charged. There's no Face ID; instead, you get Touch ID that's baked into the power button, similar to the iPad Mini and most Android foldables. Another thing that's good is the camera on the inner panel; it's visible when you're making calls, but otherwise hidden away. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android What I like is the ability to use the Apple Pencil with the iPhone Duo; that feature will come later in the year, and as someone who uses the stylus constantly, I'm excited about this. The software in general looks great; the Liquid Glass interface switches effortlessly between the outer and inner panels, and Apple moved UI elements to a vertical position to accommodate the unique size of the iPhone Duo. The dock is located vertically, giving you better real estate when using the inner panel, and there's good multitasking features — you get split-screen multitasking similar to the iPad. Coming to the internals, the iPhone Duo is powered by the latest A20 Pro silicon, which is built on a new 2nm node that delivers much better efficiency. It starts with 256GB of storage, going up to 2TB. What isn't so great is the camera system; you get a 48MP main camera and a 48MP wide-angle lens, but there's no dedicated telephoto camera on the device. This was the case on the Z Fold 8 as well, and it's annoying that the lens that most of use regularly is missing on the device. The iPhone Duo will go on pre-order starting October 16 for $1,999. Thankfully, it is getting a global launch and will be available in more than 70 countries on launch day, and heading to 28 additional regions by the end of October. What isn't great is the pricing; the iPhone Duo costs a lot more in other regions — it starts at closer to $2,700. Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd. item.title: 7 coolest things I saw at IFA 2026
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.71
IFA 2026 is back, and as expected, there's a lot to see on the show floor at Messe Berlin. IFA is traditionally more focused on consumer electronics, such as smart home devices, more than mobile products like smartphones. However, there were a few mobile devices scattered about the show, including phones and wearables, as well as a bevy of accessories that managed to catch my eye. Here are some of the coolest things I've seen while exploring IFA 2026. Xiaomi's whole thing Xiaomi's IFA debut was a big one, with the company showcasing its family of products across a massive space spanning 3,300 square meters. The company showed off how its family of products can work together using HyperOS and AI, allowing you to seamlessly move across devices as you navigate your home and even your car. But beyond that, the company also showed off a cool humanoid robot that walked around its space for photo ops. The company says it's exploring the use of humanoid robots to enhance its manufacturing, stating that it has already seen a massive improvement with tasks like nut tightening in its Auto Factory. But the thing I was most interested in was the one item attendees couldn't get their hands on: the Xiaomi 18 Fold. The device was secured behind glass in a striking red color, showing the device both closed and open. It has a wider foldable design, similar to the Galaxy Z Fold 8, although with rounder corners, which is a design cue we're expecting on the rumored iPhone Ultra. The Xiaomi 18 Fold has a triple-camera system and is powered by the company's in-house XRING 03 chip, enhanced for on-device AI. The full launch is just days away, on September 7, so we'll learn more about this exciting phone soon. Move over, Robot Phone I often ignore ruggedized phones because they serve a particular market segment I'm just not very interested in. However, the RugOne Xsnap 7 Pro from Ulefone does something unique that caught my eye. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Unlike the Robot Phone, which has a very cool robotic gimbal camera, the Xsnap 7 Pro has a detachable camera that can be used as a remote action cam. Ulefone had a number of accessories on display that the camera could be attached to, including a tripod, a selfie stick, a clamp, and more. And when you're done being adventurous, you can easily snap the camera back into place, where it's paired with a 50MP and 64MP camera system. The phone is powered by a respectable MediaTek Dimensity 8400 and is IP69K-, IP68-, and MIL-STD-810H-certified for high-grade durability. It's clear this is for a certain type of consumer, which I am not, but I can't help but want this phone. Smart rings that vibrate and much more I'm a big fan of smart rings, but the small form factor brings some limitations. Fortunately, some of the latest smart rings from Circular seem to be addressing some of them, with both rings featuring vibration alerts. This is actually something Circular has featured in previous versions of its smart ring, but it was unfortunately omitted from the Circular Ring 2. Now it's back with the Circular 3 series, which can vibrate for wake-up alarms, health alerts, bringing exercises, and more, all while being nearly as slim as the Oura Ring 5. They also feature NFC payments, which is a feature I would love to see on more smart rings. The Circular Ring 3 Slim is the thinner of the two and, as a result, misses out on some advanced health-tracking features found in the Circular Ring 3 Pro, such as blood pressure trends. However, it still gets haptic feedback, which is impressive on such a small form factor. The Circular Ring 3 series is bound to give the Oura Ring 5 a run for its money when it arrives in 2027. Your next AI running glasses I checked out BleeqUp's first smart AI glasses at last year's MWC, and this year the company has a new pair with welcome enhancements that make it an even more enticing alternative to the Oakley Meta Vanguard. Compared to the BleeqUp Ranger, the new Rover glasses feature an updated 3K60 resolution with HDR and improved low-light performance. Interestingly, the camera can tilt up or down, offering greater versatility in your sports shots. There's also more AI integration for things like emergency recording, proactive safety alerts, and for sports monitoring to track things like your breathing rhythm and provide activity summaries. Finally, there's better waterproofing, double the internal storage, and support for BleeqUp's accessories like the remote control and battery extender. Tecno bezel-less concept Tecno is no stranger to showing off cool concept at trade shows such as this (remember that cool modular phone?), but the bezel-less concept phone feels like a product I could actually see it bringing to market. At first glance, it looks and feels just like a regular phone, but turn it on, and you'll notice just how immersive the viewing experience is. It's really just display and frame, and while my hands-on time was short, it feels like a phone made for a not-too-distant future. The back is also really interesting, sporting a unique design with a 3D-like effect that thoroughly impressed myself and other onlookers almost as much as the bezel-less display. The only portable projector you'll need The Aurzen Zip Pro took what I loved about the original Aurzen Zip and supersized it. It's still one of the coolest portable projectors I've seen, and it's not much larger than the original, while still remaining easy to fold up and carry. It also weighs as much as two flagship smartphones. It has better picture quality with a higher 1080p resolution, enhanced color, and 4-point keystone correction, so the picture should look great no matter where you throw it from. Plus, it features a small top display you can use to control the device. It also has longer battery life, although at 2.5 hours, you'll wanna keep it plugged in for any "Lord of the Rings" marathons. But if you do need a charge, it now supports 65W charging speeds, which is pretty nice for on-the-go charging. This is the droid you're looking for There's always someone showing off some cool robot thing, and PrimeBot Q1 managed to steal my heart. It's a cute toddler-sized robot that you can talk to or control using your Android smartphone, and thanks to high-torque QDD joints, it moves very quickly for things like dancing (which it does surprisingly well). I also watched as someone grabbed the Q1's hand and guided it around the show floor, as if it were an actual child you didn't want to lose in the hustle and bustle of a grocery store. My heart immediately melted at the sight of this. The PrimeBot Q1 is also customizable, so you can either take it as is or dress it up to look like a Gundam, Power Ranger, and so much more. For now, availability is limited to China, but it's set to come to Europe in 2027. Here's hoping it also makes it way to the U.S.! Derrek is the managing editor of Android Central, helping to guide the site's editorial content and direction to reach and resonate with readers, old and new, who are just as passionate about tech as we are. He's been obsessed with mobile technology since he was 12, when he discovered the Nokia N90, and his love of flip phones and new form factors continues to this day. As a fitness enthusiast, he has always been curious about the intersection of tech and fitness. When he's not working, he's probably working out. The Robot Phone was crafted in collaboration with ARRI for professional camera-grade features. AI is woven in to help reduce strenuous noises and to optimize your video's high dynamic range. item.title: Samsung’s newest midrange smartphone comes with $200 of free Amazon cash
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.18
Samsung's latest 'Fan Edition' smartphone has just hit store shelves, and you can already find some solid Galaxy S26 FE deals during Labor Day sales this weekend. Buy the midrange masterpiece unlocked from Amazon, for instance, and you'll get a free $200 gift card with your purchase. No strings attached! You can even claim an additional gift card worth up to $600 if you trade in an old or broken device on the retailer's website. Not too shabby for an Android phone that was literally just announced last week! No Prime membership is required to receive the gift card, but be aware that Amazon's deal ends on September 20th — so you don't have very long to claim your free cash. The 'Fan Edition' Galaxy S26 FE comes with a free $200 gift card at Amazon Samsung Galaxy S26 FE 128GB: $699.99, plus free $200 gift card at Amazon The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE has arrived. Buy the midrange smartphone unlocked from Amazon and you'll get a free $200 gift card with your purchase, no trade-in required and no strings attached. Starting at $699, this device comes equipped with a ton of flagship-level specs and One UI 9 (Android 17) straight out of the box. Don't let its unassuming design fool you: the Galaxy S26 FE is one of the best 'Fan Edition' smartphones that Samsung has produced in years. Starting at $699.99 for the 128GB version, the device comes equipped with a lovely 6.7-inch AMOLED display constructed from durable Gorilla Glass Victus+, while under the hood you get a powerful Exynos chipset and a 4,900mAh battery that should easily last a full day on a single charge. Looking at the camera tech, the Galaxy S26 FE boasts a 50MP main lens, plus you get all of the brand's latest AI-boosted software features, such as Nightography and My FanCam. The midrange smartphone also comes with Android 17 straight out of the box, making the Galaxy S26 FE the first Samsung phone to launch with One UI 9. You even get seven years of OS and security updates guaranteed, which is extremely unusual for phones in this price range. So what's the catch? Well, the problem with Samsung's FE series always comes down to timing and price. The midrange phones generally launch months after the release of the company's S-series lineup, which means the flagship devices are often getting discounted by the time the new FE arrives. For example, you can currently buy an unlocked Samsung Galaxy S26 256GB for $721 at Amazon, which is only $21 more expensive than the S26 FE. Although, of course, you won't get the $200 gift card. item.title: I tested the POCO F9 Ultra, and it is the value flagship I'd buy in 2026
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.07
Android Central Verdict The F9 Ultra uses the same foundation as its predecessor, but comes with a new design, bigger battery that lasts two days without breaking a sweat, and a 200MP camera that takes great photos. You get the best onboard sound of any phone, but it has its share of issues — it overheats while gaming, doesn't have the latest version of Android, and video quality is average at best. That said, you're not paying anywhere as much as a regular flagship, and that makes the F9 Ultra a good all-round value in 2026. Pros - +Terrific onboard sound - +Good design and build quality - +Two-day battery life with 100W charging - +Top-notch internals - +Good 200MP camera - +Bright AMOLED - +Decent overall value Cons - -Ultrawide camera is still pretty basic - -Still runs Android 16 out of the box - -Won't get as many software updates Why you can trust Android Central Last year's POCO F8 Ultra was one of my favorite phones. It had a delightful denim-based design, powerful internals, great cameras, standout battery, and didn't cost anywhere as much as its rivals. Basically, POCO delivered one of the best value flagships of the year with the device. In 2026, the brand is continuing that trend with the F9 Ultra and F9 Pro. The F9 Ultra isn't too different to its predecessor, and that is unquestionably a good thing. There is a bigger 8,050mAh battery that lasts two days with ease, a new 200MP main camera, and a model with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, which is what I'm using. The F9 Ultra is coming to 25 countries globally, including the U.K., Germany, Spain, Italy, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Mexico, and the UAE. Annoyingly, it isn't launching in India, and I don't quite understand why that's the case — POCO has a strong userbase in the country, and the device should do well considering its intended audience. Let's start with what it costs. The F9 Ultra comes with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, and it costs the equivalent of $799, with an early-bird deal of $729. It is costlier in the west, retailing for €1,099 ($1,273), but the launch price of €829 ($961) makes it that much more accessible. Then there's the 16GB/512GB model that costs $949 ($799 at launch), and €1,199 ($1,389) (€899 ($1,042) at launch). The 16GB/1TB model is $1,199 in Asian markets with a deal price of $1,059, and it comes out to €1,399 ($1,621) in the west, with the deal lowering it to €1,199 ($1,389). The F9 Pro, on the other hand, costs $699 for the 12GB/256GB edition, and $769 for the 12GB/512GB model. Obviously, you're still paying a lot of cash towards either phone, but it isn't anywhere as much as a regular flagship. Having used the F9 Ultra for a week, it's evident that POCO once again managed to deliver a standout phone. I'm a little annoyed that it didn't retain the denim finish — it made the phone so distinctive — but the Dark Cherry model is equally good-looking this year, and the design is eerily similar to what the iPhone 18 Pro is touted to look like based on the leaks. I'm guessing that's intentional, and whatever the reason, the F9 Ultra looks great. It is on the heavier side at 235g, but weight distribution is ideal, and the matte texture makes the phone a delight to use. The camera island is wide — similar to the iPhone 17 Pro — and it doesn't lead to any wobble when using on a desk, which is a definite positive. You get IP68 dust and water resistance, an ultrasonic sensor that's fast to authenticate and is located in the right position (thankfully), and Xiaomi's interesting offline mode that lets you make calls with another Xiaomi phone without a cell signal (up to two kilometers). Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android There's a dedicated Bose woofer (like last year), and onboard audio is the best of any phone today. It gets loud and detailed, and honestly, POCO deserves a lot of credit for nailing the 2.1 audio configuration on a phone. Oh, and there's a ring encircling the Bose woofer, and it lights up — similar to HiLight on the Pixel 11 Pro Fold — and it is handy if you want to view notifications while the phone is face-down. The 6.9-inch AMOLED panel is unchanged to last year, and you get the same WildBoost engine that makes gaming a little smoother. The difference isn't big enough that I'd suggest getting this over something like the Redmagic 11 Pro, but it is better than most mainstream phones. The panel itself is bright and has good colors, and it does a good job with HDR content. Because of the accelerated launch window (the phone is launching 10 months after its predecessor), there isn't a change of silicon, and that's absolutely fine by me — the 8 Elite Gen 5 is still the best that Qualcomm has to offer. It tends to overheat while gaming, but not quite to the same extent as the F8 Ultra, so that is good to see. Another positive is the silicon-carbon battery tech. The phone gets a huge 8,050mAh battery with a decent 16% silicon-carbon content in the anode, and it easily lasts two days even with heavy use. There's 100W charging as well, and the phone takes less than an hour to fully charge the battery. I also like the camera on the F9 Ultra; there's a new 200MP main camera that takes great photos in just about any situation. The wide-angle lens is average, and the phone in general doesn't do that good a job with videos. That said, the 5x tele lens is pretty decent. The biggest annoyance with the F9 Ultra is the software. The phone runs Android 16 out of the box, and I don't understand why it doesn't have Android 17. POCO has to do better in this area, and the software in general is in need of an overhaul. Of course, that's reliant on Xiaomi, and with the brand dragging its heels, it may be a while before you see any positive momentum on the software front. On that subject, the phone will get four Android updates, which is on the lower end of the scale. All things considered, POCO has another winner in the F9 Ultra — the phone has reliable internals and cameras, standout battery life, and looks great. The software is annoying, but that's the case with every Xiaomi phone until the brand rolls out its long-overdue redesign, and for what it's worth, I prefer using POCO phones to Xiaomi or Redmi models in this category now. If you need a value flagship in 2026, the F9 Ultra is now one of the best choices. Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd.
