item.title: This AI-Developed Computer Worm Could Have Hijacked a Billion Accounts
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.83
A cybersecurity company used AI to quickly develop a computer worm capable of hacking over a billion accounts on the Chinese messaging service WeChat. Palo Alto-based Calif disclosed the already-patched computer worm to warn the public about the threat of AI-driven hacks. The attack, dubbed WeWorm, was developed after an AI model uncovered a serious remote code execution vulnerability in WeChat, a WhatsApp-like messaging service with over 1.4 billion users, mainly in China. “Exploitation takes only seconds, and gives us full control of the WeChat account. We can read and send messages, make calls, and act on the victim's behalf,” the company warned, posting a video demo of the WeWorm attack. As a computer worm, the threat can self-replicate, hacking one WeChat account and then moving to another by targeting users through their friend lists. The attack can also hit both Android and iOS WeChat accounts, spreading itself through phone calls on the app. “The victim does not need to answer the call, or interact with their phone at all,” Calif added. The good news is that WeChat’s parent company, Tencent, patched the vulnerability after Calif notified the company in July. Specifically, the flaw involved a “memory corruption issue in WeChat's VoIP stack,” or what the company described as an “unconventional” attack surface. The finding might cause some to call for a ban on AI amid signs that cybercriminals and state-sponsored hackers are using the technology, including open-source models, for their attacks. However, Calif notes that the WeChat vulnerability had existed for some time, meaning a human hacker could have uncovered it too. The problem is that AI models can discover and weaponize serious software bugs in days, whereas a human team would need months. In this case, Calif used AI to discover the WeChat vulnerability in two days. “Building the worm took one more week. A worm at this scale used to be the kind of thing that took a larger team months. AI can already do most of the work here,” the company added. To prevent hackers from unleashing their own AI-developed computer worm, Calif is urging the industry and countries to use AI models to shore up their defenses and plug potential security holes. “The US and China disagree on plenty, but keeping billions of people safe online shouldn't be one of them. AI gives us an opportunity to find and fix vulnerabilities faster than ever, and we should work together to make the world safer for everyone,” the company said. Although Calif didn’t disclose which AI program discovered the flaw, the company has been partnering with “frontier labs,” suggesting it used a leading-edge model. It fears what might happen if bad actors gain access to similar models. “All it takes is one lab accident or a person who grabs a half-finished version to unleash something like WeWorm into the world before anyone is ready,” Calif added. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: New Apple Watches Add Better Health Sensors, AI Conversation Recaps
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.76
Apple is improving its smartwatches with a more powerful health sensor to offer even better, continuous tracking and data collection. Alongside the iPhone 18 Pros and foldable Duo, the company announced the Apple Watch Series 12 and Watch Ultra 4, which feature a new “Health Sensing System” and S11 chip. The key improvement is that the sensors have been upgraded across the electrodes, photodiodes, and LEDs to better capture the wearer's electrical and biological signals for “the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable,” Apple says. The sensor can take background heart rate readings every 5 seconds, 60 times more than before. The scans of heart rate variability, or HRV, another indicator of cardiac health, are also increasing by about 24 times. “Recovery HRV is best for identifying daily signals of stress and recovery, while overall HRV is best for insights into a user’s broader health, including cardiovascular health,” the company noted. “Higher variability is generally associated with better overall recovery, while a lower variability value is an indicator of stress.” The watches support AI-focused Apple Intelligence features, including Audio Intelligence, which can tap into the microphone to listen in on your surroundings. That might sound creepy, but Apple pointed to more innocuous uses. One Audio Intelligence feature called Sound Recognition, for example, has been designed to help deaf users flag important sounds, like a doorbell or siren, when they’re away from their iPhone. Meanwhile, Live Rewind “can help users recall what was just said in conversation," Apple says. Double-pressing the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet on the watch. Another feature, called Siri Recap, can create summaries of the user’s conversations when enabled, capturing the key points. Apple emphasized that the AI-powered feature can preserve user privacy since the S11 is designed with a Secure Exclave, or “a dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.” So no secret recordings. "Users are in control and can choose whether to opt in to each Audio Intelligence feature. They can decide exactly where and when Siri Recap takes notes, and can turn Siri Recap on or off at any time, right from Control Center," the company added. "By design, Audio Intelligence features do not identify and attribute speakers, to protect the privacy of both the user and those around them." Expect Siri Recap and Live Rewind to arrive as beta later this year. The AI-generated summaries and texts can be saved to a user's iCloud, but they'll be end-to-end encrypted, meaning Apple can't even access them. In addition to the S11 chip, the watches also come with a redesigned pedometer, which means they can provide more accurate step counts during long walks or runs. That said, battery life isn’t changing much for the Apple Watch 12 series. It still offers up to 24 hours of everyday battery life, although outdoor workouts now reach up to 10 hours, a 25% increase. Meanwhile, the bigger Watch Ultra 4 has received a battery boost. “For everyday use, Apple Watch Ultra 4 now offers more than two days of battery life, up to 50 hours. In Low Power Mode, it offers up to 84 hours of battery life,” the company says. The device also charges faster; a mere 15 minutes of charging can add up to 18 hours of battery life. With watchOS 27, both devices will also be able to run the new Siri AI, Apple's upgraded voice assistant, which is rolling out in beta on Sept. 14 in English. The Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while the Ultra 4 will arrive for $799 and up; no price hikes here. Preorders are available now, and they launch on Sept. 18. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Want a New iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo? Here's How Much They Cost Through Apple Upgrade
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.44
Apple announced during its 'Surprise and Shine' event that the iPhone 18 Pro will launch on September 18, with preorders opening on Saturday, September 12. Its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, will launch one month later on October 23, with preorder starting on October 16. If you can't wait to get your hands on either of Apple's latest premium flagships but can't afford to buy them outright, you have options. You can trade in your old device to shave some money off of your bill, finance with your carrier, or lease a device through Apple's newly launched Upgrade program. Here's how much the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo will cost through Apple Upgrade, and whether or not this leasing option makes sense for you. How Much Will the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo Cost With Apple Upgrade? According to Apple, the iPhone 18 Pro will start at a retail price of $1,199 in the US. If you want to lease the iPhone 18 Pro through Apple Upgrade, prices will start at $34.99 per month for a 24-month lease and $49.99 per month for a 24-month lease. The iPhone Duo will retail for between $1,999 and $3,199. Apple Upgrade plans for the iPhone Duo will start at $57.99 per month for a 24-month lease and $82.99 for a 12-month lease. How Does Apple Upgrade Work? In partnership with "buy now, pay later" (BNPL) platform Klarna, Apple Upgrade is a new leasing program that launched on July 28, which lets you pay a monthly fee for select iPhones and Apple Watches for 24 months and MacBooks and iPads for 36 months. You'll then have the option to return the device, pay off the balance and keep it, or upgrade to a new device. Eligibility will be based on a credit check. For an iPhone, it'll need to be connected to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon when you enroll. This new service replaces Apple's iPhone Upgrade program. If you're currently a member of the iPhone Upgrade Program, your loan agreement with Citizens One remains active, and you’ll continue making your monthly payments until your 24-month term is complete, when "the iPhone will be yours to keep." How Much Does It Cost to Lease Other Apple Products? The main draw of Apple Upgrade is its low prices. Here are the starting prices by Apple device: - iPad - $11.99 per month - iPhone - $17.99 per month - Apple Watch - $11.99 per month - MacBook - $24.99 per month These are just starting prices and will vary by product (and possibly your credit score). Leasing an iPhone 17, which costs $899 to buy, starts at $25.99 per month to lease for 24 months and $36.99 to lease for 12 months. However, Apple says you can trade in your old device to lower your lease payments. For comparison, Apple's now-defunct iPhone Upgrade plan charges $42.41 per month for an iPhone 17 with 256GB of storage over a 24-month term. Does Apple Upgrade Charge Interest or Fees? Neither Apple nor Klarna mentions any interest payments. Apple's current iPhone Upgrade Program is a zero-interest installment loan, and so was Apple Pay Later, which the company ditched in 2024. Apple says there are no fees on a monthly lease payment, but notes that you could incur a damage fee at the end of your lease term if you don't take care of the device. There are also fees if you upgrade or terminate a lease early. Plus, if you don't decide what to do at the end of your lease, Klarna will start an "automatic extension period" for up to 6 months. "During this extension, your monthly payment may increase because promotional credits (such as trade-in credits) only apply to the original lease term. If you still make no decision by the end of the extension, Klarna will charge a one-time payment, otherwise known as the Purchase Option Fee, to pay off the device. You will be notified 1 month in advance if your next payment will be the final payment." There were reports that Apple would restrict access to certain apps if payments were late, but sources tell PCMag that's not the case. "If a payment cannot be collected, Klarna will retry," Klarna says. "If that also fails, Klarna will attempt to charge a backup payment method on file. There are no late fees for this program. However, missed payments can eventually be sent to debt collection after multiple failed attempts, and missed payments may be reflected in your credit report." Which Apple Products Can You Lease? While Apple Upgrade is offered for the full iPhone 17 line, some older and budget versions are not available. You cannot use Apple Upgrade for the iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, Apple Watch SE, MacBook Neo, Mac mini, iPad (A16), or Studio Display. What's the Catch? We're glad you asked. There are a few big risks you should understand before you sign up. Apple Upgrade Does Not Include AppleCare+ Apple Upgrade will not include AppleCare+, which protects your device against certain accidental damage. You'll have to add and pay for AppleCare+ Theft and Loss coverage yourself within 60 days of your lease starting. Without that protection included, you're on the hook for any damage. "You may incur damage fees if the device is...not returned in the condition required by the lease," Apple notes. If you don't have AppleCare+ Theft and Loss coverage, and the device is lost or stolen, you'll have to pay an early termination fee or the purchase option fee. If you do nothing, you'll continue to be charged the monthly lease fee. You May Get Trapped in a Cycle of Monthly Payments Much like streaming services require you to pay every month to continue to access your favorite movies, TV shows, and music, Apple Upgrade could keep you hooked on monthly payments for decades. Unlike financing an iPhone or MacBook, Apple Upgrade leases don't cover the full cost of the device, so when the end of your lease term arrives, you'll be on the hook for a large balloon payment, the Purchase Option Fee, if you want to buy your device outright. As an example, let's look at the cost of leasing the iPhone 17 (which starts at $899). Lease prices start at $25.99, so if you leased this phone for 24 months, you'd have paid $623.76 after 24 months. So, you'd need to pay at least another $275.24 to purchase and keep the phone. If you can't afford to make this large lump-sum payment on time, the easiest solution is to lease another device, essentially locking you into another couple of years of monthly payments. Suddenly, you're trapped in an endless cycle of monthly fees for a device you don't even own. Should You Use Apple Upgrade to Lease a New iPhone? There are some scenarios where leasing an Apple product makes sense. Maybe you need a MacBook for grad school, but don't plan to keep it after you graduate. Or, perhaps you're already upgrading to the newest iPhone every year, and leasing will save you money. But even if the math works in your favor, make sure you understand all of the risks before you sign up. About Our Experts As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well. As PCMag's managing editor of operations and evergreen content, I lead the operations, How To, and updates teams. I have 15+ years of experience writing and editing personal finance, small business, and financial software content. Prior to PCMag, I led the personal finance team at CNET. My work has also been published in the Chicago Tribune, NerdWallet, Investopedia, and BestReviews. Personal finance Project management software Tax software Accounting software Identity theft services Antivirus software A PC enthusiast for most of my life, I now work on a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M3) or 13-inch MacBook Air. You won't pry my Android from my hands, though! I have a Samsung S25 that has miraculously survived hundreds of accidental tumbles down my wood staircase. My first desktop was a hand-me-down Power Macintosh in the early '90s, where I spent hours trying not to get eaten by a grue in the game Zork. I'm an avid reader, and though I prefer physical books, I travel with my old Nook GlowLight 3 (yes, they still exist).

item.title: Microsoft Is Forcing a Windows 11 Security Feature That Could Slow Down Your PC
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.42
Many of Windows 11’s best security features aren’t active by default. That includes Memory Integrity protection, which uses hardware-dependent methods to prevent malware from infecting OS processes. In a good move for security, Microsoft is about to enable this Core Isolation feature on “all eligible” Windows 11 PCs. However, doing so will also likely slow down some older Windows 11 PCs. In other news, Windows 11’s big September update is out, which includes the option to move the taskbar. The release adds plenty of other features, too. Microsoft separately announced a new desktop experience called Project Zenith that “represents Windows at its best.” Despite its splashy unveiling, Project Zenith is more about making the OS less irritating for developers than adding any groundbreaking capabilities. Read on for a look at what’s actually happening to your Windows 11 PC’s performance in October, all that's new and notable in the September update, and why Microsoft’s Project Zenith should be a bigger deal for everyone. Memory Integrity Protection: A Security Win, But Older PCs Might Suffer Microsoft says a Windows Update in October will “expand memory integrity protection across all eligible devices.” Note that this feature might already be active on your PC. To check, head to Windows Security > Device Security > Core Isolation Details and look for the Memory integrity setting. As mentioned, Memory Integrity protection guards low-level Windows processes against malware by running trust checks in hardware-based virtual environments. Microsoft’s documentation says it works best with Intel Kabylake or AMD Zen 2 or later processors. The company further explains, “Older processors rely on an emulation of these features, called Restricted User Mode, and will have a bigger impact on performance.” For reference, Intel released the first Kabylake chips in 2016, while AMD released the first Zen 2 models in 2019. When I tested the impact of the Memory Integrity protection setting on a modern desktop PC with an AMD Ryzen 9 9900X CPU by running benchmarks in Doom: The Dark Ages, I couldn't find a difference with it on or off. But if you have an older Windows 10-era PC you upgraded to Windows 11, you might notice a slowdown, especially in online games and other demanding apps. Some modern PC games make you enable Memory Integrity protection; the Vanguard anti-cheat software Riot Games employs for League of Legends and Valorant requires it, for example. The extent of performance decrease will depend on your computer’s CPU and the app in question, but I encourage you to run some benchmarks if you’re unsure. If this feature slows down your PC, you can always turn it off in the Windows Security app after Microsoft enables it in October. If you have a PC with a relatively recent CPU, I doubt you will notice a slowdown. I encourage you to keep Memory Integrity active unless you have a really defensible reason to deactivate it. Patch Tuesday Brings Long-Awaited Taskbar Fixes Microsoft released a major update for Windows 11 on Sept. 8. This month’s Patch Tuesday feature drop includes the movable taskbar, a more configurable Start menu, and an optional Bing-free search experience. Unfortunately, you might not see these features on your PC immediately after installing the update. These features are going through Microsoft’s usual “gradual rollout” process, so they may take weeks to appear on your PC. Beyond the headline features, the patch notes for this update, also known as KB5124008, mention a faster File Explorer experience and a variety of other small design and performance improvements. You might notice smoother switching between virtual desktops and updated progress indicators, for example. Microsoft will likely launch Windows 11’s 26H2 update in October, but it will be a smaller enablement package. Most of Windows 11’s big new features for 2026 have already arrived in updates like this one over the last few months. Project Zenith Removes Distractions (for Developers) Project Zenith “represents Windows at its best,” according to Microsoft’s Logan Iyer, vice president of Windows Platform + Developer. This isn't a new version of Windows, but rather “a ready-to-code, distraction-free Windows experience.” AMD announced the first Project Zenith PCs at IFA 2026 in Berlin. I was able to test a similar experience when I got my hands on an Nvidia RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra at Build several months ago. On these devices, Windows gets a variety of developer-focused tweaks. For example, by default, File Explorer shows file extensions and hidden files, the OS blocks various tips to reduce distractions, and the keyboard-focused PowerToys Command Palette launcher is active. You can apply many of these tweaks to any PC via Microsoft’s Windows Developer Config project, available on GitHub. Or, you can simply customize Windows yourself. Unlike Microsoft’s Copilot+ PCs, which come with exclusive AI features, Project Zenith machines look to streamline Windows as much as possible. Many knowledge workers and average PC users would benefit from a more distraction-free OS experience and would also like to see “Windows at its best” on new PCs, so I hope this thinking extends into the development of Windows 11 itself. Is it time for Microsoft to bring back Signature Edition PCs with clean OS installs? I think many people would be receptive. Ask Our Expert: When Will My PC Get the New Taskbar? Do you have a question about Windows? I’m here to share my knowledge! You can submit your question here, and I may answer it in an upcoming Windows Guide newsletter. If you’re not subscribed to the newsletter, head here to sign up, and check your inbox each week for the latest Windows updates from me. Now, on to this week’s question! A reader asks: “When will I be able to put the taskbar at the top of my screen?” Hi, thanks so much for asking this! With most operating systems, you could simply install the latest update and access the new feature. Unfortunately, Microsoft makes this much more complex. The company’s “gradual rollout” process means I can’t say exactly when you’ll have access. You may already have this feature on your PC as you’re reading this. Or, you might have to wait weeks or even months before Microsoft turns it on. Microsoft slowly activates features like this in waves to avoid problems. Windows Insider builds have a Flags page that lets you toggle features if you don't want to wait, but that system doesn't exist for the stable version of Windows. Technical users might want to experiment with the third-party ViVeTool to forcibly enable specific features, but this could lead to OS problems down the road. I don’t recommend using it. Ultimately, I can’t tell you exactly when you’ll be able to move your taskbar. That’s a shame, and it’s a major problem with Windows. Assuming you’ve visited Settings > Windows Update and installed any available updates, I encourage you to keep checking the Settings > Personalization > Taskbar page over the days and weeks ahead. It should only be a matter of time before it appears. About Our Expert I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: ChatGPT Adds Images 2.5 Model, New Feature Turns Doodles Into AI Photos
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.23
Months after updating ChatGPT’s image generation with Images 2.0, OpenAI on Tuesday released an upgraded model and a new Sketch tool that turns your doodles into high-quality AI-generated imagery. Images 2.5 is currently rolling out to all ChatGPT users on desktop, mobile, and web. Compared with the older model, it reduces image-generation latency by 50% and is better at producing natural light and rich textures, preserving subjects from reference photos, and following edit instructions across multiple iterations, OpenAI says. The model also adds new Templates to help speed up your creative work. Instead of starting from scratch, you can now go to Images > Templates and choose from pre-set formats, including Poster and Merch, to generate desired outputs quickly. Another new tool sees ChatGPT turn your own rough drawings into detailed AI-generated images. Called Sketch, the feature opens a canvas with drawing tools. Just doodle what you have in mind, describe your vision in a short prompt, and the AI will finish the artwork. You can get started by just typing @Sketch in the prompt box. I played around with the tool for a bit, and the results were quite impressive. Though it is being promoted as a sketch-to-AI Image tool, it appears that the prompt you pair with your sketch does much of the heavy lifting. ChatGPT’s new image model arrives just days after OpenAI released GPT-6 Astra. It also introduced a new feature that lets you connect third-party messaging services directly to its chatbot, helping it better understand and emulate your writing style. Disclosure: Ziff Davis, PCMag's parent company, filed a lawsuit against OpenAI in April 2025, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: You Can Get Up to $1,200 Towards an iPhone 18 Pro with Apple's New Carrier Trade-in Incentives
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.22
The iPhone 18 Pro will release on September 18, and if you can't stomach the starting $1,199 price tag, there is some good news. Apple recently increased its trade-in values for the second time this year, making it a little easier to afford one of its new rumored iPhones. And, following the September 9 Apple Event, the tech giant also unveiled new trade-in partner incentives for anyone buying the iPhone 18 Pro. If you're preparing to trade in your old device to shave some cost off the upfront price, here's everything you need to know about Apple's boosted trade-in values and how to make sure your phone is prepped and ready to ship, so you can get the highest value in exchange. Apple's New Carrier Trade-in Incentives for the iPhone 18 Pro Max Apple has partnered with AT&T and T-Mobile to offer up to $1,200 in trade-in credits when you trade in an iPhone 14 or later to put toward a new iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max. You can also trade in your device through Apple, but the maximum trade-in value you can get this way is $885. What's the Trade-in Value for Older iPhones? Apple recently announced its trade-in values for the iPhone 17 line. It also boosted trade-in values for older devices twice this past summer. Here's the max value you can get for each type of iPhone through Apple Trade In: - iPhone 17 Pro Max: $885 - iPhone 17 Pro: $785 - iPhone Air: $585 - iPhone 17: $585 - iPhone 16 Pro Max: $720 (previously $695) - iPhone 16 Pro: $630 (previously $560) - iPhone 16 Plus: $485 (previously $465) - iPhone 16: $480 (previously $460) - iPhone 16e: $310 (no change) - iPhone 15 Pro Max: $530 (previously $490) - iPhone 15 Pro: $420 (previously $410) - iPhone 15 Plus: $340 (previously $325) - iPhone 15: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Pro Max: $405 (previously $375) - iPhone 14 Pro: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Plus: $235 (unchanged) - iPhone 14: $235 (previously $225) What to Do Before Trading in Your Old iPhone Now that you know the maximum trade-in value of your old phone, you'll want to take some steps to make sure it's backed up, unpaired, and cleaned up. Here are the steps you should take before you send in your old device. 1. Back Up Everything First, make sure you don't lose your data. Back everything up before you wipe it from your phone. To back up to iCloud from your device, go to Settings, select your name, and then choose iCloud > iCloud Backup > Back Up Now. To back up to your Mac, connect your iPhone and your computer via a cable or Wi-Fi. If you have macOS Catalina or later, go to Finder, select your iPhone, and then choose General > Back Up All of the Data on Your iPhone to This Mac > Back Up Now. If you have an earlier version or a Windows PC, you'd use iTunes. Open the program, click on the image of your phone, then select Summary > Back Up Now. 2. Unfind Your iPhone Apple’s Find My app can sometimes block activation by a new owner, so you should deactivate the app before you ditch the device. Though Find My is automatically deactivated when you erase all content and settings, which you'll do below, this is still a good step to take as a precaution. Go to Settings, select your name, then choose Find My and disable it for that device. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 3. Sign Out of Messages More than a decade ago, people who switched from iOS to Android without logging out of Messages on their iPhone found that texts were going to the old phone. The problem has since been fixed, but those still scarred by "iMessage purgatory" may want to go to Settings > Apps > Messages and disable iMessage. 4. Unpair Your AirPods Similarly, you can still connect your AirPods to a new iPhone without unpairing them from the old one, but it can't hurt to wipe the slate clean. Place your AirPods and iPhone near each other, then go to Settings > Bluetooth. Tap the information icon next to your AirPods, and select Forget this Device. 5. Unpair Your Apple Watch If you have an Apple Watch, save yourself a potential headache and unpair it from the iPhone you'll be selling. Place them near each other, then open the Apple Watch app on your phone. Go to My Watch > All Watches and select the info circle next to the watch you want to unpair. Tap Unpair Apple Watch and then confirm, which may require you to enter your Apple Account password. With a GPS + Cellular model, you're asked whether you want to keep or remove your cellular plan. Since you're selling the iPhone, you'll want to remove it. (If you don't plan to pair your watch with a new iPhone, you might need to contact your carrier to cancel.) Tap to confirm; you might need to enter your Apple Account password to disable Activation Lock. 6. Sign Out of iCloud You should sign out of iCloud, iTunes, and the App Store before selling your device. Tap Settings, select your name, and choose Sign Out. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 7. Wipe Your iPhone and Delete Data When your new phone is set up and you're ready to trade in or sell your old iPhone, head to Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Erase All Content and Settings, then approve all subsequent prompts. 8. Remove the SIM Card (If You Have One) Apple went the eSIM route starting with the iPhone 14 lineup, but older devices will have a physical SIM card. In most cases, you can just deactivate your cellphone service on the device and trade it in with the SIM card intact. But that SIM card is the repository of your phone number, various bits of security data, and all the info needed for billing. It identifies you, your phone, and a lot of your activity on your phone. So you should remove it before you sell the phone. Fortunately, it's simple. Locate the SIM ejector on your phone, then insert a paper clip until the tray pops out. Remove the SIM card, replace the tray, and say goodbye to your old iPhone. The Best Places to Sell Your Phone I've also included some of the best sites for selling or trading in your phone. Some make it easy to send in your phone and get immediate cash, others let you control the price through bidding, and there are even options for receiving store credit from places you shop. To give you an idea of your trade-in power, I priced out what you can expect to get for an iPhone 15 Pro across all of them, and it varies wildly, as you'll see below. You can also trade your phone in with your existing carrier or switch to a new one. Many offer compelling trade-in promotions, so be sure to check out AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, and others. Apple Trade In The Apple Trade In program pays you with a credit or gift card. If you pay for an Apple device in full up-front, a credit will be applied to your payment card once Apple receives your trade-in device and verifies its condition. If you're paying on an installment plan, the credit will be applied right away. Turning in an iPhone 15 Pro, for example, can get you up to $410 on a new iPhone now that Apple has increased some trade-in values by as much as $35. Best Buy If you're selling your iPhone and just want cash to buy electronics, you can cut out a step at Best Buy: Trade in your phone at a store or mail it in for a digital gift card. For a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition, expect to get about $275. eBay To sell your device yourself, there's always eBay. The site has a quick walkthrough where you can input your phone's stats. After entering my example device, a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro in good condition on Verizon, the page recommended that I list the phone at $510. GameStop Are most of your iPhone apps games? Then you'll probably do well to turn in your iPhone in for some store credit at GameStop. You can also get cold, hard cash for it there. Bring your device to your nearest GameStop, get a price quote from a sales associate, and then receive store credit or cash on the spot. I recommend getting an estimate on the site before you make the trip. I found that a 512GB iPhone 15 Pro from Verizon in very good condition will get you $267.30 in cash or $297.00 in store credit. Swappa Swappa is a marketplace where you can sell your iPhone directly. Select your phone model on the site, upload some photos, and set a price. Once someone buys it, you're paid immediately via PayPal. You're responsible for safely shipping your phone to the buyer. According to the site, an iPhone 15 Pro is selling for an average price of $544, while a trade-in to one of Swappa's partners could get me $311. uSell Want to sell your iPhone fast? One option is uSell. Select your model, carrier, capacity, and condition to receive an offer. If you choose to accept it, you ship your iPhone to uSell for free. If your device is in the condition you said it was, you're paid by check or PayPal. A 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition is currently worth about $268. Editors' Note: Trade-in values were accurate at the time of publication. Your mileage may vary. Chandra Steele contributed to this story About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. item.title: Apple's iPhone 18 Pro Boasts Big Camera Upgrade, and Price Increase
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.05
Apple just announced the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, touting “huge leaps” in the main areas customers want, including a new advanced camera, a powerhouse A20 Pro processor, and even longer battery life. But expect to pay $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pros. Both phones retain the same design as their predecessors, but the internals have been reworked to “deliver the highest sustained performance in iPhone history,” Apple says. In addition, the Dynamic Island at the top now supports three Live Activities at once. What's New in the Camera? Both models boast a 48MP Fusion Main camera, which Apple calls its biggest camera improvement in years. It's built with a variable aperture, rather than a fixed aperture, which controls how much light enters the camera. "Six laser-cut blades smoothly transition between different apertures, making it incredibly easy to capture the best shot by automatically adjusting for depth of field and lighting," Apple says. "Combined with a new sensor that improves image quality, the result is better low-light photography, crisper detail in the back of group photos, and more unique shots," Apple adds. "Variable aperture also provides more control for creative pros by giving them the ability to manually adjust any of the four aperture settings in the Camera app." (For more, see what PCMag's camera expert Jim Fisher has to say about variable aperture.) For video, Pro controls let you adjust settings such as lens aperture, shutter speed, and white balance, or use a histogram to check exposure levels across a scene. Plus, for those concerned about authenticity in the age of AI, a Reference mode will now sign the sensor data to create an unalterable reference image, viewable in the Photos app. It will act like a digital negative, allowing you to visually compare two assets and determine whether any edits were made. Chip and Performance To increase the performance, the phones feature the A20 Pro chip, which uses the latest 2-nanometer manufacturing process to fit more transistors on the silicon, an upgrade from the 3-nanometer node. The chip still contains 6 CPU cores like last year's A19 Pro. But Apple says the A20 features two “Super Cores” designed to be 20% faster and to offer desktop-class performance, alongside the four efficiency cores. The processor also comes with a 50% increase in memory bandwidth over the A19 Pro, so it can run AI workloads locally on the device rather than in the cloud. The new 7-core GPU design on the chip is also up to 40% faster, while Apple has doubled the cores on the AI-focused Neural Engine from 16 to 32. The A20 Pro processor packs enough dense computing power to potentially cause heat issues. In response, Apple touted a next-gen vapor chamber for both models that’s three times larger in surface area than the iPhone 17 Pro, meaning it can also recycle three times as much water through the cooling system. The company also used a “custom packaging” inspired by the MacBook M-series chips to place the silicon die next to the memory, paving the way for a better thermal design. Battery Life The phones promise a “massive leap” in battery life. Apple says the eSIM-only models “can offer up to 36 hours of video playback on iPhone 18 Pro and up to 45 hours of video playback on iPhone 18 Pro Max.” Users can also expect faster charging: up to 50% in 15 minutes, or wireless charging to 50% in 30 minutes. On the iPhone 18 Pro Max, charging for 5 minutes provides about 7 hours of video playback or up to 30 hours of use on a full charge. Price and Storage The iPhones have not escaped Apple's price hikes after all. Both are $100 more expensive than the iPhone 17 Pro lineup. (The iPhone 17, 17e, and iPhone Air are also now $100 more expensive.) iPhone 18 Pro - 256GB: $1,199 - 512GB: $1,399 - 1TB: $1,799 - 2TB: $2,399 iPhone 18 Pro Max - 256GB: $1,299 - 512GB: $1,499 - 1TB: $1,899 - 2TB: $2,499 Release Date and Preorder Both phones launch on Sept. 18, with preorders starting this Saturday, Sept. 12. They come in burgundy, glacier, silver, and black. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Framework Cuts Laptop Pro 13 Pricing After Securing Batch of Cheaper RAM
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.99
After several RAM-related price hikes, modular laptop maker Framework has cut the price of its Laptop 13 Pro after securing a limited batch of cheaper sticks. "We are committed to passing on savings whenever we can and keeping computers as accessible as possible in the current environment, so we are rolling out price reductions across both already shipped and a subset of currently pending preorders," Framework said in a statement. Although Framework has attempted to offer cheaper options for customers, including RAM-less builds, it has been forced to raise prices multiple times as memory costs spun out of control. But with this new batch of cheaper RAM, some Framework customers will end up with some relief. Pending orders configured with 32GB or 64GB of LPCAMM2 will receive priority, with Framework cutting the laptop's price in turn. It will also be issuing refunds to recent customers who could have benefited from the savings, and offering those with existing orders the option to switch to the higher-end configuration to secure the discount. Once those have been fulfilled, new customers will have the opportunity to buy the Laptop 13 Pro with the discounted memory. Framework has also said that if it can source more of the memory at its discounted rate, it will extend the offer to ensure as many of its customers as possible can benefit. Framework doesn't list the actual savings, but even a small cut is notable. Current standalone pricing for LPCAMM2 modules on Framework's website is $800 for the 32GB kit and $1,600 for the 64GB kit, so even shaving $50 off that would be welcome. Framework customers can also take advantage of a new batch of Core Ultra X9 chips. Intel has kept Framework on a tight leash when it came to stock of the high-end mobile processors, but a deal has been struck, and Framework now has a limited quantity of these chips to pass on. The downside is that these chips are more expensive than they were the last time around. As with the memory savings, Framework will give existing shipped orders and preorder customers the option to switch to the newer chip first, then pass the option to new order customers if stock remains. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Starlink Quietly Debuts Router 4, Confirms It Features Wi-Fi 7
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.87
UPDATE: SpaceX has published a better look at the new Router 4. The company has tweeted a video that shows a real device model from all angles. The tweet adds that the router will be "available soon in select areas." Original story: Starlink seems to be close to launching its next-gen Wi-Fi router. On Wednesday, Starlink.com published two support pages mentioning a "Router 4" device. “The Router 4 is our best-performing router yet,” SpaceX says. “It uses a Wi-Fi 7 chipset for faster peak speeds, faster client connections, and increased range. It includes two Ethernet ports, an LED indicator, a factory reset button, and water-resistant port covers.” Both Ethernet ports can support Power over Ethernet (PoE), too. One support page covers a setup guide for the Router 4, while the other compares it to past versions. SpaceX received FCC approval last month to sell a mysterious Wi-Fi 7 router, with the model number UTR-261, an apparent follow-up to the previous products. Starlink.com is now providing more specifics on why it should appeal to subscribers of the satellite internet service. The support pages include a barebones picture of the Router 4, which looks almost identical to the Router Mini, a product that launched last year as a more portable Wi-Fi router, but with limited range. The difference is that the Router 4 appears to be slightly bigger at 8 by 4 by 1.8 inches, rather than 5.4 by 3.3 by 1 inches. The company also says the Router 4 "offers improved performance and range over the Router 3," which SpaceX began selling in 2023 and features the older, but still robust Wi-Fi 6. In our own wireless tests, Wi-Fi 6 routers can offer speeds close to 1Gbps, while Wi-Fi 7 can reach even higher speeds of 2Gbps at close range. However, Starlink can usually only deliver 100Mbps to 300Mbps downloads, meaning the Router 4 won’t offer a major speed boost. Still, SpaceX notes that the Wi-Fi 7 chipset on the Router 4 promises “better performance in congested environments, as well as tri-band radios for enhanced mesh performance," adding, "If your current speed is limited by your Wi-Fi signal, the Router 4 can help improve speeds with its enhanced range and Wi-Fi 7 capabilities." The specs say the Router 4 can provide Wi-Fi coverage up to 3,500 square feet, an increase from about 2,000 square feet for the Router Mini. However, the Router 4 doesn’t support an extra slice of airwaves in the 6GHz bands, only the standard 2.4GHz and 5GHz bands for Wi-Fi 7. For now, it doesn’t look like the official Starlink shop has listed the product, so we don't know how much it costs. Also surprising: the support pages do not mention official support for the recently released V5 Starlink dish, which SpaceX has been making available across the US. Instead, it says: “The Router 4 is compatible with the Router Mini, Standard 4, Standard 4 X, Starlink Mini, Starlink Performance (Gen 1), and the Starlink Standard Circular" dish models. Still, another section says: "Router 4 is the main Wi-Fi router on Dual PoE kits (Standard 4 Upgrade Kit and kits that ship with Router 4). It is powered over Ethernet from the Dual PoE power supply. The Upgrade Kit does not include a wall power brick." This suggests the Router 4 will be bundled with Starlink dishes at some point. Although we’ve only seen the device mentioned on two support pages, its appearance suggests a product launch is imminent. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Sony Revives Its 'Terrific' 2020 Headphones, Lowers Price to $300
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.75
Most gadgets don’t return after they’re discontinued, but Sony doesn’t feel that’s right for its popular, six-year-old WH-1000XM4 headphones. After discontinuing them in 2025, Sony has decided to bring them back with new improvements as a cheaper alternative to its current flagship. Called the WH-1000XM4C, the headphones come with a few improvements over the original model, including updated sound tuning with a 10-band equalizer that Sony says matches “the latest music trends." The same noise-cancellation tech is here, but that's beginning to show its age when compared with the best headphones money can buy in 2026. The design is the same as the 2020 headphones, which many fans will appreciate, as they sport a truly foldable design that makes them more portable than recent flagship Sony options. There's also a new Lavender color alongside the Black and Platinum Silver models. Why would you buy these over the latest WH-1000XM6? Sony is selling them at $299.99 compared with the XM6 at $449.99. However, the XM4C price isn’t much lower than the original XM4, which launched at $349.99 in 2020. Given the rising prices of many gadgets, it felt inevitable that Sony wouldn't drastically lower the price. The original headphones received an Editor’s Choice badge from PCMag, a 4.5 rating in our review, and a Best of the Year 2020 award. Tim Gideon, PCMag's reviewer, said in 2020, “Sony's terrific WH-1000XM4 headphones combine top-notch noise cancellation with audiophile-friendly sound quality." Alongside the revamped headphones, Sony also introduced two cheaper models to its lineup. The WH-CH730N sits in the middle ground at $179.99, with noise-cancellation tech, a foldable design, up to 50 hours of battery life, and features like Precise Voice Pickup Technology for better call quality and LE Audio for better connectivity. The cheapest Sony model is now the WH-CH530, at $69.99. Sony says they're designed for customers seeking "dependable wireless listening at an accessible price," with a 55-hour battery life and six color options of Black, Cobalt, Coral, Mint, Pink, or White. item.title: Trade Show Groups Worry FCC Will Block Foreign Robots, Drones From CES
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.72
White House efforts to ban the sale of foreign-made drones and robots in the US are raising concerns that it could also prevent companies from showcasing them at trade shows like CES. In a Tuesday letter to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, the Exhibitions and Conferences Alliance (ECA) industry group said it’s “heard anecdotally from trade show organizers that some shippers are already declining freight bound for US trade shows this fall.” "America should be where the world comes to see what’s next," ECA President Tommy Goodwin added in a statement. Trade shows routinely display cutting-edge technologies, including robots and drones from Asia, that often wow attendees and offer a preview of what’s to come. However, the ECA says the FCC is preparing a new proposal that’ll tighten US prohibitions on certain foreign-made equipment, a list that already includes robot vacuums, Wi-Fi routers, and power inverters. The proposal seeks to block components made from foreign companies already on an FCC blacklist known as the Covered List, among other measures. But further down, the document also mentions trade shows. Electronic devices with a radio transmitter typically need an FCC equipment authorization before US sale, but the Commission’s 2.805 rule effectively provides an exemption for trade show demonstrations. As a result, prototype robots or drones—which often feature built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth—can be displayed at a US tech conference without an FCC review. However, the FCC seeks public input on whether it should change the 2.805 rule, as well as another rule, 2.1204, that permits vendors to import limited quantities of product without equipment authorization for trade show purposes. The commission is also considering changes to rule 2.803, which covers the “marketing of radio frequency devices prior to equipment authorization,” including at trade shows. The FCC notes rule 2.803 suggests that “entities might still engage in marketing of devices on the Covered List under the guise of permitted ‘preauthorization’ marketing activities, even though such devices cannot receive equipment authorizations under our rules.” “We therefore tentatively conclude that the authority to engage in marketing of radio frequency devices without an authorization should expressly exclude radiofrequency devices that are covered equipment and propose to establish a separate general rule under section 2.803 that prohibits the marketing of covered equipment that was authorized prior to inclusion on the Covered List,” the commission added. In other words, the FCC seems poised to block foreign-made robots and drones from being displayed at trade shows, even as it seeks public comment on its approach. 'The Need for Clarification Is Urgent' In response, the ECA sent an 11-page letter to the FCC, which voices the concerns of 100 groups, including the Consumer Technology Association, which runs CES in Las Vegas. The groups are calling on the FCC to “provide immediate public clarification” that the proposal “does not alter the FCC’s existing tradeshow provisions while this rulemaking is pending. The need for that clarification is urgent.” “Whatever the Commission ultimately decides in this proceeding, that uncertainty is affecting near-term events now,” the letter adds. “Such clarification would give shippers, exhibitors, and organizers greater certainty and help ensure that lawful freight is not unnecessarily rejected for upcoming US events.” The groups support the FCC’s effort to bolster national security. The Trump administration has been targeting foreign-made robots, drones, and Wi-Fi routers over concerns they could be exploited for spying or sabotage. Still, the letter urges the FCC to preserve the “longstanding” rules governing electronic devices that are merely being brought to the US for demos at trade shows and exhibitions. This includes retaining a pathway for equipment on the FCC’s Covered List, such as drones and robots, so that they can still be imported for trade show use. The letter also notes that the commission’s current proposal floats an exemption for the blocked foreign-made equipment when it comes to importing only a small quantity for “testing and evaluation or product development.” Another exemption is being made for “exclusive use of the US Government.” The groups argue: “It would be difficult to justify allowing a limited number of covered devices to enter the country for testing and product development while categorically prohibiting the same devices from entering temporarily for an equally controlled trade show demonstration. Both activities involve limited quantities of equipment for defined purposes rather than general commercial sale or deployment.” The letter adds: “If the Commission concludes that additional national security safeguards are warranted specifically for covered equipment, it should address those concerns through targeted conditions rather than eliminating the tradeshow pathway altogether. For example, the Commission could consider requirements concerning custody and control of demonstration units, documentation of the purpose of importation, prohibition of sale or transfer, and export, retrieval, destruction, or other appropriate disposition following the event.” About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. item.title: Apple AirPods 5 Are Official, Somehow Cheaper Than AirPods 4
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.60
Apple used its latest launch event to introduce its fifth-generation AirPods, which come in two different versions. For this latest generation, the more advanced option is $20 cheaper than the equivalent AirPods 4 model. The cheapest option is $129, while a more advanced pair cost $149. Both versions are up for preorder later today, ahead of a Sept. 18 launch. Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) is now available across both standard AirPods models, and it's better than on the AirPods 4. Apple claims each offers up to 50% more noise reduction than its predecessor, calling it the "best ANC on the market" for an open-ear design. A new Adaptive Audio feature lets the headphones change ANC settings depending on what's happening around you. "Providing the best of both worlds, Adaptive Audio dynamically blends Transparency mode and ANC based on the conditions of a user’s environment," Apple says. Both models feature a redesign of the earbuds' internals, which Apple says includes a new multi-port acoustic architecture and its next-generation adaptive equalizer to deliver better audio than previous models. "This makes Personalized Spatial Audio more immersive and dynamic, so the user feels like they’re surrounded by whatever they are listening to," Apple says. How do the two models differ? The design is largely similar, but the more expensive option comes with enhanced controls built into the earbud's stem, similar to those on AirPods Pro. There's also an extra hour of battery life on the more expensive model, plus a wireless-charging-compatible case. The basic AirPods 5 feature four hours of listening time and 20 hours with their paired case. The more expensive option comes with five hours of listening and 22 hours with the wireless charging case. The earbuds also come with new tied-in features that pair with other Apple services, such as access to the upgraded AI-powered Siri in iOS 27 and Live Translation on iPhone. Apple's event today also introduced the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and a foldable iPhone Duo. Apple didn't announce the long-rumored redesigned AirPods Pro, which are now expected to land next year. Rumors suggest Apple may include built-in cameras to monitor your surroundings for AI-powered features. item.title: Forget Foldables: Apple's 2nm M6 and Quad-Die Monster Just Reset the AI Race
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.57
While all eyes are on Apple's iPhone 18 event, the company's most aggressive technical leap is happening in Mac desktops. Debuting in September across updated Mac mini and Mac Studio desktops, the new M6 and M5 Ultra chips are a generational leap forward for Apple silicon. This latest wave of silicon goes beyond standard speed gains, representing a shift in Apple's architectural roadmap and placing major emphasis on AI. With a new 2nm manufacturing process on M6 and quad-die scaling on M5 Ultra, it's an evolution of Apple's most advanced chip architecture, and an increased emphasis on local AI capability for privacy-first, on-device AI compute and power for agentic AI that runs continuously in the background. For starters, the announcement introduces the M6 processor, the first of what is sure to be a wider family of sixth-generation Apple silicon. It also brings the M5 Pro to Mac desktops for the first time—that chip debuted on the MacBook Pro last spring—and pushes the Mac Studio into the M5 generation with the M5 Max and an all-new M5 Ultra, which expands on past Ultra chips with a new quad-die architecture. Apple M6 CPU Chip and the New Core Hierarchy Leading the generational transition is the M6, Apple’s first chip built on a cutting-edge 2-nanometer (2nm) lithography process. The node advancement packs greater transistor density into a smaller footprint, driving significant performance-per-watt efficiency gains. The 2nm process tech is also a step up from the "3nm Class" label Apple used for all its M5-series chips. That name was an umbrella designation for several 3-nanometer nodes and variants. They all shared the same underlying architecture, but differed in power, performance, and density parameters, hence the hedging in the name. The M6 introduces a newly structured 12-core CPU complex comprising two high-frequency super cores for peak single-threaded performance, four performance cores for demanding multithreaded tasks, and six efficiency cores for background tasks. Apple introduced the idea of "super cores" last spring, reclassifying its most recent high-performance cores under that name. With amped-up single-thread speeds and boosted throughput, Apple considered the new cores worthy of a new classification and a move to three core tiers: - Super cores: Peak single-thread speed - Performance cores: The new multithreaded workhorses - Efficiency cores: For power saving, and now only on the base M5 and M6 Combined with a dual 16-core Neural Engine and a 12-core GPU featuring integrated Neural Accelerators on every core, the M6 delivers, Apple says, up to four-times faster AI performance and up to 13.5-times faster LLM prompt processing than the M1 generation. Apple's Big M5 Ultra With Quad-Die Scaling While the M6 introduces 2nm technology, Apple is pushing its M5 architecture to extreme levels with the M5 Ultra. By upgrading its proprietary UltraFusion interconnect technology, Apple bridged two dual-die M5 Max chips to form its first quad-die system-on-a-chip (SoC). Operating across ultra-low-latency links with more than 4.4 terabytes per second of inter-die bandwidth, the four dies behave as a single unified processor, the company claims. This quad-die architecture enables the M5 Ultra to scale up to a massive 36-core CPU (12 super cores, 24 performance cores) and an 80-core GPU. Crucially, Apple integrated dedicated Neural Accelerators into every GPU core across both the M5 and M6 chip families, placing hardware-accelerated matrix multiplication directly inside the graphics pipeline. Next-Gen Unified Memory and Multi-Mac Networks Central to running large-scale AI models is Apple's high-bandwidth unified memory architecture. The base M6 provides up to 32GB of memory at 170GBps bandwidth, while the M5 Ultra scales to a staggering 512GB capacity with 1.2TBps of memory bandwidth—a 50% increase over the M3 Ultra. For enterprise workloads that exceed a single system's capacity, desktop units equipped with Thunderbolt 5 support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) clustering. By networking up to four Mac Studio or Mac mini desktops together over 120Gbps Thunderbolt 5 links, you can build a shared memory pool that delivers up to three-times faster distributed LLM inference, according to Apple. How Will M5 Ultra and M6 Improve AI on Macs? These architectural upgrades aren't just about speeding up everyday apps; they directly target local AI adoption. By pairing high memory ceilings with dedicated matrix acceleration, the new Mac lineup runs high-parameter models (such as Mistral, FLUX, and Gemma) entirely on-device, bypassing subscription token fees, network latency, and data privacy risks. On the software side, macOS 27 Golden Gate introduces Core AI and MLX framework enhancements alongside a new integrated Siri AI assistant. These built-in optimizations are designed for apps such as LM Studio, Draw Things, Cinema 4D, and Final Cut Pro. But they should also allow better support for developer tools and productivity agents—including Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Perplexity Personal Computer—to execute multi-step autonomous actions smoothly in the background. M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio: Pricing and Availability Today's chip announcements come alongside news about new-for-2026 Mac mini and Mac Studio models. Preorders for both desktop lines open today, with availability beginning Sept. 22: - Mac mini (M6): Starts at $899 ($799 for education customers), a $100 price hike over its predecessor, offset by the upgraded 12-core CPU/GPU layout and Dual Neural Engine - Mac mini (M5 Pro): Starts at $1,699 ($1,599 for education) - Mac Studio (M5 Max): Starts at $2,499 ($2,299 for education) - Mac Studio (M5 Ultra): Starts at $5,499 ($5,099 for education), with the top-tier 512GB unified memory configuration arriving in late October About Our Expert From the laptops on your desk to satellites in space and AI that seems to be everywhere, I cover many topics at PCMag. I've covered PCs and technology products for over 15 years at PCMag and other publications, among them Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, and TWICE. As a hardware reviewer, I've handled dozens of MacBooks, 2-in-1 laptops, Chromebooks, and the latest AI PCs. As the resident Starlink expert, I've done years of hands-on testing with the satellite service. I also explore the most valuable ways to use the latest AI tools and features in our Try AI column.

item.title: Everything Apple Announced at Its Sept. 9 Event: iPhone Duo, 18 Pro, AirPods, More
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.55
After months of rumors, Apple just showed off its next-gen devices, marking the formal debut of John Ternus as CEO. Apple is shaking things up this year. We won't see a standard iPhone 18 until next year; this week's event is all about the Pro versions, and making room for a new Apple form factor: the foldable iPhone Duo. But don't forget about new Apple Watches and AirPods. PCMag's Eric Zeman, Florence Ion, and Andrew Gebhart are on the ground in Cupertino to bring you all the news. They'll go hands on with the new devices soon; until then, check out all the details in our live blog below and Apple's replay above. And tune in for post-show coverage from PCMag's Executive Producer, Iyaz Akhtar, and CNET Editor at Large, Bridget Carey. About Our Expert I started out covering tech policy in DC for The National Journal, where my beat included state-level tech news and all the congressional hearings and FCC meetings I could handle. item.title: The Real Truth Behind the iPhone 18 Pro's New Variable Aperture
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.24
While unveiling the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple highlighted a cool new camera feature—variable aperture. It's uncommon among smartphones, though not a first, and will come in handy for some types of photos. Of course, in its typical fashion, Apple delivered news of the upgrade from within its reality distortion field to maximize hype. I've been reviewing cameras for more than 15 years, so I'm here to explain what variable aperture is, why you'd want it, and when you'll still need an add-on filter to reduce the amount of light entering the lens. The Basics: How Aperture Controls Light and Focus If you've only ever used a smartphone for photography, you're used to lenses that work at one and only one aperture, also called f-stop. In plain language, the aperture is a numerical value that indicates how much light a lens lets in and projects onto a digital image sensor. Phones tend to use wide-aperture lenses that let in as much light as possible to capture good photos in tough light, and default to very short shutter speeds when taking photos or videos out in the sun. The main lens of the iPhone 17 Pro has an f/1.78 aperture, which is considered quite bright and ideal for taking photos in dimly lit environments. A variable aperture uses a set of blades that close down from the sides to block some of the incoming light. Getting less light into the system lets you more easily use longer shutter speeds to introduce some motion blur, and increases the depth of field, the fancy technical term for how much of a scene is in sharp focus. One bit of housekeeping: Apertures are expressed in fractions, so a smaller number means that more light is coming in. One Lens Only: The Fine Print The iPhone 18 Pro's main lens is rated for f/1.48, which means that when it's used with the aperture wide open, it is more sensitive to light than the 17 Pro's f/1.78 lens. But instead of being stuck wide open like the 17 Pro, the 18 Pro includes a six-blade diaphragm that closes down to f/1.8, f/2.8, or f/4.0. The iPhone 18 Pro adds a variable aperture to its main lens and redesigns its optics to gather more light. When used with the Camera app in automatic mode, the f-stop changes automatically based on the light. If you're taking photos in a dimly lit interior, it'll open to f/1.48 to let in as much light as possible. For beach days and sunny landscapes, the phone will narrow the diaphragm to reduce light. One note: The variable aperture is only included in the main 24mm wide-angle lens; it's not available on the ultra-wide (13mm) or telephoto (100mm) lenses. Those are unchanged from the iPhone 17 Pro. Unlocking Creative Exposure With Pro Controls You don't have to be stuck with automatic adjustments, however. Apple includes manual exposure settings, called Pro Controls, for both photography and video. These let you adjust various aspects of your exposure, including shutter speed, aperture, and white balance. Knowledgeable photographers can use manual settings, along with the variable aperture, to take more creative control over their pictures. There are two main reasons to use a small aperture. The first is depth of field. The iPhone 18 Pro's f/1.48 lens and Type 1 image sensor will be able to create some optical blur in the right situation. iPhone photographers are used to having to go into Portrait mode and use depth mapping to blur backgrounds, but given the physics behind the 18 Pro's camera system, it will achieve similar effects when the camera is positioned close to a subject and there is some distance between it and the background or foreground. I don't anticipate the iPhone 18 Pro giving you the soft-background bokeh look without portrait mode in many situations, even when the lens opens all the way to f/1.48. Once you put enough distance between the camera and the subject, everything is in focus from an optical standpoint. Using f/2.8 or f/4 may result in slightly sharper backgrounds, but not enough to notice on a 6-inch phone screen or in a social media post. Now, sunstars are another matter. Apple showed off the iPhone 18 Pro's ability to produce bright highlights with dramatic spikes. That's something that happens optically, not computationally. When light passes through an aperture, it takes on its shape, and narrower f-stops can make light particles scatter, an effect called diffraction. These diffraction spikes, commonly called sunstars in the photo world, can add drama to landscapes, cityscapes, and portraits. You won't see them in every photo, but they're easy to get if you catch a bright reflection off a piece of jewelry, bits of sunlight peeking through leaves, or sunlight on the surface of water. The Physical Limits: Why You Still Need an ND Filter The second reason to cut incoming light is to achieve long-exposure effects. I like to use a half-second shutter speed to smooth out flowing water for landscape photos that include streams and waterfalls, and I will go even longer for urban landscapes where I want to blur out pedestrians and cars. Videographers will try for what's called a 180-degree shutter angle to record motion with just a touch of blur, an effect that reads as more cinematic. To get this angle, you want to set your shutter speed to half of your frame rate—1/48-second for 24fps, 1/60-second for 30fps, and so on. For interiors, night scenes, and twilight, the f/1.48-4.0 aperture range will give you enough leeway for photos that intentionally blur motion and cinematic shutter angles, but it's likely to fall short under sunny skies. You'll still want to add a neutral density (ND) filter over the lens if you want to get some motion blur in bright light. I'm surprised that Apple didn't add computational tricks to boost its variable-aperture lens in these types of scenes. Granted, I haven't tested the phone yet, so it could simply be something Apple chose not to mention. Is Variable Aperture Worth the Hype? I plan to test the limits of the iPhone 18 Pro's camera for long exposures and other creative shots as soon as possible. On the surface, variable aperture feels like a nice addition, but it's far from a game-changer. If you're a casual snapper who just wants to capture moments with your phone, you won't ever have to think about the aperture. Apple's Camera app will decide where to set it, and you'll still want to use Portrait mode for a blurred background, because in most situations, optical blur won't deliver the bokeh look. Knowledgeable photographers and videographers will get more mileage from the f/1.48-4.0 adjustment range and should be savvy enough to recognize its limitations. If you're in this group, you'll still want to add a neutral density filter. And don't worry, you'll have the option if you want—as I write this, the iPhone has been public for all of 90 minutes, and I've already received an email from Moment, one of the biggest makers of photo and video accessories for smartphones, letting me know that it has an adjustable Variable ND filter ready for the iPhone 18 Pro. Apple's latest killer feature isn't enough to kill the accessory market. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: Is Your TV Spying on You? The Hidden Setting Watching Everything You Do (And How to Stop It)
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.99
Your TV might be watching you. Automated Content Recognition (ACR) is a feature that can identify what you're watching to target ads and suggest content. The TV manufacturer can then sell that data to any company that wants to understand your (and everyone's) viewing habits. It's available on all major smart TV platforms and is usually enabled by default on newer TVs. Even if the device manufacturer or platform holder says the data is private, secure, and anonymized, the tech is still invasive. In fact, it's probably more invasive than you might think. I'm here to explain the privacy concerns associated with ACR and show you how to turn it off. Why Streaming Services Already Know Exactly What You Watch Anything you watch on a video streaming service is identifiable the moment you select it. That's just how streaming works. You choose a movie in an app, and the app contacts a server with that movie's name to determine which stream to send to your TV. If it's a service you sign in to, like Netflix, it'll connect your account to the movie you want to watch. The service uses that information as a convenience; after all, that's how it displays your viewing history, creates recommended watch lists, and resumes where you left off if you stop watching a movie before you finish it. If it's an ad-supported platform like Tubi that doesn't require you to log in, it can still track your viewing habits using your device's IP address or other identifying data. For example, let's say I want to watch the criminally underrated comedy-action Hudson Hawk on Pluto TV. I open the app on my TV, select the movie, and start watching. Pluto TV will know that I want to stream the movie because I chose it in its app. And if I log into my Pluto TV account to bookmark it, the service will recognize that I love Hudson Hawk and might suggest similar movies. It's simple and direct, identifying what I'm watching by its title. The service can track me, but what can I do? It's just how it works. The Bigger Threat: How Your TV Identifies Anything You Play—Even Offline ACR doesn't handle app-level data, as in the video streaming example above. Instead, it watches or listens to what you're streaming and uses that information for the TV maker's purposes. ACR analyzes everything that goes through your TV and looks for giveaways hidden in the audio or video signal. Those digital fingerprints let ACR know what you're watching, no matter which app, service, or media format you're using. As another example, let's say I want to watch Hudson Hawk on Blu-ray. I put the disc in the player (or play it from my NAS after ripping it), switch my TV to the right input, and start the film. ACR can hear Bruce Willis and Danny Aiello's duet of Bing Crosby’s "Swinging on a Star" and recognize that I'm watching Hudson Hawk. The fact that it's playing from a physical disc, not the internet, won't stop the ACR on my TV from identifying it. In fact, recent reports revealed that certain LG smart TVs were found logging nearby Wi-Fi-connected devices and capturing microphone audio even when the screen was off. How to Disable ACR (Before Your TV Collects More Data) Fortunately, you can turn off ACR, but you must dig through menus to do so. And the tech almost always has a unique name, depending on the TV brand and platform. It can also differ depending on your TV's age, since interfaces often rearrange menus when they’re updated over time. With that in mind, here's a general guide on how to disable ACR on most popular TVs. Amazon Fire TVs Amazon's Fire TV platform is used not only by Amazon but also by companies like Hisense and Panasonic. ACR might go by slightly different names on those TVs, but on first-party Fire TVs, it's simply called Automatic Content Recognition. Navigate to Settings > Preferences > Privacy Settings > Automatic Content Recognition. Turn that off, along with Device Usage Data, Collect App, and Over-The-Air Data.
