LG TVs LG TVs call ACR Live Plus, and its setting is buried pretty deep. To deactivate it, visit Settings > General > System > Advanced Settings > Live Plus. Once there, turn off Live Plus, along with any other similar-sounding options you might be concerned about. Other TVs - Roku: Go to Settings > Privacy > Smart TV Experience. To disable ACR, uncheck Use Information for TV Inputs. - Samsung: On older models, go to Settings > Support and scroll down to Terms & Policies. Here, you’ll want to turn off Viewing Information Services (Samsung’s ACR technology) and Interest-Based Advertising (for personalized ad tracking). On newer models, go to Settings > All Settings > General & Privacy > Terms & Privacy. Select and turn off Viewing Information Services and Interest-Based Advertising. - Sony: Go to Settings > Initial Setup, then choose Interactive TV Settings or Samba Interactive TV (Sony's ACR equivalent), and set it to off. - Vizio: Press the MENU button on your TV's remote or head to HDTV Settings on the TV. Go to System > Reset & Admin > Highlight Viewing Data. Press the right arrow to turn off the setting. Your TV Isn't the Only Thing Tracking You There are many ways your personal online habits might not be so personal, with tracking and data mining extending beyond your TV. For even more protection, check out these 10 essential apps for protecting your privacy. Likewise, consider getting a VPN for your computer and other devices. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s home theater and AR/VR expert, and your go-to source of information and recommendations for game consoles and accessories, smart displays, smart glasses, smart speakers, soundbars, TVs, and VR headsets. I’m an ISF-certified TV calibrator and THX-certified home theater technician, I've served as a CES Innovation Awards judge, and while Bandai hasn’t officially certified me, I’m also proficient at building Gundam plastic models up to MG-class. I also enjoy genre fiction writing, and my urban fantasy novel, Alex Norton, Paranormal Technical Support, is currently available on Amazon.

item.title: Avira Free Security Review: Strong Core Protection Paired With Heavy Upgrade Upsells
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.83
Antivirus protection for your PC is imperative, even if you can’t afford it. If your budget is limited, choose a free antivirus tool. Avira Free Security, for example, goes beyond just antivirus, offering VPN, password management, ad blocking, and more. It’s not a typical security suite, though—you won’t find firewall protection, backup, spam filtering, or other common suite components. And many of its features are fully or partially reserved for paying customers. If you're after a slimmed-down free suite, Avast One Free is a better choice. For free protection focused on core antivirus features, try AVG AntiVirus Free. These two are our Editors' Choice winners for free antivirus apps. Avira is owned by Gen Digital. Gen also owns Avast, AVG, LifeLock, Norton, and a host of other companies. This giant collection didn’t happen all at once. In 2016, Avast acquired AVG. Before long, the two product lines were using the same antivirus engine. Around the same time, Norton acquired LifeLock. In 2020, Norton acquired Avira. Shortly thereafter, Avira acquired BullGuard, but within a couple of years, Norton shut down the BullGuard brand and migrated its customers to Norton AntiVirus. Rounding out the collection, Norton acquired Avast/AVG in 2021 and created Gen as the parent company for all. Since 2023, Avast, AVG, and Norton have all relied on the same antivirus engine, called the Gen Stack. Not surprisingly, all three earned precisely the same scores in my hands-on malware blocking test. As you’ll see below, Avira scored the same as the other three. It’s not officially using the Gen Stack, but it still lined right up with the rest. Avira’s installer is seriously self-sufficient. Once you click Agree & Install, it prompts you to take a few minutes to complete the process. You can choose to continue with a free installation or purchase a license to upgrade to Avira Prime. After installation, Avira offers to run a Smart Scan. I skipped that initial scan for testing purposes. Avira’s main Status screen displays oversized icons for Security, Privacy, and Performance. A simple menu down the left lets you dig into these three feature areas or return to the Status home page. Finally, you can click a button to run the all-in-one Smart Scan. If you don’t run a Smart Scan immediately after the quick, simple installation, the antivirus will keep nagging you until you do. Smart Scan checks for active malware, of course, but it does a lot more. It analyzes your settings to identify privacy issues, looks for ways to improve performance, identifies apps that need updating, and checks the network for potential security issues. More about Smart Scan below. To supplement my hands-on testing of antivirus apps, I turn to regularly issued reports from five independent labs worldwide. The simple fact that a given antivirus appears in a report means that the lab’s experts considered it significant enough to warrant testing and reporting. The more lab results, the better, and, of course, high scores are important. When last tested, Avira had high marks from three of these labs. This time around, its lab scores are sparse and poor. Of the many reports from AV-Comparatives, I follow three. This lab doesn’t use numbers. Rather, an antivirus that passes the test earns Standard certification. Those that go beyond the basics can earn Advanced or Advanced+ certification. In this lab’s latest tests, Avast, AVG, Bitdefender Antivirus Free for Windows, Kaspersky, and Norton AntiVirus Plus managed three Advanced+ ratings. In the lab's most recent report, Avira earned one Advanced+ and one Standard certification but failed the essential Malware Protection Test. The latest test doesn’t include Avira. With SE Labs, certification comes in five levels: AAA, AA, A, B, and C. In the past, Avira routinely took AAA certification in this test, but it hasn’t appeared in this lab’s reports for the last couple of years. The latest report from this lab shows nothing but AAA and AA results. AVLab Cybersecurity Foundation is the most recent addition to my cadre of labs worldwide. Its antivirus efficacy test yields a simple percentage score. Of the products included in its latest report, all but one reached 100%. That collection of test products did not include Avira. Researchers at AV-Test Institute evaluate each antivirus on three distinct criteria. Naturally, they measure its ability to protect against malware. They also score apps on how well they avoid erroneously flagging legitimate processes as malicious, an index they call usability. And they ensure the antivirus does all this without dragging down performance. An antivirus can earn up to six points for each of the three criteria. More than half the apps tested in this lab’s latest report reached a perfect 18. Avira matched those winners in the protection and usability tests, with a perfect 6. But some serious performance problems dragged that score down to 4.5, for a total of 16.5 points, the lowest score among the tested apps. As you can see, most labs offer a range of scores to reflect varying levels of capability. Tests by London-based MRG-Effitas are scored differently. In this lab’s reports, an antivirus either exhibits near-perfect protection or fails utterly. In this lab’s all-inclusive consumer assessment, an app that totally blocks every malware attack passes at level 1. An app that misses some initially but wipes out the malware within 24 hours passes at level 2. Anything else is a failure. In the last test, only Malwarebytes Premium Security reached level 1. The rest came in at Level 2, or simply failed. Avira wasn’t tested. Since all the labs use different scoring systems, I’ve devised an algorithm that maps the scores onto a 10-point scale and generates an aggregate score. As noted, I also consider inclusion by more labs preferable. At present, only Avast and Norton appear in reports from all five, both with an aggregate score of 9.8 points. Bitdefender also holds a 9.8-point aggregate lab score, though its results come from just four labs. Also tested by four labs, ESET NOD32 Antivirus, Malwarebytes, and McAfee AntiVirus scored 9.4, 8.4, and 7.2, respectively. As for Avira, with results from just one lab and a failure among those results, it comes in at 7.0 points. I hope to see its scores back up by my next review. Lab results notwithstanding, I always perform my own hands-on tests. I start by opening a folder of malware samples that I've curated and analyzed myself. Avira immediately started quarantining those that it recognized. It eliminated 74% of the samples on sight, which is rather low. Avast, AVG, and Norton caught 85% at this stage. McAfee managed 91%, and Sophos Home Premium tops the bunch with 98% of the same set of malware samples eliminated on sight. On the plus side, Avira eliminated every ransomware sample on sight. After recording Avira’s initial reaction, I launched the samples that had passed this initial culling. Looking at both samples eliminated on sight and those caught after they launched, Avira detected 97% of the samples and scored 9.7 out of 10 possible points, the same scores achieved by Avast, AVG, and Norton. In the winners’ circle, Sophos and Malwarebytes both detected 99% overall and scored 9.9 and 9.8 points, respectively. For many years, Avira’s full scan happened in a separate window titled Luke Filewalker. I don’t know whether George Lucas found out about it, but the slightly cheesy Luke Filewalker window vanished several years ago and was replaced by fully integrated scan reporting. A full scan of a clean test system took 75 minutes, a bit faster than when I last tested Avira, and a lot faster than the current average of 120 minutes. A repeat scan took the same amount of time, suggesting that Avira doesn’t attempt to optimize scanning the way some competitors do. For example, a repeat scan by Bitdefender or ESET completed in around 8% of the time required for the first scan. Avira offers several browser extensions for Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Opera. These include a password manager, a shopping helper, and the security-centric Browser Safety extension. Browser Safety aims to prevent malware infection by steering your browser away from malware-hosting URLs. Do be sure to enable Browser Safety. Note that the Web Protection feature, whose toggle you see on the Protection Options page, is a separate feature and not included in this free suite. To test this feature, I start with a feed of malware-hosting URLs recently discovered by researchers at the British lab MRG-Effitas. I launch each URL, discarding any that are already defunct, and note whether the antivirus blocked all access to it, prevented the malware from being downloaded, or did nothing. I give equal credit for blocking the URL and for eliminating the download. Last time around, Avira aced this test, achieving 100% protection. This time, it managed 92%, evenly split between blocking access to the malware-hosting URL and eliminating the malware during download. Panda Free Antivirus reached 100% in its own test, while Aura, Emsisoft Anti-Malware, Sophos, and UltraAV managed 99%. Coding a Trojan horse or other malicious program that can steal passwords while evading antivirus utilities is a tough slog. Tricking unsuspecting consumers into foolishly handing over their login credentials is much easier. Phishing fraudsters simply create a website that’s visually identical to, say, PayPal. Sometimes, they manage a URL that’s close to the real thing, like paypal.loginuser.com. When an unwitting web surfer logs in, the fraudsters capture the username and password, and that unfortunate netizen is hosed. Yes, you can learn to spot fraudulent sites, but the best antivirus apps handle phishing protection even when you’re tired or muzzy. Avira’s web protection also detects and averts these phishing attacks. To test it, I first scraped hundreds of reported phishing URLs from websites that track such activity, including both verified fraud and pages that were too new to be blocklisted. I launched each URL in a browser protected by Avira, and simultaneously in Chrome, Edge, and Firefox, relying on each browser’s built-in protection. I discarded any that didn’t load properly in all four browsers. I also discarded any that didn’t clearly fit the profile of a phishing fraud. When I got enough data points, I ran the numbers. Just as when last tested, Avira hit the top—100% detection. A dozen recent apps have reached 100% detection in their latest tests, among them Guardio, Norton, Surfshark One, and Webroot Essentials. Phishing is completely platform-independent. If you can browse the web on your internet-aware refrigerator, you can give up your login credentials there just as easily as on your computer. However, third-party phishing protection isn’t necessarily the same across platforms. Some antivirus utilities earn wildly different scores on Windows than on macOS. Avira shields you from fraud in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Opera across all operating systems. Tested at the same time, Avira Free Antivirus for Mac earned the same perfect score. Selecting Security from the left-rail menu opens the Security page, which offers access to five security features: Virus scans, Protection options, Quarantine, Software updater, and Firewall. Selecting the Virus scans panel lets you launch a quick or full scan. By default, Avira schedules a weekly quick scan. Clicking Manage scans lets you schedule a full scan daily, weekly, or monthly. You can also schedule or run scans focusing on removable drives, active processes, or Windows system files. Once the antivirus has trapped some prey, you can click Quarantine to see just what it bagged. Here, you can permanently delete found threats or, in the very unlikely event of a false positive, restore legitimate programs that got quarantined. Clicking the Protection options panel reveals some features you don’t get for free. In the free edition, only Real-time protection is enabled. If you try to enable web or ransomware protection, you'll see a page advising you to upgrade to Avira Prime. If you decline, Avira offers a 60-day Prime trial to tempt you. Do note that web protection is a browser-independent component, completely distinct from Browser Safety. When ne’er-do-wells discover security holes in popular programs, they exploit them to the max, knowing that the program’s maker will soon release a security patch to close them. If you don’t install available patches, you put yourself at risk. The Software Updater component scans your installed apps and flags any of them that have outstanding security patches. The scan doesn’t take long and lists any important apps and components that need significant updates. A big Update All button looks tempting, but clicking it just takes you to an upsell page for Avira Software Updater Pro. Clicking the Update button next to an outdated app opens an Avira Prime upsell window that, for common programs like Chrome and Firefox, includes a link to manually perform the update. Indeed, it’s easy enough to just open each listed app and update it yourself. Avast's product line has a similar app update feature, even in the free edition. But here again, you don't get automated installation unless you spring for the top-of-the-line Avast One suite. Clicking the big Firewall button opens a window showing the status of Avira Firewall and the built-in Windows Firewall. Alas, clicking the Turn on button for Avira Firewall diverts you to an upsell page for Avira Antivirus Pro. Free users can turn the built-in Windows Firewall on and off, or switch its profile between public and private, but that’s all. When you click the Privacy option in the left-rail menu, you get six useful privacy-related components: Browser safety, VPN, Passwords, File Shredder, Privacy settings, and Secure Browser. Clicking Browser safety installs the Avira extension in your default browser (provided that your default is Chrome, Edge, Firefox, or Opera). I’ve already discussed how that feature can steer users away from malicious and fraudulent sites, but it can do more if you allow it. Browser Safety: Beyond Blocking Dangerous Websites Click the Browser safety toolbar button and click the settings gear to see this extension’s capabilities. By default, it just sends a Do Not Track header with every web page request from the browser, something most browsers can do themselves. Since websites are free to ignore this header, it’s pointless. For actual protection, you must turn on blocking web trackers. Once you’ve enabled the feature, Avira watches for tracking ads and other third-party trackers and actively stops them from tracking you. A numeric overlay on the browser extension button shows the total number of items blocked, and you can click the button for a breakdown. You can disable blocking for specific sites, but you don’t get the option to exempt certain trackers. Avira also installs its Safe Shopping extension, though I found I had to enable it manually. Safe Shopping aims to keep you from paying too much online. Its shopping cart icon turns red when you’re on a site that has been verified as safe to shop on. I spent a little time poking around shopping sites and searching for popular items. In past reviews, I’ve managed to trigger notifications of a better price elsewhere (though often the price was worse, not better). This time around, it offered coupon codes on every major site I visited, but no “better deal” pop-ups. Dedicated online shoppers may find this feature useful. VPN: Avira’s Free VPN Comes With Serious Limitations The VPN component is an integrated and feature-limited version of Avira Phantom VPN. The full-scale VPN can connect to 48 locations in 35 countries. More than half the locations are in Europe, and another 30% in North America. That geographic spread doesn’t matter to free users, as the VPN decides which server you’ll use (typically the nearest). In addition, the free VPN caps your bandwidth at 500MB per month. I found that watching a random YouTube video for five minutes used up almost 20% of my monthly allowance. Removing those limitations costs $117 per year (after a first-year discount). Paying for the all-inclusive Avira Prime is another (and better) way to get unlimited VPN protection. Clicking the Advanced Settings link takes you away from the main Avira app and opens a separate free instance of Phantom VPN, with all the same limitations. From this separate app, you can enable the VPN’s ability to block malicious websites, connect automatically when on specified networks, and launch at Windows startup. The kill switch, which blocks all traffic when the VPN connection drops, is a premium-only feature. Bitdefender includes a similarly limited VPN with a more generous bandwidth limit of 200MB per day. Lifting Bitdefender’s limits costs $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year, a good bit less than Avira charges. Password Manager: Handles the Basics But No More The password manager installs as a browser extension in Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Opera for Windows or macOS, and offers apps for Android and iOS. It handles basic tasks like capturing login credentials you enter, replaying them as needed, and syncing across all your devices. You can enable multi-factor authentication, which functions by texting a code to your smartphone. But it doesn’t offer form-filling, secure sharing, digital inheritance, or other top-tier features. Avira Password Manager is available separately as a free app with a premium upgrade. See our full review of the password manager to learn more. File Shredder: Delete Files Securely When you delete a file, it just goes to the Recycle Bin. That’s handy in case you deleted the wrong file, but not so good if you’re trying to wipe out sensitive data, such as the plaintext original of a sensitive file you encrypted. Even if you empty the Recycle Bin, forensic software can often recover deleted files. To delete files beyond the possibility of forensic recovery, just drop them on Avira’s File Shredder. Bitdefender, McAfee, and Webroot, among others, offer a similar feature. Some file shredding utilities let you choose the number of times they overwrite data before deletion, or choose specific algorithms such as the three-pass version preferred by the Department of Defense or the way-overpowered 35-pass Gutmann algorithm. Webroot can overwrite files seven times and wipe all traces, which is sufficient to foil even forensic hardware recovery. Avira doesn’t disclose its algorithm, but even a single overwrite pass is enough to prevent software-based recovery. Privacy Settings: Take Control of Your Privacy The most significant component on the Privacy page is Privacy Settings. If not configured correctly, Windows and popular apps can potentially leak information about your computer and browser usage. Avira puts you in control of over 140 settings across 17 categories, including Sharing data with Microsoft, Telemetry and user experience, Edge configuration, and OneDrive. A single click can align all your settings with Avira’s expert recommendations. Alternatively, you can dig in to customize the settings or just view exactly what they are. Curious users will want to choose Custom settings and view the many dozens of privacy settings. Who knew that by default, you were subject to “Microsoft experiments,” for example? In the Custom view, you can see what settings Avira marks as Recommended and what additional settings it changes when you switch to Enhanced. Secure Browser: Lots of Features But Little Substance Avast, AVG, Avira, and Norton all include a privacy-focused secure browser. When you click Secure Browser on the Privacy page, it installs the secure browser and, with your permission, makes it the default. This browser is Chromium-based, so if you use Chrome, it will be familiar. What sets it apart is the Security & Privacy Center, a collection of special-purpose items. The Security & Privacy Center page has undergone a radical change in appearance since my previous review. The page is now divided into four regions: Browser Modes, Security Check, Settings, and Tools. Security Check simply reports statistics on things like phishing sites blocked and dangerous downloads intercepted. As for browser modes, choosing Private Mode just invokes your browser's built-in privacy, such as InPrivate in Edge or Incognito in Chrome. In between those two is a third mode called Screen Sharing. This mode hides sensitive browser elements so you can share your screen without risking exposure. Under settings, you have Privacy Guard (not to be confused with Private Mode), Web Shield, Password Managers, and Extension Guard. The Tools panel has just two items, Avira Security and Privacy Cleaner. In terms of quantity, this is an impressive collection of features, but most of them don’t offer much. Clicking Avira Security just opens the antivirus, and the Password Managers feature pointlessly lets you swap between using Avira's password manager and the browser’s built-in password feature or turn both off. As for Privacy Cleaner, it’s almost identical to Chrome’s Clear browsing data feature and is reached by the same Ctrl+Shift+Del key combo. Extension Guard promises to block untrusted browser extensions. Really, though, shouldn’t the antivirus just wipe these out, just as it would any other malware? I didn’t find a way to test this feature. In the Secure Browser, Web Shield replaces Browser Safety. I don’t know why Gen antivirus products insist on providing two separate components that do the same thing, but I’ve learned they are not exactly the same. To check this, I ran my malicious URL-blocking test again, but this time using Web Shield for defense. Browser Safety protected the test system against 92% of the malware-hosting URLs, with its success split evenly between blocking all access to the URL and deleting the malware download. With Web Shield protection, it was more of a 60/40 split, with more samples being totally blocked in the browser. While Browser Safety leaves downloading to the browser (except when it interrupts the process), Web Shield takes over the download. When it blocks a dangerous download, it marks it with a red icon right in the browser’s downloads list. Safe downloads get a green icon. In total, Web Shield scored 94% to Browser Safety’s 92%. That’s not much of a difference. Privacy Guard is an ad and tracker blocker with more flexibility than Avira’s Browser Safety extension. At its default Basic level, it blocks items that “disrupt your browsing experience.” Leveling up to the Balanced level tells it to block more ads, including ones on social media. At the Strict level, it blocks ads, trackers, browser notifications, and attempts at browser fingerprinting. If you do select Strict blocking, the browser pops up a plea asking you to relent and not block “partners that fund us through…user-friendly ads.” This feature is both less flexible and less informative than what some competitors offer. For example, Bitdefender’s Anti-Tracker breaks down blocked ads by category and lets you choose its response at the category level. Tracker defense in the IronVest privacy tool shows which trackers it blocked and lets you exempt any specific tracker or site from its scrutiny. Avira Secure Browser flashes a collection of security features, many of which don’t do much. It is configured for the best security, but you can configure most of the same settings in Chrome. It’s not hardened against attack like some other secure browsers are. It’s a cut above basic Chrome in terms of security, so use it if you like. A user who blames security software for performance problems (reasonably or not) may just turn off security altogether. That’s not good. Avira heads off that problem with a collection of features aimed at improving performance. Clicking Performance in the left-rail menu reveals a page with six button panels: Optimizer, Battery saver, Driver updater, Duplicate finder, Advanced tools, and Game Booster. First: There Aren’t as Many Distinct Features as It Seems Out of these six performance features, Game Booster isn’t available without an upgrade. Three of the buttons (Battery saver, Duplicate finder, and Advanced tools) just launch the corresponding components within the separate Avira System Speedup application. Even more than the rest of this suite, System Speedup is loaded with locked Pro-only features, scans that find problems but won’t fix them without payment, and other upsell attempts. The simple Optimizer aims to free up space by removing junk files, speed up your device’s performance, and clean up things like cookies and erroneous Registry data. On my sparsely populated test system, it found about 830 MB of junk files and one slow-startup app. One click of the Optimize button cleaned up the junk files, but did nothing about that slow app. The results page offered to unlock my “full cleaning potential.” After clicking the Unlock button, I learned that I could either pay $90.99 per year for Avira’s System Speedup Pro or get it all with Avira Prime. Driver updater is similar in purpose to the Software updater described above. However, rather than finding missing security patches, it scans your system for device drivers that could be updated for better performance. During testing, the scan ran quickly, reported no drivers requiring an update, and listed all the up-to-date drivers found. In past reviews, clicking to update all outdated drivers took me to an upsell page. However, clicking Update next to a single driver caused Avira to handle the update even in the free edition. Avira System Speedup: Many System Optimization Features, Mostly Locked As noted, several items on the Performance page simply open corresponding features within the separate Avira System Speedup. For example, selecting Battery Saver launched Avira System Speedup with the energy management component open. Of course, the virtual machine test system has no battery, but it still lets me choose among five modes, ranging from best energy saving to best performance. Or rather, it offered me three of those modes, as choosing either extreme triggered an offer to purchase System Speedup Pro. Storing useless temp files and other junk wastes space on your hard drive, but so does storing multiple copies of documents and other files. Clicking Duplicate Finder opens the corresponding component in System Speedup. By default, this scan checks your Music, Documents, Pictures, and Videos folders. You can add other folders if desired and control which types of files it searches for. By default, it ignores “small-sized” duplicates, but you can remove this restriction if it seems appropriate. In testing, Avira quickly found groups of identical files, marking all but one for deletion in each case. However, clicking the delete button for those redundant files just brought up an upsell screen. If you don’t want to pay up, you’ll have to reference Avira’s report when performing deletions manually, then run the duplicate scan again to be sure you've removed them all. Going back to the Performance page and clicking for Advanced tools once again opens System Speedup, this time with the Startup Optimizer page selected. After a quick scan, the utility listed apps that may slow down the device and offered to perform a basic optimization. I wasn’t at all surprised to find that full use of this feature required an update to System Speedup Pro. I ran through the other features of System Speedup and got similar results. Quick Optimizer performed a partial cleanup but noted that its Pro edition could do more. Power Cleaner identified 5.5GB of items that should be cleaned up, but wouldn’t perform the cleanup without payment. Pulling down the Tools menu reveals that there’s even more to this cleanup tool. You can open a page of features designed to free up disk space and another that aims to improve system performance. You can reach the battery saver page mentioned earlier from this menu. There’s a full page of backup and restore options, though almost all are flagged as Pro-only. A file shredding system goes way beyond Avira’s built-in, with options to choose the file-overwrite algorithm, wipe a disk completely, and overwrite the disk’s free space. That last feature effectively shreds all deleted files ex post facto. Maintenance tasks get their own page, but they’re mostly locked. The app’s many pages are riddled with orange Pro-only flags. At least when you see those, you know the feature’s not available before you spend time scanning something. Even so, I found the preponderance of Pro-only features in the separate System Speedup component to be seriously annoying. I’d be happier if Avira’s designers continued the integration trend by pulling the handful of available speedup features into Avira Free Security. Back at the beginning, right after installation, Avira asked to run a Smart Scan. Now that I’ve explained the suite’s many features, I can spell out just how Smart Scan puts them all to work. You click a button on the main page to start the fun. Smart Scan checks for privacy issues and performance issues. It runs a quick scan for malware and checks for outdated apps. Finally, it scans for network threats. That last item refers to any time you’ve connected to an insecure Wi-Fi network. The whole thing just takes a few minutes. When the scan finishes, it summarizes its findings, broken down into Security, Privacy, and Performance issues. You can click a button to fix everything or choose to view detailed results. Well, fix everything may be the wrong phrase. Avira clears cookies, fixes Registry problems, and frees up some disk space. If you want to fix the rest, including outdated apps, privacy settings, and more wasted disk space, you’ll have to pay for an upgrade. Final Thoughts Avira Free Security - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The core antivirus component Avira Free Security gets good scores in our hands-on tests, but its lab test results are lacking. While its Privacy and Security components are completely integrated, most of the Performance features still call on the separate Avira System Speedup app. This suite is bursting with features and utilities, but it doesn’t cover the full range of expected suite components, and many of its features aren’t fully functional without payment. Avast One Free roughly matches Avira feature-wise, but its lab scores are vastly better, its VPN bandwidth limit is much more generous, and it includes protection aimed squarely at ransomware. It's an Editors’ Choice for free antivirus protection, sharing that honor with AVG AntiVirus Free, which sticks to typical antivirus features. Of course, when you’re looking at free antivirus tools, you have the luxury of evaluating as many as you want to pick the one that suits you best. STILL ON THE FENCE? About Our Expert When the IBM PC was new, I served as the president of the San Francisco PC User Group for three years. That’s how I met PCMag’s editorial team, who brought me on board in 1986. In the years since that fateful meeting, I’ve become PCMag’s expert on security, privacy, and identity protection, putting antivirus tools, security suites, and all kinds of security software through their paces. Before my current security gig, I supplied PCMag readers with tips and solutions on using popular applications, operating systems, and programming languages in my "User to User" and "Ask Neil" columns, which began in 1990 and ran for almost 20 years. Along the way, I wrote more than 40 utility articles, as well as Delphi Programming for Dummies and six other books covering DOS, Windows, and programming. I also reviewed thousands of products of all kinds, ranging from early Sierra Online adventure games to AOL’s precursor Q-Link. In the early 2000s, I turned my focus to security and the growing antivirus industry. After years of working with antivirus, I’m known throughout the security industry as an expert on evaluating antivirus tools. I serve as an advisory board member for the Anti-Malware Testing Standards Organization (AMTSO), an international nonprofit group dedicated to coordinating and improving testing of anti-malware solutions.

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro Expected Today. Here Are the Rumors That Look Legit
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.81
Tim Cook is out, and John Ternus is in, and he'll introduce himself to Apple fans today, when the company hosts its "Surprise and shine" event. It's set to be a packed presentation. What can we expect? And how much more expensive will Apple's latest and greatest be, given the memory crunch? Apple already raised prices across several major product lines in June, but iPhone pricing has remained steady, helping drive iPhone 17 sales during the last quarter. However, "For September, we expect to pay even higher memory costs,” Cook said during a recent earnings call. With Apple's foldable expected to cost north of $2,000, the iPhone 18 Pro is probably the more economical choice if you're looking to upgrade this fall. To help you know what to expect, we've rounded up the biggest iPhone 18 Pro rumors we have heard so far. iPhone 18 Pro: Revised Lineup The biggest rumor around the iPhone 18 lineup is its release timeline. Unlike previous years, where Apple released four phones in the same series in one go, Bloomberg reports Apple could take a two-pronged approach to ensure consistent revenue throughout the year. Flagship phones, such as the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max, and the foldable iPhone, will be unveiled in September, while the base iPhone 18, iPhone Air 2, and the iPhone 18e could be launched in spring 2027. We discuss the foldable iPhone in detail in a separate rumor roundup, so we’ll just stick to the Pro models here. iPhone 18 Pro: Design and Colors The iPhone 17 Pro models brought a major overhaul to Apple’s smartphone design language, with a new camera “plateau” and two-toned color scheme. This year, Apple isn’t expected to drastically change the device's appearance, but it could add a few bold colors and return to a more uniform color scheme on the back. Several leakers, including Sonny Dickson and Instant Digital, claim that Apple could go with a never-before-seen cherry red and a new light blue, alongside the regular dark gray. Dickson also shared pictures of potential dummies, including one in light gray. In a fresh leak last week, Fixed Focus Digital backed dark cherry, sky blue, and dark gray colors for the new models, but noted that light gray or white/silver was highly unlikely. While the appearance of the rear is expected to remain the same, the in-hand feel could be a lot different. Ice Universe says the battery could get slightly larger on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, contributing to increased weight and bulk. More precisely, the leaker expects the device to be 0.25mm thicker and 7 grams heavier. iPhone 18 Pro Display On the front, we might see one significant change. The Dynamic Island, or the camera cutout, could be reduced by 35%, Ice Universe says. This won’t shrink the feature's overall functionality, but it could move the Face ID sensor’s illuminator to one corner below the screen. When it comes to display sizes, the consensus is that the iPhone 18 Pro will come in its usual 6.3-inch screen, while the Pro Max will have a 6.9-inch screen. Apple, however, has reportedly been pushing suppliers to provide much brighter displays and could use the more power-efficient LTPO+ display tech. iPhone 18 Pro Cameras The iPhone 17 Pro lineup bumped all three cameras to 48MP. For the iPhone 18 Pro, the biggest camera-related rumor we have heard is around variable aperture. While the iPhone 17 models had a fixed aperture, the iPhone 18 Pro may introduce a variable aperture. ETNews reports that the modified system has already entered production and would help the cameras deliver more light to the sensors in dark conditions and reduce light in bright conditions. Apple may also modify its relatively new Camera Control button. Introduced with the iPhone 16, the capacitive button at the bottom right of the phone lets you quickly launch the Camera app, take pictures, and adjust settings for zoom, exposure, depth, and other controls. Mastering the capacitive button, however, has proved difficult, with users noting that they have been accidentally launching the Camera app. Apple may finally fix the problem by removing the touch-sensitive components of the button and delivering a more user-friendly experience, 9to5Mac reports. iPhone 18 Pro Performance The iPhone 18 Pro is likely to receive a performance boost with the A20 chip. It will use TSMC’s 2nm technology, an upgrade from the previous generation’s 3nm tech. The transition will allow more transistors on each chip but also raise chip costs by 50%, MacRumors reports. The chip is also rumored to have TSMC’s Wafer-Level Multi-Chip Module (WMCM) technology, which infuses RAM into the same wafer as the CPU, GPU, and Neural Engine. Overall, it is expected to be 18% faster and 30% more power-efficient than previous generations, according to leaker Fixed Focus Digital. Apple usually reserves the base variant of its chip series for the standard iPhone models, while the Pro models get the corresponding Pro chip. With the iPhone 18 series, Apple is reportedly considering offering just the high-end variant across the lineup. Another expected upgrade is for the modem. The iPhone 17 Pro models had an unspecified third-party modem, but the iPhone 18 Pro could get the company’s proprietary C2 modem. It will support 5G satellite connectivity and reduce the scope of location data retained by networks, according to MacRumors. iPhone 18 Pro Battery Apple never reveals its battery capacities, but multiple leakers have indicated a larger and more efficient battery for the iPhone 18 Pro Max. According to Digital Chat Station, the top variant will have a capacity of up to 5,200mAh, slightly better than the 5,088mAh capacity of its predecessor. With a more efficient modem and processor, the battery life could be significantly longer. The iPhone 18 Pro, on the other hand, could see a minimal bump from 4,252mAh to 4,288mAh. More recently, leaks posted on Korean and Chinese social media sites tip a US iPhone 18 Pro Max model with a 5,567mAh battery, a nearly 10% increase over the iPhone 17 Pro Max, MacRumors notes. iPhone 18 Pro: Pricing and Release This is what much of the decision-making hinges on. According to The Wall Street Journal's estimate, rising component costs would push the iPhone 18 Pro to start at $1,299. If you couple that with recent Apple trends, the iPhone 18 Pro Max could be priced $100 higher, taking its starting price to $1,399. In comparison, the iPhone 17 Pro starts at $1,099, while the 17 Pro Max starts at $1,199. When asked on a recent earnings call about potential price hikes for the iPhone, Cook said it's "too early to come to a definitive conclusion of what happens there. Because it takes a little while for the channels to adjust since there's channel inventory, it takes a while for the consumer to respond. We'll understand that more in the weeks ahead." With the event scheduled for Sept. 9, preorders will likely begin a few days later, ahead of the launch the following week. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Is It Worth It to Upgrade to Switch 2 Games? We'll Run You Through the Actual Costs
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.71
Video game prices have been slowly creeping up for years. When the Nintendo Switch first launched in 2017, full-priced games were $60. Then, PlayStation and Xbox first-party releases jumped to $70 in 2020. Nintendo followed suit in 2023 with The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom. But Switch 2 pricing has made everything more complicated. Mario Kart World costs $80. Donkey Kong Bananza is $70. Yet Final Fantasy VII Remake Intergrade is just $40. Want to buy physical games? That will cost you more than the digital versions. And even though some of the Switch 1 games I own are backward compatible, if I want to upgrade to the Switch 2 version for better performance or additional DLC, the upgrade pricing is all over the place. In some cases, upgrading costs $0, while others require you to break out your credit card. Here's the full breakdown of how much it costs to upgrade your old Switch game to the Switch 2 versions. The 3 Types of Switch 2 Games Before I talk about how much the upgrades cost, I need to explain the three (yes, three) different kinds of games you can play on the Switch 2. - Switch 2 games: These are native Switch 2 games made exclusively for the console. They feature the Switch 2 logo and are designed to take advantage of the latest hardware. This includes Mario Kart World and Donkey Kong Bananza, as well as third-party releases like Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition. - Switch 2 Edition games: These are Switch games that have performance and visual upgrades over their Switch 1 counterparts. The physical versions of these titles will have the Switch game and Upgrade Pack on the same cartridge. Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Pokémon Legends: Z-A are Switch 2 Edition games, and are labeled accordingly. - Switch 1 games: Finally, there are just Switch 1 games, since (most of) these can be played on the Switch 2. This means you can play Breath of the Wild or Metroid Dread for free if you already own those games. They won't have the significant upgrades that come with the Upgrade Packs, but should gain some small benefits simply by running on more powerful hardware. How Much Does Nintendo Charge for a Switch 2 Upgrade Pack? Instead of having to buy new games to get upgraded versions of the titles you already own, Nintendo allows you to upgrade your Switch games into native Switch 2 games, turning them into Switch 2 Edition games. However, the cost of that upgrade varies widely, depending on how much new content is included. - $20: Upgrade Packs that include DLC-sized additions for the Switch 2 cost $20. This includes Super Mario Party Jamboree, Kirby and the Forgotten Land, and Super Mario Bros. Wonder, which add new gameplay features and content to the base game. The Switch 2 Edition versions of these games cost $80, so it's the $60 base game + $20 DLC. - $10: Games with smaller performance and visual upgrades, such as Metroid Prime 4: Beyond and Pokémon Legends: Z-A, cost $10. Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom are also priced here because a new copy of BOTW for Switch 2 costs $70 and TOTK costs $80. However, they're actually included as part of Nintendo Switch Online + Expansion Pack. It's interesting to note that the Xenoblade games add some additional content. - The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild - The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom - Metroid Prime 4: Beyond - Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy - Pokémon Legends: Z-A - Xenoblade Chronicles: Definitive Edition - Xenoblade Chronicles 2 - Xenoblade Chronicles 3 - $5: Nintendo introduced a $5 upgrade path for the Switch 2 Edition of Animal Crossing: New Horizons to coincide with the game's free version 3.0 update. This upgrade adds enhanced visuals, GameChat functionality, and mouse controls. Xenoblade Chronicles X is another $5 upgrade, but it just includes performance improvements. Interestingly, both games are getting new physical editions, so is this the one common thread? - Free: Finally, some games have received free upgrades from Nintendo, including Arms, Pokémon Scarlet/Violet, The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom, Super Mario Odyssey, Bowser's Fury, and more. These updates mainly focus on visual upgrades, though some gain frame rate bumps, HDR, and even GameChat support. - Arms - Big Brain Academy: Brain vs. Brain - Captain Toad: Treasure Tracker - Clubhouse Games: 51 Worldwide Classics - Donkey Kong Country Returns HD - Game Builder Garage - The Legend of Zelda: Echoes of Wisdom - The Legend of Zelda: Link's Awakening - New Super Mario Bros. U Deluxe - Pokémon Scarlet and Violet - Splatoon 3 - Super Mario: 3D World + Bowser's Fury - Super Mario Galaxy + Super Mario Galaxy 2 - Super Mario Odyssey How Much Are Third-Party Games? It's not just Nintendo games that have unlockable updates for the Switch 2; all developers have the option of offering an upgrade path to players. Many of these updates come with graphic and performance improvements, but some may add additional content. However, how much this costs will depend on the game and the publisher. For instance, games in Hamster's Arcade Archives line cost $2.99 to upgrade. Meanwhile, Marvelous has multiple games at the $10 price point. However, many developers have opted not to charge for the Switch 2 Edition of their game. This means if you own the Switch version of the game, the upgrade pack is available to you as a free download. - 1000xResist - Free - 4PGP - $5 - A-Train: All Aboard! Tourism - $7 - Another Crab's Treasure - Free - Another Eden Begins - $5 - Asdivine Knot - $1 - Asphalt Legends - Free - Atelier Yumia: The Alchemist of Memories & the Envisioned Land - $10 - Ball x Pit - Free - Bang! Bang! Bandits - $3 - Beyblade X Evobattle - $10 - BlazBlue Entropy Effect X - $2 - Blood: Refreshed Supply - Free - Botany Manor - $4 - Braid: Anniversary Edition - $3 - Broken Sword - Shadow of the Templars: Reforged - $5 - Brotato - Free - Card-en-Ciel - $10 - Cast n Chill - Free - Chippy&Noppo - $2.40 - Citizen Sleeper - Free - Citizen Sleeper 2: Starward Vector - Free - Core Keeper - Free - Cozy Grove - Free - Cozy Grove: Camp Spirit - Free - Culdcept Begins - $10 - Dark Auction - $1 - Dave the Diver - Free - Deltarune - Free - Demon Castle Story - $4 - Dinkum - Free - Disney Dreamlight Valley - Free - Disney Speedstorm - Free - Dispatch - Free - Divinity: Original Sin II - Free - Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake - Free - Dream Town Island - $4 - The Drifter - Free - Dungeon Village 2 - $4 - Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim - $20 for Anniversary Edition - Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Anniversary Edition - Free - The Exit 8 - $1 - Factorio - Free - Fantasy Life i: The Girl Who Steals Time - $2.59 - Final Fantasy Tactics - The Ivalice Chronicles - Free - Fitness Boxing 3: Your Personal Trainer - $10 - The Fox's Way Home - $3 - Fruit Mountain Party - $1.88 - Game Dev Story - $4 - Go-Go Town - $3 - Gunvolt Chronicles: Luminous Avenger iX 1+2 Dual Collection - $5 - Hades II - Free - Hello Kitty Island Adventure - $10 - High on Life - Free - Hogwarts Legacy - $10 - Hollow Knight - Free - Hollow Knight: Silksong - Free - Human Fall Flat - $5 - Inazuma Eleven: Victory Road - $2.59 - Isekai Rondo - $1 - Isekai Villain - $1 - It Takes Two - Free - Jumbo Airport Story - $4 - Kingdom's Return: Time-Eating Fruit and the Ancient Monster - Kuukiyomi 4: Consider It - $5 - Lego Party! - Free - Little Rocket Lab - Free - Lollipop Chainsaw RePop - $5 - Lorelei and the Laser Eyes - Free - Lou's Lagoon - Free - Lynked: Banner of the Spark - Free - Memory of Memorie : A Chill Story - $2 - Mina the Hollower - Free - Minecraft - Coming soon - Minishoot' Adventures - Free - Moonlight Peaks - $5 - Nicktoons & The Dice of Destiny - Free - No Man's Sky - Free - Novel Rogue - $1 - One Piece: Pirate Warriors 4 - Free - Overcooked 2! - $10 - Outlaws + Handful of Missions: Remaster - Free - Overrogue - $1 - Pipistrello and the Cursed Yoyo - Free - Planet of Lana II - Free - The Prince of Tennis Doki Doki Survival - $5 - The Prince of Tennis Sweet School Festival - $5 - Pritto Prisoner - $1 - Psyvariar 3 - Free - R-Type Tactics I • II Cosmos - $5 - The Ramen Sensei - $4 - Red Dead Redemption - Free - RollerCoaster Tycoon Classic - $5 - Romancing SaGa 2: Revenge of the Seven - $10 - The Rumble Fish 2 - $5 - Rune Factory: Guardians of Azuma - $10 - Sail Forth - Free - Sayonara Wild Hearts - Free - Shadow Labyrinth - Free - Shuten Order - $2.49 - Sid Meier's Civilization VII - $10 - Simogo Legacy Collection - Skyship Quest Story - $4 - Sonic Racing: Crossworlds - $10 - Stardew Valley - Free - Storm Lancers - Free - Story of Seasons: Grand Bazaar - $10 - Subnautica - Free - Subnautica: Below Zero - Free - Super Bomberman Collection - $5 - System Shock Remake - Free - System Shock 2: 25th Anniversary Remaster - Free - Tales of the Shire: A The Lord of the Rings Game - Free - Tamagotchi Plaza - $10 - Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Splintered Fate - $2.49 - Tomb Raider I-III Remastered - Free - Touhou Yukkuri Mountain - $1.50 - Trails in the Sky 1st Chapter - $1 - Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter - $5 - The Touryst - $6 - Unrailed 2: Back on Track - Free - Wobbly Life - $5 - Woodo - Free Not All Games Have Upgrade Paths Keep in mind that not all titles will offer upgrade paths. Square Enix, for instance, seems to shy away from making the Switch and Switch 2 versions of their games compatible or upgradeable. Some Sega games do the same. That has also typically meant save data can't be carried over either, so be careful before buying a game on Switch that you plan to upgrade down the road on Switch 2. You'll need to re-buy these games—at full price—to get them on the new console: - Atelier Ryza Secret Trilogy Deluxe Pack - Dragon Quest I & II HD-2D Remake - Dragon Quest VII: Reimagined - Dragon Quest XI S: Echoes of an Elusive Age - Definitive Edition - Final Fantasy Resonance - Final Fantasy X & X-2 HD Remaster - No Sleep For Kaname Date - From AI: The Somnium Files - Nobunaga's Ambition: Awakening - Octopath Traveler - Octopath Traveler 2 - Octopath Traveler 0 - Raidou Remastered - Shinobi: Art of Vengeance - Sonic Frontiers - Definitive Edition - Sonic X Shadow Generations - Star Ocean: The Second Story R - Suika Game Planet - Suikoden I & II HD Remaster Other games may also receive free patches that allow them to take advantage of the new hardware without the need for a true upgrade path. About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: 'This Is Just the Beginning': Our Review of the First iPhone in 2007 Was Pitch-Perfect
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.64
Editors' Note: Welcome to our ongoing An Apple a Day series, where we’ll share Apple stories and video from our archives daily from now through late September. In addition to PCMag, this series includes pieces from our sibling sites CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, and Popular Science. The excitement surrounding the original iPhone was electric. From the moment Apple CEO Steve Jobs held the product on stage at Macworld in January 2007 until it reached Apple and AT&T retail stores in June, the iPhone captivated the entire tech sphere. The six-month timespan in between felt like an eternity. Even before it was released, the iPhone was loved and reviled equally. Some hailed it as the "Jesus phone," a device to save us all from tech drudgery, while others judged it more for what it wasn't than what it was. Whether you were an early believer or not, the first iPhone's release was a watershed moment that emphatically shoved the industry in a new direction. Looking back at the review (which you can read in full here), it's amazing to see how on-point it was, despite some skepticism from our expert reviewers. "The Apple iPhone is a great first try from Apple," Sascha Segan and Tim Gideon noted. They added, "Apple's smart, though, and this is just the beginning. Think of this as the 128K Mac of the 21st century—a vanguard product, maybe not perfect or the most usable machine ever...but heralding some insanely great products to come." How the Industry Largely Wrote the iPhone Off I still vividly remember the iPhone pre-release news cycles. At the time, I was a writer for a small website called Phonescoop. Apple announced the iPhone in San Francisco on January 9, when most of the industry was in Las Vegas for CES. The next day, I actually sat with PCMag's then-lead phone reviewer, Sascha Segan, at the Hilton in Las Vegas, at a joint press briefing held by Apple and its network partner, AT&T. The small group peppered the Apple and AT&T folks with questions during a sometimes contentious session. Sascha loudly questioned Apple's decision to ship the phone with EDGE (2.5G) rather than UMTS or CDMA (3G), which was catching on with many competing devices at the time. On paper, the original iPhone was sort of a loser in the eyes of the tech-obsessed. It lacked so much technology compared with the BlackBerrys, Communicators, Treos, and Windows Mobile devices of the day. It didn't have 3G, didn't support stereo Bluetooth, couldn't run third-party apps, and the stated one-day battery life was less than half the endurance of others. It packed a 2MP camera with a single function at a time when Nokia was shipping advanced 5MP cameras with multiple capture modes. The original iPhone couldn't send picture messages, nor could it record video at launch. The industry largely wrote it off. "There's no chance that the iPhone is going to get any significant market share," said Microsoft's then-CEO, Steve Ballmer. It took 74 days for Apple to sell 1 million of them. And things only exploded from there. Tomorrow, Apple is expected to introduce the iPhone 18 Pro, the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and its first foldable phone. Not a Very Good Phone, But It Did Change Everything In person, it turns out, the device was remarkable in many ways. It was the first phone to have only a finger-touch user interface. Until then, most devices relied on resistive screens that supported stylus input but still required directional buttons or scroll wheels to navigate. And while the iPhone wasn't the first phone to support multi-point touch (up to 10 fingers at a time), it was the first to put it to such effective use, with swiping and pinching gestures that moved you through the home screen and menus. We all still use this UI paradigm every single day. Meanwhile, the iPod app's UI was colorful, fun, and just so different from text-heavy, folder-based menus on every other device. And, despite its limitations, browsing the web on Safari was worlds different from the text-heavy WAP browsers on many other phones, thanks to its broader support for HTML and imagery. Segan captured all this in his initial review, co-written with then audio reviewer Tim Gideon. "The seamless integration of the internet, iPod, Maps, Phone, and email functions flaunted in the commercials is no exaggeration," they wrote. "The iPhone is intuitive, interconnected, and impossible to get lost in—just hit the home button to get to the main screen." Enamored as he was with the user interface, Segan didn't hold back about the iPhone's faults: "It isn't a very good phone. Call quality was the worst we've heard on a high-end device in years." "What sort of smartphone doesn't have corporate email?" critics quipped.
The iPhone was widely panned for its limited support for enterprise email and messaging, features considered vital to the smartphone-toting crowd of the era (mostly traveling professionals). PIM (personal information management) was the crux of Research In Motion's and Microsoft's mobile businesses at the time, and licensing access to Exchange was big money. "What sort of smartphone doesn't have corporate email?" critics quipped. There's no doubt the first iPhone had many limitations, but plenty of people saw it for the new dynamic it introduced. And it did change everything. For the next year, LG, Motorola, and Samsung tripped over themselves to create "iPhone killers," and they all failed for one reason or another. Nokia, RIM, and Microsoft could hardly be bothered to respond. It wasn't until Google launched Android in October 2008 that a truly competitive platform arrived. PCMag's initial review was well-informed, praised the phone on its merits, and docked points where it came up short. The original iPhone was not the most technically advanced device of its day, but it offered one of the best experiences, merged multiple products into one (phone, music player, camera), and shook things up in just the right way. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Managing Editor for Consumer Electronics content, overseeing an experienced team of reviewers and product testers. I’ve been covering technology for more than 25 years. Prior to PCMag, I worked at outlets such as Android Authority, Fortune, InformationWeek, and Phonescoop.

item.title: Intel Will Reportedly Increase CPU Prices by 10% Next Month
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.61
If you’re waiting for PC prices to drop, you may be in for a long wait. According to a new report from Chinese outlet Digitimes, Intel is set to raise its CPU prices for the third time this year. After increasing prices by 10% in Q1 2026 and by an unknown margin in July, the company is reportedly set to impose another 10% price hike on Oct. 5. Citing industry sources, Digitimes reports that Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan is conducting a comprehensive review of CPU prices, gross profit, and manufacturing costs amid a global memory crisis and rising demand for some specific processors. As part of the plans, Tan may also consider discontinuing some low-margin product lines and letting go of a few more employees, the report adds. Intel’s headcount has been dropping steadily since 2024. The company cut 15,000 jobs that year and reduced its global workforce by another 15% the following year. A few more employees were laid off in July, and Intel is now planning to cut 5-10% more jobs soon, Digitimes says. The company is estimated to have about 75,000 employees. Qualcomm imposed a similar price hike on Sept. 1. Microsoft, too, is reportedly considering a price hike for Windows licensing fees. Whether PC manufactures absorb the rising costs or pass them on to consumers remains to be seen. According to June data from IDC, PC shipments are expected to decline by 11.3% this year, with Q4 projected to decline by 20% year-over-year. A recent survey by PCMag’s parent company, Ziff Davis, also found that 73% respondents were willing to hold on to their old devices for as long as they worked. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: iPhone Duo Is Apple's First Foldable Phone. Surprise, It's Expensive!
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.50
Apple was in no rush to launch a foldable phone, even as many of its rivals released various versions over the last eight years. But with John Ternus now at the helm, he kicked off his first Apple event as CEO by introducing a new form factor for the company: the foldable iPhone Duo. Though rumors suggested the device might be the iPhone Ultra, Apple likely opted for the Duo name to keep it short and snappy, aligning it with its other monikers, such as Air, Neo, and Pro. (Though it does have an Apple Watch Ultra, so who knows?) iPhone Duo Design and Display The Duo is a passport-style foldable phone, meaning it's shorter and wider than a lot of rivals. The inner display is 7.6 inches, while the outer display is 5.4 inches, with both sporting a 1:4 aspect ratio to help transitions between screens feel more seamless. The Duo is 11.3mm thick when closed and 5.2mm when open; during today's presentation, it was touted as the thinnest iPhone ever, though that's only when it's open, of course. (The iPhone Air is 5.64mm thick.) The left-hand corners of the outer display are right angles, while the right-hand corners are rounded to make it easier to use with one hand. It's unclear how easy that will be if you're left-handed, though. Touch ID is how you unlock the phone; it's built into the power button on the right-hand edge. On durability, Apple says it feels "exceptionally solid every time you use it." It's also IP68 for water and dust resistance, and there's a nano-texture finish on the display, designed to minimize damage on the inner screen. Apple says its hinge uses over 100 tiny components to close smoothly and last a long time, although it has yet to say how many folds it expects to handle over its lifetime. Apple's press release notes, "Internally, support ribs reinforce the structure for added stiffness, while antenna splits with ceramic fiber inserts enhance the frame’s rigidity." iPhone Duo Chip and Performance The iPhone Duo comes with a new A20 Pro chipset built on 2nm tech, enabling what Apple calls "upgrades across the entire chip," with up to a 50% increase in memory bandwidth. There's a 6-core CPU that's 20% faster than A19 Pro, a 7-core GPU with 40% faster graphics performance, and a 32-core Neural Engine. Plus, there's a larger vapor chamber for improved performance. The Duo has Apple's N1 wireless networking chip found in the iPhone 17 and Air, and the C2, Apple's next-generation cellular modem system (also in the iPhone 18 Pros), which brings AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability, as well as mmWave support in the US. iPhone Duo Camera Specs Foldable phones often fall short in their cameras, but Apple may have addressed this by including a 48MP Fusion Main rear camera and a 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide. That's one fewer than the iPhone 18 Pro series, so it may not be as capable as the brand's other top-end phones. The main camera uses the iPhone 18 Pro's Fusion tech, which includes a variable aperture that adjusts automatically to let in up to 50% more light. On the front of the phone is a 12MP selfie camera designed for video calls and for shooting when the phone is folded. iPhone Duo Battery Life and Charging Speed The phone is powered by two batteries, allowing for up to 31 hours of video playback on the inner display or 44 hours on the outer display. We'll have to wait for our upcoming full review to know how long it lasts on a full day of use. New fast-charging features are also here, meaning the iPhone Duo gets from zero to 50% in around 20 minutes. If you're using a wireless charger, it takes 30 minutes to get to the same battery level. iOS 27 on the iPhone Duo The iPhone Duo will support an adapted version of iOS 27 for the wider, foldable screen. Apple detailed some of the changes during its launch, such as moving controls to the right-hand edge rather than at the bottom of the display. The software also shows whatever you were doing on the outer display when you move to the inner display. That includes access to the new AI-powered Siri for better assistant connectivity across Apple apps. Siri AI is rolling out with iOS 27 as a beta on Sept. 14 for users with a supported device set to English. (Support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish is coming in October; it's not coming to the EU and China.) The bendable screen also means new features such as dual-screen use for the camera, alongside innovations for running multiple apps at once across iOS. The iPhone Duo also works with the Apple Pencil USB-C version. iPhone Duo Price and Storage Options The iPhone Duo doesn't come in a 128GB option; it starts at 256GB of storage for $1,999. That's lower than some had expected, and only slightly higher than rivals; the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold are both $1,899.99. Here's the breakdown: - 256GB: $1,999 - 512GB: $2,199 - 1TB: $2,599 - 2TB: $3,199 If you want to test it out without dropping thousands, the Duo is available to lease via Apple Upgrade for $34.99 per month for a 24-month lease or $49.99 per month for 24 months. Meanwhile, if you were hoping to save some money and get a discount on the older iPhone, Apple has instead increased the starting price of the iPhone 17, iPhone 17e, and iPhone Air by $100. iPhone Duo Release Date and Preorder Preorders for the iPhone Duo start on Oct. 16, and the official release date is set for Oct. 23. iPhone Duo Colors, Cases, and Accessories The phone comes in two colors: Night Sky, a black shade, and Star White, a light white option. There are also two official cases. The $129 iPhone Duo Folio comes in navy blue or taupe and features an integrated kickstand so you can place the phone on a desk. The $79 iPhone Duo Case comes in two parts, in either sand or navy blue. Both will be available to order on Oct. 16. The ongoing Apple launch just introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, but it's thought that it will skip the standard iPhone 18 to launch it early next year. Other new gadgets include an Apple Watch Series 12, an Apple Watch Ultra 4, and new AirPods 5. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: FCC: Satellite Constellations Don't Need Environmental Reviews
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.49
The FCC has decided to exempt satellites from federal environmental reviews, despite concerns about light pollution and potential effects on the atmosphere. The agency plans to make it official during its Sept. 30 meeting, where it will vote to reform its environmental regulations. “For too long, outdated and unnecessary environmental rules have slowed America’s builders down,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr wrote in a blog post on Tuesday. Specifically, the commission wants to revise its approach to the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), which requires federal agencies to “assess the environmental effects of their proposed actions prior to making decisions.” In his blog post, Carr cited the need to “cut billions of dollars in red tape" while clearing the way for more investment in new telecommunications infrastructure both on the ground and in orbit. “The decision will also clarify that bureaucratic NEPA reviews have no place across a range of innovative space-based activities regulated by the FCC.” The FCC plans on publishing the exact text of the reforms on Wednesday. That said, in a press briefing, a senior official noted they call for exempting the on-the-ground NEPA rules from satellite systems and other constellations in orbit. Historically, the FCC has refrained from conducting environmental reviews of satellite systems. But in 2022, the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) urged the commission to revisit its approach, given that tens of thousands of satellites, such as those from SpaceX, could be in orbit by 2030. “Stakeholders have expressed concerns about changes in the temperature of the upper atmosphere from emissions from launches or deorbiting of satellites and effects on astronomical research from radio transmissions or sunlight reflections. They have also expressed concerns about effects on amateur astronomy and astrophotography and the general public from changes to the night sky,” the GAO report said. Those concerns have only grown as SpaceX looks to launch another 100,000 satellites for Starlink and up to 1 million for its orbital data center system, Starmind. In 2024, a group of astronomers and space experts even called on the FCC to halt future Starlink launches so that the US could study the potential environmental effects, including whether retired satellites can harm the ozone layer when they burn up in the atmosphere. But a year ago, Carr’s FCC signaled it would continue excluding satellites from NEPA reviews when it kicked off a process to modernize its environmental regulations. In doing so, the commission described them as "'extraterritorial activities' with effects located entirely outside of the jurisdiction of the United States.” In July, the Commission also approved the US startup Reflect Orbital’s plan to launch a controversial satellite featuring a giant space mirror that reflects sunlight back to Earth during nighttime hours. Despite objections from astronomers and environmental groups, the FCC found the space mirror-related concerns “beyond the Commission’s authority,” involving NEPA. “The Commission’s authority pertains to the licensing and operation of a radio station using radiofrequency spectrum, and it does not have regulatory authority over the licensing and operation of a solar reflector,” the FCC said, noting it was merely clearing one satellite from Reflect Orbital. Although environmental groups are expected to object to the reforms, Carr's FCC has made maintaining US dominance in space and the satellite industry a major goal, citing the threat of China. "Our decision will ensure that outdated environmental rules do not hold back America’s space economy and the novel activities underway in orbit. It is time to build," Carr said. Meanwhile, SpaceX has long worked to prevent its satellites from causing light pollution. The company has also told the FCC it plans on starting small with its orbital data center project "to monitor actual atmospheric effects." About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. I'm always eager to learn more, so please jump in the comments with feedback and send me tips.

item.title: Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini Review: A Powerhouse Mini PC for Work and Play
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.21
This isn't your father's NUC—or even the NUC you may remember from five or 10 years ago. The PC industry keeps finding ways to pack beefier silicon into tinier and tinier machines. Case in point: the Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini. Our punchy test model (expected to sell for around $3,000), kitted out with an Intel Core Ultra X7 358H processor and 64GB of memory, is one of the most powerful mini PCs of its size class we've tested to date. It delivers enough CPU performance to handle tough workflows—managing complex datasets, casual content-creation work, even light AI development—while taking up almost no space on your desk. Plus, this NUC's integrated graphics can challenge an entry-level discrete GPU for graphics acceleration, and even gaming—outside of office hours, of course. Asus' individual pricing ranges wide: The base model, which is peppy in its own right, comes in at $559 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 CPU. (Mind you, that's a barebones model, so you'll need to add your own memory and storage, which are today's big-dollar components.) While our exact configuration was not yet available in the US as we published this (it's expected to show up in Q4), the highest-end build available at this writing still runs a sobering $2,799. If your workflows justify the payout, however, this NUC will deliver peak power per cubic inch. It displaces the Geekom A9 Max as our Editors’ Choice pick for the best overall Windows mini PC. The NUC 16 Pro comes in several configurations, all based on mobile (that is, laptop-grade) hardware. The base-level barebones model, as I noted, carries an Intel Core Ultra 5 325 chip that features four Performance cores (P-cores) and four Low-Power Efficient cores (LPE-cores) in the CPU portion, plus four Xe cores in its integrated graphics processor (IGP). The model I reviewed contains a far more powerful Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU. That "Panther Lake" chip features four P-cores, eight Efficient cores (E-cores), and four LPE-cores, making it significantly faster for CPU-intensive tasks. The Arc B390 IGP in the Ultra X7 358H processor also delivers a lot more graphics punch than the base model's chip, with a dozen Xe cores. It's a major advantage and one of the keys to this mini PC’s appeal. Our review model, available soon according to Asus, came with 64GB of LPDDR5X RAM, clocked at a speedy 9,600MHz and set in a dual-channel configuration. That setup will give you an abundance of memory bandwidth, boosting performance in demanding applications. It also boosts the IGPs performance with games. If you're looking to upgrade the machine, though, you're out of luck: The memory installed for the X7 chip (as well as for X9 models that Asus says will also come) is soldered to the motherboard; Asus says X7/X9 models with 16GB. 32GB, 64GB, and 96GB will be available. A 96GB memory allotment, paired with the X7 chip's robust neural processor (NPU) and IGP, would make for a lively, very small local-AI computing platform. This level of AI capability goes well beyond the Copilot PC functions that Windows 11 provides and can be useful even for AI product development. The appeal is that any sensitive AI work can be done directly on the device and stay off the cloud. The CPU also features hardware-based Intel vPro security options for managed environments. Asus also offers versions of the NUC 16 Pro Mini with ordinary Core Ultra 5 and Ultra 7 chips, and these rely instead on DDR5 SO-DIMMs (compact memory modules, the same kind some laptops use). The entry-level NUC model, with the Ultra 5 325 processor, is designed to be hands-on. As it's a barebones kit, you need to plug in your own SO-DIMMs, as well as an M.2 SSD, before you can fire up the system. (You’ll also need to install your own OS, in this case.) This model is worth keeping in mind if the NUC piques your interest, but a prebuilt model like our lavishly appointed tester is too expensive. As noted up top, the model with the Ultra 5 325 CPU starts at $559, which makes it far more affordable if you don't need that all the performance the X7 model packs. Bear in mind, though, that shelling out for the needed RAM, SSD, and operating system will set you back a few hundred dollars more. The top-most configuration available at this writing, at $2,799, has the same Intel Core Ultra X7 chip as in my test model, but with just 32GB of memory and a 1TB SSD. If you're buying as an IT fleet manager, you might have access to bulk pricing for this NUC, whether barebones or prebuilt, which will differ from these single-unit prices. All Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini models come with a three-year warranty that includes 24/7 support, which should appeal especially to business owners and IT buyers.
