The real selling point of a mini PC is the size, and the NUC delivers on that front, measuring just 1.65 by 5.7 by 4.6 inches (HWD). A sleek black exterior gives the system a premium sheen. Opening the case is simplicity itself: Press the latch on the bottom of the system and lift, and the bottom comes right off. You won’t need to open up a system like this often—unless you get the barebones model, of course—but on the rare occasions you do, accessing the hardware is a cinch. The exterior, meanwhile, delivers a plentiful array of ports for a machine this size. Up front, you get a 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C port and two 10Gbps USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A connections. Around back, the NUC gives you two more USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports, alongside a pair of Thunderbolt 4 connections that also support DisplayPort 2.1 video-out. You'll also find two HDMI 2.1 ports, two RJ-45 Ethernet jacks, and the DC-in power connection. It's an impressive spread that will satisfy most buyers, but particularly professionals. (For instance, those dual Ethernet jacks are useful for either connection redundancy or connecting to two networks separately, say, to isolate internal corporate and external net traffic.) This is a lot for such a small computer, and most of you will likely be happy with this configuration. I would have liked to see an SD or microSD-card slot, too, but that's just a quibble. A single fan handles active cooling inside the NUC 16 Pro Mini, pushing air out through two small heatsinks. These are connected to a few thin copper heat pipes. The whole works keeps operating noise exceedingly mum, even when you push the system. I never heard this NUC strain or whoosh while running benchmarks. Asus, in fact, rates its maximum noise generation at an impressively low 38dBA. To see how it stacks up, I sent the NUC head-to-head against the systems listed below, all of them mini PCs with relatively powerful hardware for their sizes. Among these peers was a $3,039 HP Z2 Mini G1a review configuration (the most powerful of the bunch, a compact workstation), as well as the Geekom A9 Max 2026 Edition ($2,079 as tested), an upgraded version of our previous Editors’ Choice pick for the best overall Windows mini PC. The words "previous pick" say a lot about which machine won these contests. Rounding out the list, we have the $1,699 HP Eliteboard G1A AI configuration we reviewed, and the ECS Liva Z11 Plus ($699 as tested) as a representative budget mini PC. Our primary overall benchmark, UL's PCMark 10, puts a system through its paces in productivity apps ranging from web browsing to word processing and spreadsheet work. Its Full System Drive subtest measures a PC's storage throughput. Three more tests we rely on are CPU-centric or processor-intensive: Maxon's Cinebench 2024 uses that company's Cinema 4D engine to render a complex scene; Primate Labs' Geekbench 6.3 Pro simulates popular apps ranging from PDF rendering and speech recognition to machine learning; and we see how long it takes the video transcoder HandBrake 1.8 to convert a 12-minute clip from 4K to 1080p resolution. Finally, workstation maker Puget Systems' PugetBench for Creators gauges a PC's image-editing prowess in a variety of automated operations in the seminal photo editor Adobe Photoshop 25. The NUC 16 Pro Mini beat the field in both PCMark 10 tests—showing it has a speedy SSD, too—as well as the single-core Cinebench test. It fell to second in Cinebench multi-core speeds, HandBrake, and the multi-core Geekbench test. Meanwhile, it placed technically third in single-core Geekbench speeds (though, really, second, third, and fourth were a virtual tie in this lot) and came in third in Photoshop. First place (or a near-tie for first) in most tests beyond the PCMarks went to the HP Z2 Mini G1a, which has the strongest multicore performance among the systems. These results suggest that power-user productivity performance is this NUC's forte. You can still see a clear step up for content-creation tasks with HP's workstation-grade Z2 Mini and its AMD Ryzen AI Max+ Pro 395. For all desktops we test, we challenge the graphics silicon with a quintet of animations or gaming simulations from UL's 3DMark test suite. The first pair, Wild Life (1440p) and Wild Life Extreme (4K), uses the Vulkan graphics API to measure GPU speeds. The second set, Steel Nomad's regular and Light subtests, focuses on APIs more commonly used for game development, like Metal and DirectX 12, to assess gaming geometry and particle effects. Last, we turn to 3DMark Solar Bay to measure ray-tracing performance. The NUC 16 Pro Mini came in second in all of the 3DMark tests, with most of the other competing desktops trailing far behind. The HP Z2 Mini G1a, though, pulled ahead of the rest. Its processor tops the rest, and it has the punchiest graphics solution, too, AMD's Radeon 8060S. (The Radeon 8060S also distinguished itself in our recent review of the Asus TUF Gaming A14 gaming laptop, a rare gaming model with no discrete graphics chip.) Typically, for mini PCs, especially business units, our graphics tests end there. But I was curious to push its IGP further, given its promising results in the 3DMark trials. I ran some additional tests with the games Total War: Three Kingdoms and Shadow of the Tomb Raider. I ran these same tests on the Geekom A9 Max 2026 Edition, which employs a different flavor of Radeon integrated graphics. I didn’t have the other mini PCs I mentioned above available to test these games on them. Instead, I compared these game results against the IGPs from some other hardware that I had previously tested. I test the IGP on all desktop CPUs that I review with these two games, using medium graphics settings for Total War and low graphics settings for Shadow of the Tomb Raider. I also test all graphics cards with these games using Total War’s Ultra graphics preset and Shadow of the Tomb Raider’s Highest preset. So, I chose some representative desktop components for comaprison. Below, you can see how the NUC 16 Pro Mini's Arc B390 shapes up against the integrated graphics on these desktop CPUs: - AMD Ryzen 9 9950X (which uses integrated AMD Radeon Graphics) - AMD Ryzen 5 8500G (which uses an integrated AMD Radeon 740M) - Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus (which uses integrated Intel Xe LPG graphics) Also, you can see some comparisons against some of lowest-end graphics cards from the last five years: Here's how the NUC 16 Pro Mini shaped up in those face-offs... First off: I was surprised by how far behind the NUC the Geekom A9 Max performed in these tests. While I expected the NUC to be faster, I didn’t anticipate quite this difference. This is likely due, in part, to the different RAM supplied with these two mini PCs. The NUC’s RAM operates at 9,600MHz, while the Geekom’s DDR5 RAM is clocked far slower, at 5,600MHz. This is a massive difference in bandwidth, and GPUs are heavily reliant on memory bandwidth to maintain fast performance. This likely hampered the Geekom’s speed somewhat. Now let's look at the IGPs on the three desktop chips. Powerful IGPs are more common on mobile processors, used for PCs in which adding a graphics card is impossible. While desktop IGPs are capable of more than they are typically given credit for, they tend to struggle against the best of their mobile competition, and it showed here. Take the Intel Core Ultra 7 270K Plus: It's equipped with the fastest IGP that Intel provides on a desktop platform, and it lagged far behind the NUC's Arc B390 IGP in both tests. That's despite this being a socketed desktop chip with much more aggressive cooling than the NUC. As for the comparisons against the low-end graphics cards, the Arc B390 was competitive with all three of the basic GPUs here in Shadow of the Tomb Raider. Meanwhile, it trounced them all in Total War, likely down to that game's heavy reliance on the CPU and the high memory bandwidth available to the NUC. (Plus, these three cards are all between four and seven years old.) This mini desktop isn't designed as a gaming PC, by any means, but it can hold its own against the low end of discrete graphics. I expect this will vary heavily by game, though. The size of this system would make it perfect for sitting on a TV stand in your living room. I could also see it as an attractive option for travel. While at a usability disadvantage against laptops, due to it lacking a built-in screen, a battery, a keyboard, and a mouse, its small size makes it a sensible option for, say, connecting to a TV in a hotel room, where maybe you want something faster to work on (or game on!) than a basic laptop can provide. Final Thoughts Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini, in the configuration that we tested or one like it, will set you back quite a bit when purchased individually. But the performance for the size is pretty impressive. It will power through any general office tasks you throw at it, as well as light content-creation work. It's also packed with features that IT managers and other business users will appreciate, like an extended warranty with direct support, hardware-level security, and deep AI development readiness. On top of that, its CPU and graphics speeds make it a capable pinch-hitter gaming PC. All of this comes in a compact package that's easy to tuck away on any desk. Among the mini PCs in our head-to-head tests, only the HP Z2 Mini G1a gave the NUC any real competition. The Z2 is technically a mini workstation with an even bigger price tag, making the pricey NUC 16 Pro Mini look even more attractive if you need density of performance at the smallest possible size. Even the more affordable version of the NUC should deliver good value for the price. It won’t be quite as fast, but that trade-off may well be worth it. For eclipsing the previous title holder, we give the Asus NUC 16 Pro Mini our Editors' Choice award among mini PCs. About Our Expert I have been interested in science and technology for as long as I can remember, spurred on by a fondness for video games. I learned to work in Windows and manipulate files to get buggy games to work, and I learned to build and upgrade PCs for better performance. In my role at PCMag for the past four years, I’ve deeply enjoyed the opportunity to share my knowledge and expertise. Before PCMag, I wrote for Tom's Hardware for three years, where I covered tech news, deals, and wrote some hands-on reviews. After working as a PCMag contributor for a time reviewing desktops, PC cases, budget processors, and motherboards, I now focus on testing and reviewing processors and graphics cards and sharing my insights on the industry.

item.title: We May Get the iPhone Ultra This Week. Every Rumor We Think Is Legit
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.86
It's no surprise that Apple is late to the folding phone party while its major rivals—Google, Motorola, and Samsung in the US, and many more abroad—take massive bites out of the hinged-handset pie. Apple has long taken a "wait and see" approach to emerging form factors. As a phone expert, I've tested intriguing foldables, from the not-so-great Microsoft Surface Duo to the more successful Samsung Galaxy Z Flip series, as well as the Google Pixel Fold and Motorola Razr lines. But where's Apple's fun and flexible iPhone Flip? I vividly remember when, in 2019, Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak told Bloomberg that "[Apple] is not the leader in areas like the folding phone, and that worries me because I really want a folding phone." Well, if the rumors are anything to go by, it looks like The Woz is finally getting his wish. Whispers about Apple's foldable project date back to 2016, but this year, reports have skyrocketed. As someone who's obsessed with both iPhones and foldables, I'm excited that these worlds may collide in an ambitious new piece of hardware that could make Apple's rivals sweat. Foldable iPhone: All the Credible Rumors So Far Given Apple's long-standing iPhone naming conventions, you may expect the company to announce the iPhone 18 Fold. However, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, one of the most credible Apple leakers, there may be a twist: Apple might go with iPhone Ultra, instead. Gurman claims the foldable is still on track for this fall, despite chatter about manufacturing snags. That said, the so-called iPhone Ultra is expected to launch at the Surprise and Shine Sept. 9 event, alongside the iPhone 18 series. What will Apple's foldable look like? Gurman called it "the most significant overhaul in the iPhone’s history and the first actual form-factor change." It won't open vertically like the Samsung Z Flip 7 or the Motorola Razr Ultra. Instead, it will open from side to side, like a book, revealing a larger display that's roughly the same size as the iPad mini. For reference, it won't be like the skinny Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7, which is thinner than some regular phones. According to a recent interview with Tom's Guide, Gurman said that the iPhone foldable will more closely resemble the Galaxy Z Fold 8, adopting a wider footprint for its inner display. Apple reportedly plans to pitch the iPhone Ultra as a device that's more beneficial for web browsing, framing subjects with a gigantic viewfinder, and most importantly, watching video. Samsung leaned heavily into the fact that the Z Fold 8 reduced letterboxing for a more pleasant streaming experience—Apple may roll out similar marketing plans. Gurman also expects the larger display to make the iPhone Ultra “awesome for gaming,” delivering a far more immersive experience similar to handheld gaming consoles. Having tested the Z Fold 8, I completely agree. Gaming on a wider foldable screen is glorious. For the first time in years, I actually want to play mobile games because I’m no longer confined to a cramped, narrow display. Similar to the Z Fold 8, the iPhone Ultra won’t have a dedicated telephoto camera, so you’ll miss out on the enhanced zoom capabilities Apple will likely offer on its iPhone 18 Pro models. The rumored Apple foldable may also lack Face ID, meaning users could have to rely solely on Touch ID for biometric security. Bloomberg's sources say Apple will introduce "apps [that] look more like iPad software" to accommodate the upcoming foldable. Similar to the experience you'd find on rival foldables, the foldable iPhone will reportedly launch side-by-side apps. However, unlike the iPad, it can't run multiple windows at once. Although Gurman's reports often liken the rumored iPhone Ultra to a tiny iPad, it's worth noting that it's expected to run iOS, not iPadOS. We've already seen early glimpses of foldable-friendly software at WWDC. Apple's documentation emphasizes to developers the importance of creating apps that support a "dynamic range of sizes and aspect ratios." As for the processor, there's speculation that the foldable iPhone will run on Apple's A20 Pro chip, which is also expected to power the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. The real question is, how does Apple plan to stand out from the crowd? As mentioned, the Z Fold 8 appears to be quite similar to the rumored iPhone Ultra. On top of that, Apple faces stiff competition from devices like the Motorola Razr Fold and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which we recently reviewed. Sources close to Apple's foldable project claim the iPhone Ultra will solve issues that other rivals struggle with, including that pesky crease in the middle of the display. Gurman acknowledged that Samsung has made “serious strides on the crease,” but told Tom’s Guide that Apple’s approach to tackling the center trench will be “a little bit better,” thanks to the stronger hinge rumored to be coming to the iPhone Ultra. Reportedly called Liquid Metal, the hinge is said to use a teardrop-shaped internal structure that helps distribute and reduce stress when folding. Another way the iPhone Ultra could stand out is with MagSafe. The iPhone Ultra will reportedly feature MagSafe support for case-free magnetic charging. Samsung’s foldables, on the other hand, aren’t quite there yet. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 support wireless charging, but without built-in magnets, you’ll need a compatible case to use magnetic chargers. The Cupertino company's forthcoming foldable is expected to be priced between $2,000 and $2,500, which is not a surprise for envelope-pushing tech or for Apple. Apple's Surprise and Shine event is set to kick off in Cupertino at 10 a.m. PT / 1:00 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Sept. 9. We'll be there to bring you all the news. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

item.title: Don't Miss These Still-Available Labor Day Deals on Laptops and Desktops
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.81
I spent the weekend tracking Labor Day sales across multiple retailers to spotlight the deepest discounts on laptops and desktops, focusing on top-rated machines that we've tested in the PC Labs. If you were too busy grilling and having a good time to get any shopping done, don't stress. Some—but not all—of the deals we found are still good as of Tuesday morning. We've still got Alienware gaming machines, mini desktops, all-in-ones, and everything else you could want at the summer's best prices, but there's no guarantee they'll stay discounted much longer. Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x Laptop Labor Day Deal For a solid budget-priced option, you can't go wrong with this $200 post-Labor Day discount on the capable Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3x. While this isn't a portable that you're going to squeeze top-tier gaming performance out of, it's an absolutely dependable daily driver with excellent battery life thanks to the power-efficient Snapdragon X processor. We put it through its paces in a comprehensive review and overall felt positively about it, commenting that it felt solid and sturdy, ran for nearly 30 hours in our testing, and handled productivity tasks with ease. We did note that the keyboard felt a little cramped, one downside of the 15-inch form factor, but aside from that it was very pleasurable to use. Dell 2K Touchscreen Laptop Labor Day Deal For a budget-priced Windows machine, this Dell is an absolute steal. Typically portable PCs under $500 have dire loadouts and murky monitors, but this one is a full 2K IPS touch display with good color and contrast. Under the hood, you're getting great component value, with a peppy but affordable Intel Core i5 processor running the show and 512 gigabytes of internal storage. I would say that the 8GB of DDR5 RAM is slightly skimpy, but memory prices are absolutely out of control right now so it's not surprising. Just don't keep a million browser tabs open and you'll probably be fine. The keyboard and touchpad are both good-sized and well-built, and port selection is solid but not exceptional. Battery life is also a strong point, with fast charging taking you from zero to 80% full in just an hour. Lenovo Legion Pro 5i Gen 10 Gaming Laptop Labor Day Deal For something with a little more horsepower, Lenovo's delivering a discount of over a thousand dollars on its Legion Pro 5i gaming laptop. We gave this one an Editors' Choice award in our review, with our expert Charles Jefferies declaring that it "offers compelling value for gamers" thanks to a solid component loadout, including a Blackwell-series RTX 5070 graphics card, tons of system memory, and top-flight connectivity with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4. Although some versions of this laptop ship with an OLED display, this particular offer has an IPS screen, which is not as high-end but still quite good, with 500 nits of brightness and a 240Hz refresh rate. Because it's a Lenovo, the keyboard and touchpad also both feel spectacular. Alienware 16 Aurora Gaming Laptop Labor Day Deal Here's a huge deal that's still good post-Labor Day. Dell is offering $900 off of an entry-level Alienware 16 Aurora laptop, and just from sheer component value you're getting your money's worth. While it's not pushing the envelope in terms of resolution, the RTX 5050 graphics card is more than capable of whip-fast framerates to the crisp 2560x1600 display. We have a review of the similar 16X Aurora, where it took home an "Excellent" rating for its sturdy but compact design, with no thermal shelf for a more modest profile, along with a well-considered port selection. While Alienware machines typically land on the higher end of the price spectrum, this discount cuts it down well into a more competitive bracket. Asus ROG Strix G16 Gaming Laptop Labor Day Deal For a gaming portable with a little more juice to squeeze, this is a very nice 28% discount on a midrange Asus that brings the heat. We have an extensive review of this model, awarding it an Editors' Choice nod for its 165Hz ultra-high refresh rate Nebula display, lightning-fast performance both in synthetic benchmarking and real-world testing, and surprisingly long battery life. The RTX 5060 graphics card is one of the best current-gen options for gaming laptops, easily keeping up with the 1200p screen. Visually, it's a treat as well, with a full-sized RGB backlit gaming keyboard, attractive styling, and plenty of ports. This bundle comes with a wireless gaming mouse and headset. The Dell Slim has a relatively small footprint without compromising on performance, featuring a perky 20-core Intel Core Ultra 7 processor that we consider an excellent value for the money, easily capable of handling everyday productivity and entertainment tasks all day long. A full terabyte of internal storage is also a surprise, given how spendy SSDs are these days. item.title: Someone might be in your PayPal account. Here’s a quick way to check
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.53
According to the FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report, the number of reported cybercrimes exceeded 1 million last year, with trends showing a year-on-year increase. A common vector of online crime is the unauthorized access to online accounts. Payment services such as PayPal are a particular target for fraudsters. This quick test shows you how to tell whether your PayPal account has been affected. The key warning signs: What you should check first Not every unusual account activity automatically means you’ve been hacked. But these signs should set alarm bells ringing: - Unfamiliar transactions in your transaction history are the clearest sign. In your PayPal account, go to “Activity” to view your transaction history and check the most recent entries. Payments to unknown recipients or amounts you cannot recall are a serious warning sign. - Your password no longer works. After a breach, criminals often change the password first to lock out the actual account holder. If your usual password is suddenly rejected without you having changed it yourself, take immediate action. - You are receiving confirmation emails for activities you did not initiate. These include login notifications from unfamiliar devices or locations, password reset requests you never made, or emails about added payment methods. - Unfamiliar devices linked to your account. In PayPal, click the cog icon in the top right-hand corner, open “Security” and click “Manage” next to “Manage logins.” If a smartphone, computer, or browser appears there that you do not recognize, someone else has logged into your account. - Unexpected SMS codes. Have you received a 2FA code even though you’re not currently logging into PayPal? This means someone knows your password and is trying to log in. You still have access: These steps are crucial now If you can still log in to your account, act as quickly as possible. Every minute counts. Step 1: Change your password immediately Open PayPal directly in your browser. In your account, click on the cog icon in the top right-hand corner, then select “Security” and “Password.” Change your password straight away to a new, secure one containing at least 16 characters, including upper- and lower-case letters, numbers, and special characters. Only use this password for PayPal. Tip: If you haven’t yet started managing your passwords with a password manager, now is a good time to do so. Foundry Step 2: End all active sessions Click on the cog icon, then on “Security,” and next to “Manage logins,” click on “Manage.” Here you’ll see all active logins, along with the device, location, and timestamp. Remove any entries you don’t recognize. Step 3: Check linked payment methods In the top navigation bar, open “Wallet,” check all saved bank accounts and credit cards, and remove anything you didn’t add yourself. Next, check which merchants are authorized to make recurring direct debits from your account: Click on the cog icon, then on “Payments,” and a little further down, open “Direct Debit Payments.” If an unknown entry appears there, click on it, select “Cancel,” and confirm by clicking “Cancel direct debit payments.” You should also inform your bank if your credit card or current account is linked to the compromised account. Step 4: Report unauthorized transactions You can dispute any payment that you did not initiate yourself via the Resolution Center. Click on “Help” in the top navigation bar, then on “Resolution Center” further down the page. There, select the transaction you wish to dispute and click “Continue.” Then select “I want to report unauthorized account access” and follow the instructions. Foundry Alternatively, click on the suspicious transaction under “Activity,” select “Get help,” and report the transaction as unauthorized via the PayPal AI Assistant. PayPal usually processes such cases within 10 days and will refund the money, provided you report the transaction within 180 days of the debit. Step 5: Enable two-factor authentication If you haven’t already done so: Click on the cog icon, then on “Security” and finally on “Two-step verification.” This ensures that nobody can log in without your confirmation code, even if they know your password. Our 2FA guide explains exactly how this works. An even more secure option is a passkey, which PayPal also offers under “Security.” This eliminates the need for a password altogether. No longer have access? Here’s how to regain access to your PayPal account If your password no longer works, the attacker has already locked you out. Follow these steps in this order: - On the login page, click on “Forgot your password?” and enter your email address. PayPal will then send a reset link to that address. If the attacker has also changed your email address, you’ll need to contact PayPal’s customer service directly. The quickest way to do this is via www.paypal.com/us/cshelp/personal or by telephone on the freephone number 1-888-221-1161. - Have your personal details to hand: date of birth, recent account activity, and payment details. With this information, PayPal can verify your identity and restore access. - You should also report the incident to the police. This may sound like a bureaucratic hassle, but it is important: You will often need a reference number for a chargeback via your bank or for any subsequent legal action. How to protect your account in the long term A hacked account is a real nuisance. To prevent this from happening in the first place, you should take the following measures or follow these rules: - Use a password for PayPal that you don’t use anywhere else. A password manager such as Bitwarden or Dashlane helps ensure you don’t have to remember it. - In your account, under Settings (cog icon) > Security, enable “Two-step verification.” Even better: Set up a passkey. Then attackers won’t be able to do anything even if they have your password. - PayPal will never send you emails asking you to enter your password via a link. If in doubt, always go directly to the settings via paypal.com and never via links in emails. Our guide shows you the most common phishing warning signs in emails. - Avoid logging in via open networks in cafés, hotels, or at railway stations, as these are a gateway for attackers. Instead, use a VPN or log in via your mobile data plan. - Your email account is the key to everything. If attackers gain access to your emails, they can reset your password for virtually any online service. You should therefore also secure your email account with a strong, unique password and two-factor authentication (2FA).

item.title: Microsoft’s September updates fix a record 973 security flaws
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.18
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft’s September update patches a record 973 security vulnerabilities, doubling the previous month’s total, with 113 classified as critical. - Two zero-day exploits are already being actively used by attackers, and flaws in Windows, Excel, SharePoint, and Windows Hello could allow remote code execution or privilege escalation. - Users are strongly urged to update their Microsoft software immediately to protect against these serious risks. Yesterday was September Patch Tuesday, which means Microsoft released security updates addressing 973 new security vulnerabilities. That’s more than twice as many as last month and a new record. Along with Windows and Office, other products have been updated, including Defender, Exchange Server, Hyper-V, Skype for Business, Visual Studio, and Microsoft’s cloud services. Microsoft classifies 113 of the 973 vulnerabilities as critical, including 83 remote code execution (RCE) issues. The remaining vulnerabilities are classified as high risk, and two are already being exploited in the wild. The next Patch Tuesday is scheduled for October 13th, 2026. Windows security vulnerabilities A large number of the vulnerabilities—over 700 this time—are spread across the various Windows versions (10, 11, Server) for which Microsoft still provides security updates. This month, two Windows vulnerabilities classified as high risk are already being exploited in the wild. The CVE-2026-81963 vulnerability in the Windows Update stack allows attackers to gain elevated privileges, enabling them to execute code with system privileges by combining this exploit with an RCE vulnerability. The second zero-day vulnerability, CVE-2026-85880, is in Windows Advanced Local Procedure Call (ALPC) and it’s also an elevation of privilege (EoP) vulnerability. In this case, the exploit code must be concealed within a document so that a user can trigger it. For both zero-days, it’s unclear how widespread the attacks are. Critical Windows vulnerabilities Microsoft has classified 77 Windows vulnerabilities as critical, including 56 RCE vulnerabilities. These include CVE-2026-69525 in the Windows Remote Desktop Service, a use-after-free (UAF) vulnerability that an attacker could exploit to remotely execute injected code without authentication or user interaction. Windows Hello also has nine vulnerabilities, eight of which are EoP vulnerabilities classified as critical. Microsoft had to patch 64 vulnerabilities in the biometric service, most of them very similar to one another and following the same pattern. In 56 cases, there are buffer overflows. CVE-2026-69727 allows elevated privileges over the network, while CVE-2026-73008 exposes personal data—hardly what one would want or expect from a biometric service. Microsoft Office security vulnerabilities Microsoft has fixed 137 vulnerabilities in its Office products, slightly more than in August. These include 22 RCE vulnerabilities classified as critical, five of which are in Excel alone. In the case of critical RCE vulnerabilities in Office, the preview pane is often an attack vector—a user doesn’t need to open a malicious file for an attack to succeed. Meanwhile, RCE vulnerabilities classified as high risk can be exploited when a user opens a malicious file in a vulnerable Office product (called “open-and-own”). In SharePoint, Microsoft has patched 16 vulnerabilities, six of which are RCE vulnerabilities. Microsoft Exchange Server vulnerabilities This month, Microsoft has fixed nine vulnerabilities in Exchange Server, all of which are classified as high risk. These include two RCE vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-55007 and CVE-2026-69355. In the case of CVE-2026-55007, an attacker need only send an email containing a malicious Visio file. The exploit is triggered when the email is processed, without the need for a preview pane. Microsoft Edge security vulnerabilities The latest security update to Edge 152.0.4191.66 is dated September 4th and is based on Chromium 152.0.7977.83. It addresses one zero-day vulnerability as well as other Chromium vulnerabilities that aren’t included in the total number of vulnerabilities mentioned above.

item.title: Windows 11’s next security feature may cost you gaming performance
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.14
Next month’s Patch Tuesday falls on October 13th, and with that update, Microsoft will be enabling “Memory Integrity” on all Windows 11 systems that are still receiving updates, according to this Windows IT Pro blog post. Memory Integrity (also known as Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity, or HVCI) has been around for some time, but it hasn’t been enabled yet on many PCs. Starting October 13th, 2026, all supported Windows 11 PCs will enable Memory Integrity by default. While Memory Integrity is primarily intended as a security feature, gamers may find it a hindrance. What does it actually do? Well, Memory Integrity ensures that only verified kernel-mode code is loaded on the PC, blocking unsigned rootkits and raising the barrier to driver-based kernel attacks. The goal is for Windows 11 to be better protected against malware attacks. Before Windows enables this feature, it will check eligible computers and verify whether the machine is ready for it. According to this support page, Memory Integrity requires the following hardware: - 8th-generation Intel processor or newer - AMD Zen 2 or newer - Qualcomm Snapdragon 8180 or newer - At least 8GB of RAM on x64 systems - A 64GB SSD with firmware-enabled virtualization - Drivers with confirmed compatibility with Memory Integrity However, this feature has a major drawback: Memory Integrity can apparently slow down games. Tom’s Hardware measured years ago that HVCI combined with VBS (Virtualization-Based Security) causes games to run up to 15 percent slower. VBS is also enabled as part of this update, providing additional security features. According to Tom’s Hardware, Microsoft confirmed in 2022 that “Memory Integrity and Virtual Machine Platform could affect gaming performance on some Windows 11 configurations, and advised gamers prioritizing performance that they could temporarily disable these protections while playing, warning that doing so reduces security.” Gaming performance losses are most likely to be noticeable on computers with older hardware. Tom’s Hardware continued, saying that Microsoft’s guidance for gamers recommended “temporarily disabling Memory Integrity and VMP where they interfere with gaming performance.”

item.title: Office 2021 loses support in October. This tool keeps it safe anyway
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.71
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft will end support for Office 2021 on October 13, 2026, leaving users without official security or feature updates and potentially vulnerable to threats. - A third-party tool called 0patch offers unofficial micropatches that fix vulnerabilities without altering original software code, providing security coverage for up to three years. - 0patch costs €24.95 annually for private users and €34.95 per PC for businesses, though Microsoft recommends upgrading to Microsoft 365 or Office 2024 as the primary alternative. Microsoft plans to end support for Office 2021 once and for all on October 13th, 2026. This means users of this version will no longer receive updates—both feature updates and security updates. Because of that, continued use of Office 2021 will be unsafe past that date. However, if you still wish to continue using Office 2021 after support ends, you can do so with 0patch. As the company explains in this blog post, 0patch will provide Office 2021 with unofficial security updates for up to three years (and possibly longer if there’s sufficient demand). You may already be familiar with 0patch. Back when Microsoft ended support for Windows 10, the company stepped in and promised updates for Windows 10 until 2030. Although the official end of extended Windows 10 support has been postponed once again, 0patch continues to provide its own updates for critical issues. 0patch operates with what are known as “micropatches.” These micropatches don’t require direct access to Office 2021’s code, but instead integrate their own code fragments externally. Not only do these micropatches help to patch vulnerabilities and resolve issues, but they can also be removed in case of errors and bugs. What 0patch costs (plus alternatives) 0patch is a promising way to continue using Office 2021, but it’s not completely free. Although the company provides select updates free of charge to private users, it’ll cost €24.95 per year per PC for the full range of security updates. For business customers, the price is €34.95. If you don’t use 0patch, Microsoft’s recommendation is to either switch to Microsoft 365 or Office 2024. Not sure which one is right for you? See our guide to choosing Microsoft 365 or Office 2024. Note: 0patch doesn’t offer traditional support for the software being patched. That’s still the responsibility of Microsoft, although they’re unlikely to be of much help once official support ends.

item.title: Google Earth’s flight simulator now works right in your browser
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.65
Google sometimes releases fun bonus features for its products and services. Recently, Google Earth gained a kind of flight simulator. Google has long been working with maps, satellite and aerial images, and street views—these are packaged in various ways. Google Maps is the most widely used service, but there’s also another popular option in Google Earth. With it, you can do everything from viewing the Earth from above to zooming all the way down to street level. But the most recent feature is a simple flight simulator. You can’t make any advanced technical adjustments to your aircraft in the way that’s possible in something like Microsoft Flight Simulator. Instead, it’s simply a way to fly around and view the Earth from the skies. While the built-in flight simulator was previously only available in the desktop version of Google Earth, it’s now accessible via web browser. Here’s how to start using it: Joel Lee / Foundry Go to earth.google.com, then click the “Explore Earth” button at the top. You might be prompted to pay for a premium subscription, but you can ignore this. There’s no need to log in either. Go to the location where you want to start your flight. You can do this using the “Search Google Earth” bar at the top left or by manually zooming and panning around the Earth view. Once you’re ready, click on Tools → Flight simulator in the menu. Your flight will now begin and you can control your airplane using the arrow keys or mouse to turn and the Page Up and Page Down keys to increase or decrease the throttle, respectively.

item.title: 4 ways to get Windows 11’s newest features sooner — from safe to experimental
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.34
A new Windows update does not automatically mean that every user receives the same features on the same day. Microsoft rolls out many new features in stages. Even if a feature is technically already part of the installed version of Windows, it may initially remain disabled on your PC. There’s a method to this: With phased rollouts, Microsoft can initially deliver new features to a subset of users and monitor whether any issues arise. If errors occur, the rollout can be halted or adjusted before millions of computers are affected. Some new features are also only enabled in specific versions of Windows or in certain regions. For those who are impatient, there are therefore several ways to speed up the official rollout. The simplest involves going directly to the Windows Update settings. If you want to test the updates even sooner, you can install optional preview updates or join the Windows Insider Program. Finally, with ViveTool, you can even activate hidden settings in Windows to gain access to new features. It’s important to note that the further you stray from the standard Windows Update process, the greater the risk of errors. For an everyday PC or an important work computer, the most radical method is therefore not always recommended. Four ways to access new Windows features How soon do you want to try out new features? Depending on the method you choose, you’ll gain access to new Windows features at different speeds: - Enable the latest updates: In the Windows Update settings, there’s a toggle that lets you receive new features and updates as early as possible. This is the simplest and safest way. - Install optional updates: Microsoft releases preview updates towards the end of the month. These often already contain bug fixes and improvements that are later rolled out as standard updates. Installation is carried out manually via Windows Update. - Use Windows Insider: The Insider Program gives you access to pre-release versions of Windows. For keen users, the Beta Channel is usually the best balance between new features and day-to-day usability. If you prefer maximum stability, choose the Release Preview Channel. - Enable hidden features with ViveTool: The open-source tool ViveTool can unlock certain features that are already included in Windows but have not yet been activated. However, this requires some experience and a willingness to experiment. 1. Get new features sooner Foundry The easiest way to access new Windows features is via an inconspicuous toggle in the update settings. This tells Microsoft that you’d like to receive new features and updates as early as possible. To do this, open ‘Settings > Windows Update.’ There, enable the option ‘Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available.’ Windows will then continue to check for updates as normal, but will prioritize your device when Microsoft rolls out new features or improvements. What the toggle does — and doesn’t do This setting is particularly useful for users who want to try out new features as early as possible without having to install pre-release versions of Windows. You’ll continue to receive security updates regardless. However, at Microsoft, “immediately” does not necessarily mean that a new feature will appear straight after activation. Many new features are rolled out gradually. Microsoft may initially enable a feature for only some compatible computers and expand its availability later. So if an announced new feature still doesn’t appear despite the toggle being activated, this isn’t necessarily a fault. In such cases, a little patience often helps — or one of the following methods. 2. Manually install optional updates Foundry If you’d like to get your hands on new improvements a little earlier, you can take a look at the optional updates. These are often preview versions of upcoming, non-security-related updates. They contain, for example, bug fixes, drivers, or improvements that Microsoft will later roll out to all users via a regular update. These updates usually appear towards the end of the month and must be installed manually. They are therefore not part of the automatic update service. How to find the preview updates: Open ‘Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Optional updates.’ If updates are available there, you can select the packages you want and then install them. Depending on the update, relevant offers may also appear directly on the Windows Update homepage. The optional quality updates can be particularly interesting. They sometimes already contain improvements that will only be automatically installed on your computer on the next regular patch day. If you want to fix specific bugs or try out new improvements earlier, you can often access them here in advance. Please note, however, that an optional update is not automatically a major feature update. Nor does it necessarily include every new Windows feature. Whether a new feature is already included and enabled for your device also depends on the specific rollout. For users keen to experiment, however, this method offers a sensible middle ground: You stick with a standard and generally stable version of Windows, but get certain improvements slightly earlier than others. 3. Windows Insider: Test new features much sooner Foundry If you find the standard Windows updates aren’t quick enough, you can get a head start yourself: through the Windows Insider Program, Microsoft provides preview versions of Windows that may already include new features and changes before they are officially released. Participation in the Insider Program is free and can be enabled directly within Windows. Open ‘Settings > Windows Update > Windows Insider Program’ and follow the instructions. Then select your preferred channel. Which Insider channel is the right one? Microsoft divides the Insider Program into four channels. They differ primarily in how early — and therefore how experimental — the Windows versions they contain are. Release Preview: This channel is closest to the next final version of Windows. New updates usually appear here shortly before general release. It is suitable for users who want to try out upcoming features early on, while taking as few risks as possible. Beta: The Beta channel offers the best middle ground for many users. New features are often made available here much earlier than in the Release Preview channel, but the builds are generally considered to be significantly more stable than those in the Dev or Canary channels. Ideal for anyone who wants to test new Windows features whilst still being able to use their PC reliably in everyday life. Dev: This channel is aimed at users who want to try out new Windows developments at a very early stage. However, the features included are often still at an early stage of development and may change significantly or even be dropped before release. Important: Switching back may require a fresh installation of Windows. Canary: This is where Microsoft is most keen to experiment. The builds may contain very early innovations that are still a long way from being intended for general release. This channel is therefore not well suited for a PC used for important work or day-to-day tasks. Here too, switching back may require a fresh installation, depending on the build. Our recommendation: If you want to try out new features as early as possible but still use your PC productively, the Beta channel is the best choice. If, on the other hand, your main priority is to test upcoming features in advance with as little risk as possible, stay on the Release Preview Channel. | Channel | New features | Stability | Suitable for | | Release Preview | Shortly before the official rollout | ★★★★☆ | Users who want to test new features early on, whilst ensuring they are as stable as possible | | Beta | Well ahead of the official rollout | ★★★☆☆ | Ambitious users and curious everyday users | | Dev | Very early | ★★☆☆☆ | Testers and Windows enthusiasts | | Canary | The earliest | ★☆☆☆☆ | Developers and power users keen to experiment | ⚠️ Important: Insider builds are pre-release versions and may contain bugs, compatibility issues, or changes to functionality. You should therefore back up your important data before joining. You should be particularly careful with Dev and Canary: Depending on the build, switching back to a regular version of Windows may not be possible via the settings and may require a complete reinstallation! 4. ViveTool: Unlock hidden features Don’t want to wait for Microsoft to enable a feature on your PC? That’s where ViveTool comes in. This free, open-source program can activate hidden feature toggles in Windows, thereby unlocking certain functions that are already present in the system but haven’t yet been made available to all users. However, this approach does require a certain level of technical understanding. Many features are hidden for a reason: They may still be unfinished, could change at any time, or might cause unexpected errors. ViveTool works with what are known as Feature IDs. These switches can be selectively enabled or disabled via the command line. Which IDs are relevant for a particular version of Windows depends on the specific build and the function in question. Important: Do not randomly activate Feature IDs found on the internet. An incompatible or as yet unfinished feature may lead to error messages, crashes or other problems. You should therefore create at least one system restore point and back up important data before experimenting. ViveTool explained in detail: In our guide, we explain which commands you need, exactly how the tool works, and what you absolutely must bear in mind when using it. ViveTool is the most powerful, but also the most demanding method when it comes to gaining early access to features. For most users, the options provided by Windows itself are sufficient. Conclusion: Test new features earlier For most users interested in new Windows features, the toggle in Windows Update is sufficient. Those who wish to test them even earlier can use optional updates or the Insider Program. ViveTool, on the other hand, is intended for experienced users who want to experiment specifically with hidden features. Please note, however: The more experimental the method, the more important it is to make a backup. You should therefore back up important data before experimenting with Insider builds or ViveTool.

item.title: 12 ways to make your old PC feel new again
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.27
There’s no denying that all of our next PC upgrades are likely to be more expensive than they’ve been in a long time. Memory shortages, SSD shortages, graphics card shortages—it’s all driving prices up. And if history is anything to go by, they won’t come all the way down again. (They will come down at some point, it’s just not clear when.) So, one strategy to survive this current crisis in PC components? Outlast it. Stave off your next upgrade as long as you can, hope prices stabilize soon, then retreat as demand falls off. But if your current PC isn’t cutting it—if your gaming or workflows are starting to struggle under the age of your system—there are ways you can refresh your system, make it feel new, and keep it going long enough to squeeze more juice out of it. Enable XMP/EXPO This is one of the easiest and most useful performance boosters for any PC that has anything beyond the most basic DDR memory. If you aren’t running your RAM sticks with XMP/EXPO enabled, you could be leaving a lot of performance on the table. Ian Paul / Foundry Duck into your BIOS and make sure you have one of the profiles enabled for your memory: XMP for Intel or EXPO for AMD. Enabling this will boost your memory clocks up to their rated speeds. Enable Resizable BAR (ReBAR) AMD Resizable Bar (ReBAR), also known as Smart Access Memory for AMD, gives your CPU full access to your GPU’s VRAM without the need to break it up into chunks. It can make your graphics card perform notably faster, especially if it’s an Intel GPU. Check your graphics drivers (or the BIOS) to make sure this is enabled to make the most of your GPU. Clear out SSD storage Jon Martindale / IDG If you’re running low on storage, you aren’t just lacking the space you need to install your next game or app—it can actually have a significant impact on your SSD’s performance, too. Modern SSDs need between 10% and 20% spare capacity to efficiently move data around and make the most of their ultra-fast random access capabilities. Freeing up spare capacity is one of the easiest ways to boost SSD performance—and it’ll even increase overall SSD lifespan. So, if your main SSD or game library drive is getting full, delete a bunch of unused apps, games, and/or files. You should notice a real uptick in system responsiveness. (Don’t know what to delete? Use the free WizTree app, one of my favorite hidden gem apps on Windows.) Update your drivers Jon Martindale / Foundry I know it’s boring and takes a minute, but keeping your drivers up to date is one of the best ways to make sure your system is running at peak performance and efficiency. The main ones to update are your graphics drivers, but chipset drivers are also important, and if you’re feeling a little braver, BIOS updates can help improve system stability and give you more options for tweaking hardware. Bonus points if you use Display Driver Uninstaller (DDU) to make sure the old drivers are really cleared out. Update your operating system Microsoft Keeping your operating system updated is as unexciting as keeping your drivers current, but it ensures you’re enjoying the most efficient and performant experience you can get on your PC. Updates often include security features, too, so making sure you’re up to date with all the latest patches is just good practice in general. Any light performance bumps along the way are just icing on top. Take care of your battery Panos Sakalakis / Unsplash If your daily driver is a laptop, then keeping the battery in peak condition is paramount to making that laptop last the long haul. Don’t overcharge it. Use plugged-in power when you can. Keep the screen brightness down when you don’t need it. That’s just scratching the surface! Heed all my tips for ensuring long battery life and you’ll extend the lifespan of your battery by quite a bit. Do an annual spring cleaning Whether it’s blocked laptop vents or dust-clogged heatsinks, dirt and debris can easily build up in PCs and laptops. Not only is it gross, but it absolutely does lead to weaker performance. If the heat can’t escape, the fans have to spin harder to stay cool, and then it’s a slippery slope to thermal throttling and system instability. Make sure you’re giving your PC a regular clean at least once every six months. That’ll help keep it working as it should over the long term. For a more advanced refresh of your system, consider some in-depth cable tidying. You can re-paste your CPU if it’s been a few years. You can re-paste your GPU, but that will void your warranty on many cards, so double-check you’re happy risking that before proceeding. Lightly overclock your hardware Overclocking can be complicated and time consuming, but there are plenty of apps out there that’ll help ease the learning curve and let you enjoy a modest overclock at the press of a button. Nvidia Nvidia, AMD, and Intel all have apps for automated GPU overclocking, and that alone net you a few percent of extra performance. The same goes with CPUs from AMD and Intel, though not all of them can be overclocked like this. Learn more in our article on cheap/free ways to make an old computer run faster. Memory overclocking is an option, too, but beyond enabling the XMP/EXPO profile (which I mentioned above) it can get quite complex. Just make sure the memory profile is enabled and you should be good. Need more storage? Go external If you can’t just delete stuff from your main SSD but you need more storage space, just get an external SSD and call it a day. But you don’t need a PCIe 5.0 SSD that costs hundreds of dollars. If you’re tight on cash, maybe resort to an older PCIe 3.0 design. Consider even buying a small SATA drive to tide you over. Nor Gal / Shutterstock.com Most external SSDs these days are fast enough to play games from, but even if they’re not, storage is storage if you don’t have enough. You could even consider buying a classic hard drive if you just need somewhere to put stuff. They’re cheap and they’re great for holding large files like games and videos. Factory reset your PC This one’s more drastic, but if you can easily back up your most important files, then performing a PC factory reset is a great way to get it back to what it was like when you first bought it. Foundry It clears out any lingering malware and bloatware, dumps all the old drivers that are still kicking around, and lets you reinstall only the apps, games, and services that you actually use. Not convinced? Check out these crucial signs that it’s time to reset your PC. Just be extra sure you’ve backed up important data first. Don’t forget browser bookmarks, any offline password manager databases, sensitive work and personal documents and files. Get it all on an external drive or in the cloud before you clear everything with a clean reset. Upgrade one part, not the whole PC If you absolutely have to upgrade your PC hardware, then try to stick to components that won’t be hit by the RAM crunch. If you need a new CPU, don’t also upgrade the memory, even if it’s tempting to pair it with faster sticks. If you need a new GPU, make sure you aren’t buying one that’s too fast for the rest of your kit. And if you need more memory? Outsmart the shortage with these tips. Roll the dice on a pre-owned If you really, really need a whole new PC, you can skip a lot of the issues with sky-high PC prices by going with a pre-owned model. You’re rolling the dice with this since AI has made it easier to scam with older hardware, and price hikes have hit the second-hand market, too. But if you buy from a trusted seller on a trusted platform with reliable refund opportunities, you should be relatively safe. If you can, view the system in person. If you can’t, at least get a video from the seller (with today’s date) to see the PC in working condition.

item.title: Windows 11’s new update finally fixes its biggest taskbar complaint
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.25
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft is finally addressing long-standing Windows 11 taskbar complaints through a new update packed with customization options. - Users can now resize the taskbar, reposition it to any screen edge, and adjust Start menu layouts, restoring features many had missed. - The update also cleans up Windows Search by hiding Bing and Microsoft Store clutter, while legacy tools like WMIC are being removed to modernize the OS. With yesterday’s Patch Tuesday for September, Microsoft not only fixed a record number of security vulnerabilities but also released several new features for Windows 11, which you can try out now (or soon). Microsoft gradually rolls out new features across eligible Windows 11 PCs. That means most users will gain access to the new features within the next few days or weeks. Windows 11’s new features For the first time since the launch of Windows 11, the taskbar can be repositioned to any edge of the screen. In doing so, Microsoft has addressed one of the biggest criticisms of Windows 11. You can now find the new taskbar setting under Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Taskbar behavior → Taskbar position. There, you can choose from Left, Top, Right, and Bottom. An option for a smaller taskbar reduces both the size of the icons and the height of the bar. However, there are some limitations, such as the search box and the compact version only being available when the taskbar is positioned at the top or bottom, not the sides. The Start menu now features the size options Small, Automatic, and Large, as well as separate buttons for Pinned, Recently Used, and All. Windows Search now hides results from Bing and the Microsoft Store if you disable those result types, making it faster to use and find what you want. Further updates relate to administrator protection and device preparation using Windows Autopilot. Microsoft is also introducing process isolation for Microsoft Execution Containers, which are designed for agent-based tasks and programming tasks. Lastly, Microsoft is completely removing WMIC from Windows 11, and there are also some minor fixes to Outlook’s search and touchpad reliability.

item.title: GMKtec NucBox K17 review: This Lunar Lake mini-PC punches above its price
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.05
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Arc 130V is faster than the older Radeon 680M graphics card - PCIe 4.0 SSD reads at over 7,000MB/s - USB4 leads the way at 40Gbit/s, plus six USB-A ports - Two HDMI 2.1 outputs, one of which supports 8K at 60Hz - Windows 11 Pro 25H2 pre-installed Cons - 16GB of RAM permanently integrated and not expandable - Only one USB-C port (USB4) - Eight threads limit performance under parallel loads Our Verdict The NucBox K17 brings Intel’s Lunar Lake technology to the under-$700 price bracket, provided the mini-PC is on offer. The Arc 130V graphics deliver adequate performance for an integrated GPU, the SSD is fast, and the range of ports is extensive. The limitations lie in the integrated 16GB of RAM and the processor’s eight threads. The K17 is well suited for office work, media playback, and occasional gaming. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Price When Reviewed $619 Best Prices Today: GMKtec NucBox K17 Mini PCs featuring Intel’s Lunar Lake chip were a rarity until recently. GMKtec first incorporated the platform into the NucBox K13 and is now following up with the K17, a more affordable model. Instead of a Core Ultra 7, this model features a Core Ultra 5 226V. We put the device through our benchmark suite. The test shows how the more affordable model stacks up against the K13 and Ryzen competitors. GMKtec NucBox K17 design and build quality The K17 returns to the classic rectangular shape that GMKtec had most recently abandoned in favor of the flat K13. The case measures 5 x 5 x 1.75 inches and weighs 16.2 ounces. This results in a volume of around 0.76 ounces. Although the K13 is smaller at 0.63 ounces, its elongated shape means it occupies a similar amount of space on the desk. Christoph Hoffmann The top panel is made of light gray brushed aluminum and features the engraved manufacturer’s logo. Fingerprints are barely visible on it. The edges are generously rounded, and the gaps are uniform. A yellow-green power button on the front breaks up the understated design. Right next to it is the recessed reset button. It restarts the computer and, when pressed in the correct manner, also serves to clear the CMOS settings. The cooler draws in air through slits on both sides and expels the heated air towards the rear. There, three wide ventilation grilles span the entire rear panel. Under the hood, two copper heat pipes and a turbine fan are at work. The external power supply delivers 100 watts at 20 volts and is compact in design. A Kensington lock is located on the left-hand side. Christoph Hoffmann GMKtec NucBox K17 specifications Inside, the Intel Core Ultra 5 226V is at work. Lunar Lake utilizes, among other things, TSMC’s 3-nanometer manufacturing process and combines four Lion Cove cores with four Skymont Spark cores. As Lunar Lake does not support Hyper-Threading, the eight CPU cores can process a maximum of eight threads simultaneously. The clock speed ranges from 2.1- to 4.5GHz, and the Smart Cache measures 8MB. HWiNFO reports a base processor power of 17 watts. GMKtec provides three profiles set at 20, 25, and 35 watts. A peak of 37 watts is permitted for short periods. Graphics are handled by the integrated Arc 130V with seven Xe cores and a clock speed of up to 1.85GHz. Some diagnostic tools report an Arc 140V here, but the number of Xe cores confirms the smaller variant. The NPU achieves up to 40 TOPS. The advertised 97 TOPS also includes the graphics unit and CPU. Christoph Hoffmann In Lunar Lake, the RAM is integrated into the processor package. HWiNFO lists eight Samsung chips, each with 2GB, connected via four channels. Together, this amounts to 16GB of LPDDR5X running at 8,533MT/s. An upgrade is not possible, and GMKtec does not offer a higher-capacity version either. For memory-intensive applications or virtual machines, 16GB can quickly become insufficient. Two M.2-2280 slots are available for mass storage. The test unit features a 1TB EXT X200E SSD, connected via PCIe 4.0 with four lanes. The system features one M.2 slot with PCIe 5.0 x4 and a second with PCIe 4.0 x2, allowing for a total capacity of up to 16TB. Christoph Hoffmann At the front are two USB-A ports with speeds of 10- and 5Gbit/s respectively, a USB4 port with 40Gbit/s and a 3.5mm jack. The USB4 port accepts up to 100 watts via Power Delivery and outputs DisplayPort signals. Christoph Hoffmann Unlike the K13, this means there is a USB-C/USB4 port located directly on the front panel. At the rear are three USB-A ports at 5Gbit/s, an older USB 2.0 port, two HDMI 2.1 outputs, and the power socket. One of the two video outputs supports 8K at 60Hz, while the other supports 4K. Together with USB4, three monitors can be operated in parallel. Christoph Hoffmann Network speeds remain at 2.5Gbit/s via an Intel i226-V adapter. The K13 has the edge here with its 5Gbit port. The K17 connects wirelessly via Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.2. Christoph Hoffmann It comes pre-installed with Windows 11 Pro version 25H2, build 26200; the BIOS is dated March 2026. Upon first start-up, several security updates were pending, which we installed before carrying out the measurements. Christoph Hoffmann Computing performance In PCMark 10, the NucBox K17 achieved a total of 7,789 points. It scored 9,934 points for everyday tasks. PCMark 10 recorded 14,350 points for productivity and 8,996 points for content creation. Photo editing performed particularly well, scoring 15,417 points. Spreadsheet and writing tasks also performed strongly, scoring 14,059 and 14,648 points, respectively. Rendering and visualization scored 7,246 points, while video editing scored 6,518 points. The K13 with Core Ultra 7 256V achieved 7,695 points in our tests. Christoph Hoffmann The CPU profile in 3DMark clearly highlights Lunar Lake’s distinctive characteristics. At full load, the processor scores 4,614 points, putting it almost on a par with the K13, which achieves 4,698 points. Both processors are limited to eight threads, which restricts scaling under high levels of parallelization. The K16, with its 16-thread Ryzen, scores 6,691 points, while a Ryzen AI 9 scores over 9,700 points. In the single-core test, the picture changes: 1,093 points are on a par with the most powerful AMD models. The high single-core performance benefits applications that utilize only a few threads. Christoph Hoffmann The K17 performs significantly better in terms of graphics. In Time Spy, the Arc 130V achieves 3,789 points, of which 3,521 are graphics points. Depending on the system, the Radeon 890M achieves around 3,000 to 3,900 points in the Time Spy graphics test, whilst the Radeon 680M in the K16 manages just 1,762 points. The K13, with its larger Arc 140V, is around 6 percent ahead with 4,006 points. In the Steel Nomad Light test, the gap is even wider: 2,575 points and 19.1 frames per second compare with 3,176 points and 23.5 fps. The Fire Strike Ultra score stands at 2,000 points. In all three runs, our test unit outperforms the average for comparable systems as reported by 3DMark. Cyberpunk 2077 runs in Full HD with low detail settings and XeSS enabled at an average of 38.1 frames per second, with a minimum of 31 fps. Reduced detail settings are required for demanding, modern games. Less demanding titles should run significantly more smoothly. Christoph Hoffmann Geekbench AI Pro could not be run on the K17 via the NPU. The test ran via the AVX2 path and thus via the CPU. It scored 2,657 points in single-precision, 1,262 in half-precision, and 5,522 in the quantized test. These figures reflect the CPU’s performance, not that of the NPU. The NPU test via OpenVINO could not be launched in Geekbench AI Pro, even with two different versions of Intel’s NPU driver (32.0.100.4778 and 32.0.100.4841). Christoph Hoffmann The SSD also achieves high transfer rates. In CrystalDiskMark, it reads sequentially at 7,123MB/s and writes at 6,335MB/s. This means the sequential read rate is close to the practical maximum for fast PCIe 4.0 x4 SSDs. The K16, with its PCIe 3.0 drive, achieves only about half that speed in sequential operations. Christoph Hoffmann Noise levels and power consumption When idle and during office tasks, the turbine fan remains in the background. It only picks up speed slightly when the graphics unit is under sustained load. From a distance of 3 feet, the fan remained below our reliably measurable threshold while idle. Measured directly at the ventilation slots under full load, we recorded 27.3 dB(A). In terms of power consumption, the K17 proves to be economical. In idle mode, the mini PC draws less than 7 watts from the outlet; under combined load during the benchmarks, this figure rises to between 25 and 35 watts. The supplied 100-watt power supply is therefore more than adequately rated. No thermal issues arose during the test. After prolonged use, the SSD registered 42 degrees Celsius. The case surface warmed up noticeably but did not become uncomfortably hot. We found no evidence of throttling in the benchmark measurement logs. Should you buy the GMKtec NucBox K17? The NucBox K17 makes Intel’s Lunar Lake platform accessible at a list price of around $650. The Arc 130V graphics deliver high performance for an integrated solution and significantly outperform the Radeon 680M, for example. The SSD reads at over 7,000MB/s, and the range of connectivity options is extensive. With six USB-A ports, the K17 offers plenty of space for peripherals. Added to this are USB4 ports on the front and an 8K-capable HDMI output. Its weaknesses are clearly defined. The RAM is limited to 16GB; a higher-capacity version is not available. Under multi-core workloads, the K17 lags behind Ryzen systems with 16 or more threads, and the network is capped at 2.5Gbit/s. For workstation tasks, a model with higher multi-core performance and more RAM makes more sense, such as the EVO-T2S. We take a critical view of the pricing within the brand’s own range. The better-equipped K13, featuring a Core Ultra 7, Arc 140V, 5Gbit LAN, and two USB4 ports, costs only slightly more. Anyone who does not need the K17’s six USB-A ports will get the more powerful spec with its sister model. Warranty details vary depending on the sales channel. GMKtec specifies a warranty of either one or three years. Regardless of this, when purchasing as a consumer from a commercial retailer, you are entitled to statutory rights in respect of defects against the seller. The K17 is a great value computer for office and multimedia work and is also suitable for gaming to a limited extent. The numerous USB-A ports are particularly handy for extensive peripheral setups. Technical specifications - Processor: Intel Core Ultra 5 226V (Lunar Lake), 8 cores/8 threads, up to 4.5GHz, 17 watts base power; profiles with 20/25/35 watts, up to 37 watts for short periods - Graphics: Intel Arc 130V, 7 Xe cores, 400MHz to 1.85GHz - NPU: Intel AI Boost, up to 40 TOPS; total AI performance up to 97 TOPS (Int8) - RAM: 16GB LPDDR5X, 8,533 MT/s, integrated into the processor package, not expandable - Internal storage: 1 TB M.2 2280 SSD (PCIe 4.0 x4), test unit with EXT X200E - Expansion: 2 × M.2 2280 (1 × PCIe Gen5 x4, 1 × PCIe Gen4 x2), up to 16 TB in total - Graphics output: 1 × HDMI 2.1 FRL (8K/60 Hz), 1 × HDMI 2.1 TMDS (4K/60 Hz), 1 × USB4 (4K/60 Hz), up to three displays - Front ports: 1 × USB-A 3.2 Gen 2 (10Gbit/s), 1 × USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 (5Gbit/s), 1 × USB4 (40Gbit/s, DP, PD 100 W), 3.5 mm jack, Power, Reset - Rear ports: 3 × USB-A 3.2 Gen 1 (5 Gbit/s), 1 × USB-A 2.0, 2 × HDMI 2.1, 2.5 Gbit RJ45 (Intel i226-V), DC-In - Other: Kensington lock on the left-hand side of the chassis - Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6E (RZ616), Bluetooth 5.2 - Operating system: Windows 11 Pro 25H2 (Build 26200) - Power supply: 100-watt external (DC 20 V / 5 A) - Dimensions: 5 x 5 x 1.75 inches - Weight: 16.2 ounces

item.title: Windows 11 is getting faster boot times and 8GB RAM performance
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.28
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft is working on performance improvements for Windows 11, targeting faster boot times and better Windows Hello responsiveness. - Upcoming updates appear focused on optimizing the operating system for devices with only 8GB of RAM, which remains common in many Surface models. - No specific release dates have been announced yet, but users with lower-end hardware may soon experience noticeably faster startup speeds. Microsoft confirmed at IFA 2026 that upcoming updates for Windows 11 will include faster boot times. According to Mark Linton, head of Windows & Devices at Microsoft, the company has already made significant progress in both the startup times and responsiveness of Windows Hello, and further improvements are expected. At the same time, Microsoft reaffirmed its earlier promise to optimize Windows 11 for PCs with only 8GB of RAM. According to Linton, Microsoft is still committed to this goal of making weaker Windows PCs run well, but he didn’t provide any specific plans or features. This renewed commitment is important because Microsoft recently halved the RAM in its own Surface laptops. The newest entry-level Surface models only have 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, which isn’t even enough to meet the minimum requirements of Copilot+. Even for Windows 11, a minimum of 32GB of RAM was recommended for a long time… until Microsoft quietly removed this recommendation from its support pages. It’s disappointing but not surprising, as the ongoing RAM crisis has spiked prices of memory and storage, forcing companies to rethink their strategies and shift to other solutions. It’s not yet clear when the upcoming improvements to boot times and memory usage will be rolled out to regular Windows 11 users. All we know is they’re expected to come as part of future updates. Further reading: Speed up Windows 11 on PCs with less RAM

item.title: Windows 11’s desktop is now a full-screen ad for Harry Potter movies
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.71
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft used its Bing Wallpaper app to display full-screen ads promoting Harry Potter and Fantastic Beasts movie collections on Windows 11 desktops. - The ads appear randomly based on user region, exploiting small print that allows Microsoft to show advertisements within wallpapers meant for scenic daily backgrounds. - Reddit users expressed strong disapproval, especially given that Microsoft previously acknowledged showing too many ads to its users. Microsoft recently caused a stir among some users with an ad that fills the entire Windows 11 desktop background. It’s a wallpaper that ends up on the computer via the Bing Wallpaper app. The full-screen wallpaper advertises a collection of the eight Harry Potter films plus three Fantastic Beasts films. The caption “Available Now” makes it clear what the whole thing is about: Windows 11 users are being encouraged to buy this film collection via wallpaper. However, this marketing stunt was not received well on Reddit. Not all Windows users are seeing this Harry Potter ad, mainly because Bing rotates its wallpapers and varies them depending on the user’s region. According to Windows Latest, “One user told Windows Latest that they used four PCs on the same day, and only one showed the Harry Potter ad. The other three had a nice view of Bamberg, so not everyone appears to be getting the same wallpaper.” The fact that the Bing Wallpaper app is now pushing full-size ads to Windows PCs is surprising. Microsoft recently admitted that it has been displaying too many ads in Windows, but the fact that the entire desktop background is being commandeered as a new avenue for marketing was never explicitly announced by Microsoft. (However, if you look at the small print, Microsoft reserves the right to display ads within wallpapers.) Bing Wallpaper is part of Windows 10 and 11 and facilitates automatic desktop background changes, primarily intended to liven things up and treat users with a new visual image and vibe every day.

item.title: This $40 Anker dock turns your laptop’s USB-C port into 8 connections
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.38
If your laptop has just one or two ports and you’re always swapping between them to plug in monitors, flash drives, keyboards, mice, and whatever else, you deserve to treat yourself with a proper docking solution. This Anker 8-in-1 Laptop Docking Station is $40 at Amazon, which is a 26% discount off its usual $54. Like any hub or dock, this one plugs into your laptop’s USB-C port and turns it into a bunch of usable ports, but this one stands out for two reasons: it’s eight full-blown connections, two of them 4K HDMI and one 85W USB-C Power Delivery. That makes this perfect for productivity laptops, allowing you to expand your setup with dual 4K/30Hz monitors and keep your laptop charged despite taking up its USB-C port. The other ports are useful too, including double USB-A for data or peripherals, SD and microSD slots for cards, and Ethernet for a stable internet connection as needed. One thing to keep in mind, however, is that if you’re on a Mac, using both HDMI outputs will show the same image on both (mirrored) instead of treating them as separate spaces (extended). Also worth noting is that this dock is only compatible with Windows, macOS, and Chrome OS—it will not work with Linux machines. At $40, this 8-in-1 hub is a solid value for any thin-and-light laptop that’s lacking in usable ports. If you want to expand your laptop into a capable workstation, this is a great entry-level option. For more options, check out PCWorld’s picks for the best USB-C hubs and best Thunderbolt docks.

item.title: Best monitor arms 2026: Tested picks for single- and dual-monitors setups
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.88
A monitor arm is a sure way to boost the effectiveness of a home office setup. A good-quality arm not only frees up usable space on your desk’s surface, it aids ergonomics by allowing you to move and position your display/s for optimal comfort. Plus, a monitor arm makes your office setup look really pro. The only catch is the price. Most monitor arms worth buying will cost close to $200, and heavy-duty arms capable of holding two large displays can be priced even higher. The good news is that a good-quality monitor arm is likely to last you for a very long time. That’s why it’s important to make the right choice when you purchase a monitor arm. To help you with that, we’ve tested several popular monitor arms, for both single- and dual-monitor setups. Below you’ll find our curated list of recommendations, with detailed explanations of what features and qualities make them stand out. We even have some good budget recommendations.
