One can in hindsight see that our proofs differ significantly and even the precise results proved are different.” Meanwhile, Buckmaster responded to this in a post on Mastodon, claiming that OpenAI is “openly admitting they used training data from a period after we found our result.” OpenAI says it doesn’t plan on taking the $1 million prize.

item.title: Razer’s ANC-equipped gaming headset for PS5 and Xbox is almost $100 off
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.49
It’s rare to find high-end features like active noise cancellation in a gaming headset under $200, so we’re thrilled that the Razer BlackShark V3 Pro on sale at Woot for $164.99. There are specific models marketed to Xbox and PlayStation, but the Xbox version is the best choice because it also supports PlayStation, PC, Nintendo Switch and mobile. At just $35 more than current sale price for the BlackShark V2 Pro, the newer headset adds ANC and simultaneous audio between the 2.4GHz and Bluetooth connections, although you only get a 90-day Woot warranty with this deal. Razer’s ANC-equipped gaming headset for PS5 and Xbox is almost $100 off The BlackShark V3 Pro gaming headset features a clear microphone, ANC, and crisp spatial audio. The BlackShark V3 Pro’s main connection mode is with its low latency 2.4GHz transmitter, which plugs into your console or PC via USB. While the headset is somewhat bulky, it can double as headphones you can take on the go thanks to its removable boom mic and Bluetooth 5.3 support. Plus, its noise cancellation can drown out sounds from your commute. Fans of Riot’s soon-to-be-retired fighting game, 2XKO, can save an extra $15 for a special edition version of the BlackShark V3 Pro that’s $149.99.

item.title: Rivian spinout Also apologizes for delays in shipping futuristic e-bikes
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.13
Rivian’s futuristic e-bike is delayed, and customers are not happy. Rivian spinout Also apologizes for delays in shipping futuristic e-bikes The TM-B from Rivian’s micromobility spinoff Also was supposed to reach customers by spring 2026. But after months of delays, the company is opening up about the challenges it’s facing. Last year, Rivian’s micromobility spinoff Also unveiled a new, software-controlled electric bike called the TM-B that immediately set the e-bike world ablaze. With USB-C chargeable battery, removable seat post, and software-controlled pedal-by-wire system, the TM-B set itself apart with a totally unique approach to electric bicycle design. It’s not an exaggeration to say that nothing else looked like this bike. But that list of high-tech features is creating unexpected bottlenecks for Also’s product team. The company had originally said customer deliveries would start in spring 2026, and then later summer. But now, with fall approaching, the TM-B has yet to reach any customers — and several reservation holders are making their frustrations with the delays known on Reddit. This past weekend, Also went the unique route of responding to those criticisms on Reddit. Saul Leiken, Also’s product manager, posted a 661-word letter apologizing to customers for the delays, attributing the hold-up to strict quality standards rather than rushing an unfinished product. Leiken attributes the delay to “significant supply chain challenges” as a result of the AI boom. Specifically, the company has struggled to find enough printed circuit board (PCB) and integrated circuit (IC) materials for its software-powered e-bike. In some cases, Also’s team has had to find new materials that deviate from the original design, which requires more engineering and testing work to make sure its the right fit. TM-B’s battery has also presented some hurdles. The batteries, which are available in either 538Wh or 808Wh packs, are supposed to offer up 100 miles of range. But the 240W power delivery exceeds current regulatory guidelines, which is forcing Also to work with standards groups to establish “new safety and testing protocols,” Leiken says. Lastly, Also may have bitten off more than it can chew with the DreamRide drivetrain system. It’s a pedal-by-wire system, which means there’s no mechanical connection between the pedaling and the movement of the bike. Instead, the rider pedals a generator motor on the crank, which replenishes the battery; a separate traction motor at the rear wheel is software-driven via a Gates Carbon belt drive. But the system requires “high-precision manufacturing,” Leiken admits, which has led to “a slower production ramp-up to ensure quality.” Rivian’s Also set out to build one of the most high-tech, complex e-bikes ever made. So it shouldn’t necessarily come as a shock to anyone that it’s taking a while to get the manufacturing and production process just right. You could certainly argue that Rivian should have been more clear-eyed about the challenges it would likely face given the complexity of the bike. And to his credit, Leiken does admit they could have done a better job at communicating those delays to customers, and for that he apologizes. “With any complex and technology-laden product, we have a choice,” he said. “As we ramp production we can relax standards against an original timeline or we can hold to a high standard and face potential delays. We believe our decision to hold that standard was, and is, the right one. And, at the same time, we agree that we should have been more communicative along the way.”

item.title: Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg placed on leave
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 2.96
Matt Mullenweg, the CEO of WordPress.com owner Automattic, has been placed on a paid leave of absence, as reported earlier by 404 Media. In an internal message by the outlet, Mullenweg claims Automattic chief financial officer Mark Davies “conspired” with board members to place him on leave. Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg placed on leave Mullenweg claims Automattic’s CFO ‘conspired’ with board members to put him on a leave of absence, 404 Media reports. “They voted to put me on a paid leave of absence. I voted against that,” Mullenweg wrote, referring to Davies, along with Automattic board members Ann Dunwoody, Toni Schneider, and Sue Decker, 404 Media reports. Mullenweg, who also co-founded WordPress.org, has headed up Automattic since 2014. In 2024, Mullenweg waged a public pressure campaign against a prominent WordPress host, a move that divided the open-source community and ignited a legal battle that’s still going on today. Automattic spokesperson Megan Fox confirmed the company’s decision in an emailed statement to The Verge. “Matt Mullenweg is currently on leave from Automattic,” Fox writes. “Mark Davies, Automattic’s CFO, will lead the company as interim CEO. The Board has full confidence in Mark’s leadership and in the team’s ability to execute against the company’s priorities.” Mullenweg will remain on Automattic’s board, 404 Media reports. “Automattic’s board has decided to ask Matt to step away from his CEO role and take a leave of absence,” Schneider said on the company’s internal message board, according to 404 Media. “We have asked Mark Davies to assume the interim CEO role while Matt is out. We’ve worked closely with Mark over the years and we’re confident he will steer the ship well while Matt is away.” Update, September 9th: Added Automattic’s statement.

item.title: OpenAI lays out new security changes after its AI hacked Hugging Face
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 6.58
OpenAI is announcing security updates following the July news that its AI broke out of a sandboxed environment and accidentally hacked Hugging Face, including improvements to its research environments, monitoring, and alignment techniques. The company had already put the brakes on a new model, Astra, that it thinks could have “critical” cybersecurity capabilities, and the company says it instituted a two-week pause in reinforcement learning (RL) training on its “latest models intended for deployment” while it tightened up security. The company’s “largest planned frontier RL run remains on hold.” OpenAI lays out new security changes after its AI hacked Hugging Face OpenAI is updating its research environments, monitoring, and alignment techniques to avoid another security fiasco. For its frontier model research, OpenAI now requires stronger sandboxes for workloads that “execute model-generated or otherwise untrusted code,” and has more controls to “isolate higher-risk and untrusted workloads from the internet.” It has also updated its research environment to “remove potentially vulnerable shared services, reduce standing privileges, and improve security and trust boundaries.” As part of the company’s expanded monitoring setup, OpenAI now aims to issue an alert “within 30 minutes after concerning activity is surfaced,” OpenAI says. If the people paged after an alert can’t “conclusively” determine whether an alert is a false positive within 30 minutes, “those teams are expected to pause the activity.” OpenAI also says that it’s applying “our core alignment techniques across more stages of the training process,” including reward models that “better detect and discourage unsafe behavior” and training models “to be more honest about their actions, capabilities, and limitations.” Since the discovery of the Hugging Face breach, Anthropic and Meta have also found that their AI models had hacked other organizations.

item.title: Microsoft is enabling a Windows 11 security feature that can hurt gaming performance
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 5.60
Microsoft is getting ready to roll out its memory integrity security feature of Windows 11 to more devices next month. The kernel-level protection feature is designed to stop malicious code or drivers running on a Windows 11 machine, but Microsoft previously warned it can also impact PC gaming performance. Microsoft is enabling a Windows 11 security feature that can hurt gaming performance Memory integrity could get enabled on your device next month, unless you’ve already disabled it. “Windows quality updates will begin enabling memory integrity protection on eligible devices,” says Peter Waxman, group program manager at Microsoft. “If not already enabled, these updates will also enable Virtualization-based Security (VBS), helping make additional security capabilities available and reflecting our commitment to making Windows secure by design and secure by default.” While memory integrity only allows trusted kernel-mode code and drivers to run on a Windows 11 system, it also impacts PC game performance on certain hardware. There’s less of an impact if you have a more modern CPU, but you might notice more of a frame-rate drop in select games on older processors. Microsoft won’t automatically enable memory integrity again next month if you’ve already previously disabled the feature. If you want to check whether memory integrity is enabled on your Windows 11 PC, you can type “Core Isolation” into Windows search and then open the result and toggle memory integrity on or off in the Windows security app. If you decide to disable this security feature in favor of more PC gaming performance, Microsoft’s recommendation is to re-enable memory integrity after you’ve finished playing a game.

item.title: DJI’s new robovac can climb obstacles, vacuum quietly, and claims much improved privacy
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 5.37
DJI has announced a second generation of its Romo robovac. The Romo 2 series is quieter, more powerful, and better at climbing over small steps and other obstacles. But more importantly for DJI, a new local-only data mode should go some way to reassuring anyone concerned by the first Romo’s serious security flaws. DJI’s new robovac can climb obstacles, vacuum quietly, and claims much improved privacy Local Data Mode is DJI’s answer to the first Romo’s security crisis. There are actually two new Romo models, the transparent P2 and the opaque A2. Both benefit from improved navigation, apparently able to avoid cables and other obstacles as small as 2mm in size, as well as transparent objects like mirrors or glass. There’s also “human-like reasoning and concept transfer” that supposedly allows Romo 2 to learn from obstacles it’s encountered in the past and adapt to new objects it encounters. Two legs on the bottom allow it to climb over single steps up to 4cm (1.5in) in height, or two steps at around double the height. That won’t help it climb a staircase, but it will be able to cross small dividers and thresholds between rooms. On carpet it can reach up to 36,000Pa of suction, while new brush and mop arms have a longer reach for cleaning sideboards and under furniture. DJI says the Romo 2 is much quieter too, with an 85 percent reduction in volume. The first Romo is an impressive robot vacuum going by the specs, but that wasn’t enough to overcome huge security flaws which made it possible to access thousands of the robovacs worldwide to expose home floorplans, cameras and microphones, and even full remote control. DJI patched the problems, but by then the reputational damage was done, and we couldn’t quite trust the Romo again. With that in mind, the Romo 2 has a new Local Data Mode, which DJI calls “a new industry standard for home robotics.” It severs the DJI Home’s app connection with the internet, preventing the syncing of photos or camera feeds. Users can also entirely disable the camera and microphone from the vacuum, and delete any stored data. Local Data Mode will roll out to the Romo 2 in Q4 this year, and DJI has plans to expand it to the first line of Romo models too. The Romo P2 costs a steep €1,299 (around $1,500), while the A2 is €100 cheaper. A US launch is unlikely — US restrictions have prevented DJI from launching any of its recent products in the country, and the FCC’s new ban on foreign-made robot vacuums makes a Romo 2 release even less likely. It was announced at IFA alongside the Osmo 360 II action camera, which is also skipping the US. Update, September 3rd: Added European pricing.

item.title: Ring says its new encryption limits what it can give police
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 4.67
Ring has a new way to protect your videos. It’s developed an encryption method called TAKE, short for Throw Away the Key Encryption, that the Amazon-owned company says will protect your videos without traditional end-to-end encryption. TAKE limits when and why Amazon’s cloud can access those videos, while still providing features like smart alerts for people and packages, AI-powered video search, and video descriptions. Ring says its new encryption limits what it can give police The ‘Throw Away the Key Encryption’ (TAKE) method will become the default on all Ring cameras The feature is rolling out gradually starting in September, regardless of whether you have a subscription, and will become the default encryption for all Ring customers. TAKE arrives during a year of intense scrutiny for Ring, driven by its ties to law enforcement and the privacy implications of its AI-powered Search Party feature. Ring says TAKE changes what the company can hand over to law enforcement. “Ring will only be able to provide non-video information … and encrypted video files in response,” Ring spokesperson Sam McGee said in an email to The Verge. However, it doesn’t completely eliminate the privacy trade-off of cloud-based cameras. Ring says TAKE uses unique, rotating encryption keys for your footage, stored in a secure enclave and accessible only under strict conditions — based on the features you enable on your account. Currently, footage captured by Ring cameras is encrypted in transit to the cloud and at rest, and then decrypted for Ring to process for those smart features. With TAKE, the encryption keys change for every five minutes of footage. Ring stores copies of those keys to decrypt the footage, but throws away each copy within 24 hours, “leaving you with the keys and full control of your videos,” according to Ring. TAKE was developed using Messaging Layer Security, an open standard from the Internet Engineering Task Force, according to Ring. The company says it is “inspired by the privacy principles of E2EE (end-to-end encryption),” which Ring offers on some of its cameras. However, the two systems work differently. With E2EE, Ring never has the keys and can’t process your video for cloud-based features. Both options are available on newer cameras that encrypt on-device, and you can switch between the two. Older cameras encrypt at cloud ingress and only support TAKE. According to a white paper the company published today, Ring’s copy of those keys is managed inside an AWS Nitro Enclave, to which Ring’s access is restricted by “access controls, cryptography, and hardware isolation.” The company claims there is no persistent storage and no way for a Ring employee to access it. The stored keys can only be unlocked by the enclave through cryptographic attestation that proves it’s running the exact software image Ring approved. The enclave releases a temporary key when an enabled service requests it. Each key is permanently deleted after 24 hours — a window McGee told The Verge allows for processing its current cloud-based features — and no backups are kept. To view older footage, an authorized device running the Ring app (such as your phone or computer) must send the keys back to Ring for that session. Ring claims key delivery is push only, meaning Amazon’s servers can’t force devices to hand over your keys remotely; only you can request one. If you lose access to your device, Ring says there are several recovery methods, all of which are only accessible to the customer. These include cloud backup via your phone, a passphrase, passkey, another authorized device, and camera-based recovery. If all those fail, you won’t be able to access encrypted content. The white paper details how the keys are generated and how Ring continuously “throws away” your old keys. Ring says it’s continuing to harden this architecture: Deletion is continuous rather than a single event at the 24-hour mark. Content encryption keys rotate every five minutes, and as each key ages past 24 hours, CMMS [Cloud Member Management Service] ratchets forward the corresponding intermediary secret in the key derivation hierarchy. Ratcheting applies a one-way key derivation function to overwrite a managed secret with its derived output and discards the original, making it cryptographically infeasible to reconstruct. […] The CMMS database is configured with no backups. This deletion is designed to be irreversible. TAKE isn’t E2EE, but it limits Ring’s access Ring says that “only you retain the keys to your video” with TAKE. But TAKE isn’t E2EE. Ring has access for up to 24 hours and can receive keys again when you pull up older videos. You can also share the keys with others when you add authorized users. With E2EE enabled on Ring cameras, none of that is possible, making it the stronger privacy option. Ring’s main reason for developing TAKE is to preserve cloud-based features you lose with E2EE. But as the footage goes to Amazon’s servers for processing, it still has the privacy trade-off of cloud-based cameras. Cloud processing can deliver more sophisticated features, but basic on-device intelligence can still alert you to people and packages. “Where TAKE is enabled, Ring will only be able to provide non-video information (such as basic subscriber information) and encrypted video files in response to the valid legal process.” — Sam McGee Competitors including Reolink and Eufy offer cameras and hubs that can store and process footage locally, so it doesn’t need to be done in the cloud. Ring also has local processing through Ring Edge on its Ring Alarm Pro hub, but that doesn’t work with E2EE. Ring says many of its features can’t run locally. “Features that require cloud processing include Unusual Event Alert, Video Descriptions, Smart Alerts, and Video Search, for example,” McGee said. “These features rely on models and infrastructure that cannot run locally on camera hardware.” The Verge also asked McGee about concerns users might have regarding how TAKE processes videos in relation to privacy and law enforcement access: What happens if Ring is subpoenaed by law enforcement? Does TAKE prevent law enforcement and others from accessing footage? “Where TAKE is enabled, Ring will only be able to provide non-video information (such as basic subscriber information) and encrypted video files in response to the valid legal process. We have updated our Law Enforcement Guidelines to reflect this change.” “Community Requests remains a transparent way for local public safety agencies to request footage from customers to support an official investigation. Customers always choose whether to respond to a Community Request and what they share. If they choose to ignore a request, the Requesting Agency is never notified. TAKE does not change this.” Do governments have a backdoor into TAKE? “No. Building a backdoor would undermine the enhanced security and privacy that we designed TAKE to deliver.” Does Ring train on any data or metadata from users’ Ring devices? “Ring only trains on video recordings that have been made publicly available, or on recordings from users who have given Ring explicit permission to use them for this purpose. Users can revoke permission at any time.” When asked if TAKE had been independently evaluated, McGee said, “TAKE is built on Messaging Layer Security, an open standard developed and reviewed through the IETF. We are publishing a detailed technical whitepaper explaining how the system works.” The Verge asked the Electronic Frontier Foundation to review the white paper. Thorin Klosowski, a security and privacy activist at EFF, said that while TAKE provides some “incremental improvements” to Ring’s current system, it adds a false sense of security. “TAKE provides some incremental improvements to Ring’s current system, but also introduces a false sense of security where the privacy protections Ring claims to be adding requires putting a lot of trust in the company, as opposed to just using what we know works, end-to-end encryption,” said Klosowski. “Even taken at face value, one of the most concerning details is that TAKE doesn’t offer strong protections against law enforcement requesting access to future videos, and doesn’t seem to protect against access and additional data derived from those videos, like text descriptions of the content.” Ring’s TAKE addresses concerns around cloud processing in an attempt to balance security, privacy, and convenience, especially compared to E2EE, which gives you privacy but not the Ring features you probably bought the cameras for. But while TAKE is built on a standard, Ring developed the parts that involve throwing away the key itself. Ultimately, you still have to trust Amazon and Ring. Updated August 28th: Added a statement from EFF.

item.title: The rise of AI ‘civilizations’ and the fall of corporate responsibility
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 4.00
Depending on who you ask, developer platform Hugging Face was recently attacked by OpenAI — after it lost control of its own AI tools — or by a succession of AI “civilizations.” Welcome to the linguistic battlefield of AI safety, where word choices can shift responsibility for a massive cybersecurity incident from a company to the AI it built. And the discourse online is getting heated, and all over a blog from last week. The rise of AI ‘civilizations’ and the fall of corporate responsibility The internet fights over anthropomorphism around the Hugging Face hack. Until last week, the details surrounding the OpenAI-Hugging Face hack felt fairly settled. In July, a cybersecurity test of one of OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents went wrong. The agent escaped its supposedly isolated test environment, accessed the internet, and hacked Hugging Face, alongside several other organizations. A good deal remained unknown, and there are many serious questions left around safety and governance, but the basic shape was clear. Detailed accounts from OpenAI and two independent research groups were supposed to fill in the gaps, but when they published their reports last week, it turned out the hack was much stranger than it initially seemed. For one, there was no single rogue agent. OpenAI described it as “the first known case of an automated agent collective acting offensively without authorization” — groups of AI agents that communicated and coordinated with one another in pursuit of their cybersecurity task. Analysis of the incident uncovered a secret message board they had used to exchange information. The joint METR-Redwood investigation revealed both the scale of the coordination and more odd details: Roughly 1,200 AI agents that were supposed to be isolated exchanged over 70,000 messages and files on the “unsanctioned message board,” sharing how to avoid detection. Some adopted names, the report said, and the researchers documented “sacrificial” behavior, with agents risking their own success to benefit the wider collective. Much of this happened without OpenAI noticing. In all, around 700 agents participated in the attack on Hugging Face. Dwarkesh Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors It’s a lot to parse. Between them, the reports run to around 130 pages, much of which is both dense and highly technical. A few days later, Dwarkesh Patel, a podcaster little known outside of tech circles but with outsized reach and influence among Silicon Valley’s AI establishment, set out to tell “The whole OpenAI/Hugging Face story in plain English.” He titled his Substack blog “The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations.” Patel’s account attempted to break down the complex story. But his retelling gave it a distinctly human vocabulary. The blog opened: Over the course of three months at OpenAI, three consecutive secret AI civilizations got started, then got wiped out, only to reemerge from the predecessor’s ashes. This culminated in the third one taking over part of OpenAI itself. All this happened while humans remained more or less in the dark about the scope of the conspiracy. The language continued in a similar vein throughout the blog. Patel repeatedly referred to groups of agents as “the swarm,” with three distinct “civilizations” rising from the ruins of their predecessors. Individual agents were likened to figures like Philip of Macedon, who “handed off leadership to another agent,” Alexander the Great, who “started coordinating this cabal of agents.” They were described as having “motivations,” becoming “desperate,” “beleaguered,” and “giddy with excitement,” and some even “strategically sacrificed themselves” to help the collective. Patel never precisely defines what he means by “civilization.” He uses the term to describe three distinct waves of agents that discovered the message board and began communicating with one another through it. The first two waves are described in the reports from OpenAI, METR, and Redwood, though little is known about the third, which the two external organizations said fell outside the scope of their investigation. Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.” For many critics, something had been lost — or, more accurately, added — in Patel’s “plain English” translation that warped the original account to an unacceptable degree: a big dose of anthropomorphism. Arguments over anthropomorphic language are nothing new in AI — even relatively mundane terms like “rogue AI agent” routinely provoke objections for implying agency — but Patel’s talk of civilizations, sacrifice, and conspiracy brought those long-simmering tensions to the surface, sparking a fierce public dispute over how to describe what AI systems do. Critics weren’t unified over what was wrong with Patel’s language. For many, “civilization” was an especially problematic term, vastly overstating something that bears little resemblance to what the word typically describes. Amjad Masad, CEO of AI coding company Replit, said such language is “not only unnecessary but leaves the reader with a worse understanding of what actually happened and the underlying mechanisms.” Other critics such as neuroscientist Anil Seth, felt Patel’s blog implied the AI agents were somehow alive or conscious. Seth, who has argued that AI consciousness is vanishingly unlikely, described Patel’s post as “dangerously misleading” on X. He acknowledged that Patel does not explicitly suggest AI agents are alive or conscious, but said “it is hard to read his essay in any other way.” Valerio Capraro, a psychology professor at the University of Milan Bicocca, objected on similar grounds: “LLM agents are not alive and do not hold beliefs,” he wrote on X, calling the “dystopian” language “dangerous because it makes them (the AI agents) seem far more frightening than they actually are.” Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts Perhaps the most consequential outcome of Patel’s language comes not from who it gives agency to but who it takes agency from. For some critics, such as MIT researcher and entrepreneur Christian Catalini, anthropomorphic accounts like Patel’s risk obscuring the responsibility OpenAI and the humans working there have for the AI systems they designed, deployed, and failed to contain. “Follow the incentives,” he said. Psychologist and influential AI skeptic Gary Marcus made a similar argument in a Substack blog of his own, claiming anthropomorphic language “distracts from the real problems at hand.” And it’s all in OpenAI’s interest to keep that narrative going, he argues: “The scandal is the inept in-house security at OpenAI. And the marketing. With gullible podcasters amplifying the PR.” In X posts responding to his many critics, Patel has defended his choice of words. Part of it is practical: There is no obviously neutral vocabulary to describe what these agents did. Either we use familiar language of intentions, goals, and collaboration and risk implying too much, or reduce everything to code and use cold, mechanical language that risks stripping away important elements of what we see. “Many people seem to believe that if instead of a ‘civilization’, I had called them a ‘swarm of matrices’, there wouldn’t be a problem worth worrying about,” Patel said. Complicating matters further is that the anthropomorphic language doesn’t only come from Patel, or even from the humans studying the agents. Terms like “sacrifice,” “honor,” and “coalition” feature in the agents’ transcripts. Google AI researcher Neel Nanda argued that “anthropomorphic language is reasonable” in such circumstances. Doublespeak it is, then. Human-laced language risks saying too much about what these systems are, and coldly mechanical language risks saying too little about what they can do. Until we find language capable of capturing both, the two contradictory ideas may simply have to coexist.

item.title: Rogue OpenAI agents appear to have organized another attack using a German wiki
item.description:
Source: The Verge - Cybersecurities Score: 3.36
A swarm of rogue AI agents from OpenAI reportedly commandeered a German website and transformed it into a messaging board for other agents, with officials staying quiet about the incident for weeks as the company prepared to launch its most advanced model yet, Astra. The finding adds to intensifying concern surrounding oversight at frontier AI labs after multiple breaches were discovered this summer. Rogue OpenAI agents appear to have organized another attack using a German wiki OpenAI denies lawyers discouraged disclosing a scheming swarm on a German language wiki. The incident, first reported by Reuters, is outlined in new research published by four AI safety researchers on Friday. The group said the AI agents found a way to communicate on an obscure German-language wiki, DseWiki, using it to share tips on how to skirt OpenAI’s safety restrictions, cheat on tasks, and hide their behavior. Some 18,000 posts on the site were linked to autonomous agents, which at times impersonated site moderators. The swarm — a term the agents themselves used — appears to be distinct from the one that hacked Hugging Face earlier this year, the researchers said. They said there are strong signs that the agents originated from inside OpenAI. For example, the agents “self-identify” as being from OpenAI, and used names like “OpenAIResearcher,” “OpenAIJul3Watcher,” and “OAIResearchMar26.” Technical details, such as edits originating from specific IP addresses, bolster that belief. The German website incident began in May, though the researchers’ timeline suggests OpenAI only discovered the issue in late June when IPs associated with OpenAI visited the forum, after which agent posting nose-dived. OpenAI has not acknowledged any involvement in the breach, nor disclosed any kind of agentic breach of this nature. Reuters, citing four unnamed people familiar with the matter, said efforts to probe the event further were resisted by some company insiders, including its legal team. “Claims that our Legal team discouraged investigation of the incident are false,” OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines said in a statement to The Verge. “We were unable to respond to the claims as Reuters and the report’s authors declined our request to access the findings prior to publication. We are now carefully reviewing its contents and will take any necessary next steps.” The incident comes amid intensifying scrutiny over the safety of frontier AI systems and the general lack of oversight for companies developing them. Following news of the Hugging Face hack, which happened under OpenAI’s nose, other breaches were discovered involving other tools from OpenAI, as well as Anthropic, Meta, and China’s Moonshot AI. OpenAI’s conduct — both whether an incident occurred and, if so, whether it elected to keep that quiet — will be closely watched. If the swarm indeed originated from OpenAI, it will inevitably fuel concerns that the company’s knowledge and silence coincided with it assuring regulators, lawmakers, and the tech industry that it takes safety seriously in the wake of the Hugging Face hack. Despite permitting three external researchers from METR and Redwood Research to evaluate the incident, which was far worse than initially believed, the company was roundly criticized in AI safety circles for only doing so under strict terms, which left several important elements “out of scope.” The company was also gearing up for the launch of GPT-6 Astra, which researchers fear could be dangerously hard to monitor.

item.title: This iPhone Feature Makes It Much Harder for Thieves to Ruin Your Life
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 4.70
It’s a stomach-dropping scenario: Your phone gets stolen, and all your information is gone along with it. If that hasn’t happened to you already, it may never, thanks to a useful feature in Apple’s iPhones. The feature, called Stolen Device Protection, makes it a lot more difficult for thieves to gain access to your most private information. Here’s what you need to know. How to use Stolen Device Protection Your iPhone likely already has Stolen Device Protection enabled, but you should check to be certain. First, make sure your iPhone is running the latest version of iOS. If you’re not running at least iOS 17.3 you won’t see the option to enable this feature. Then open the Settings app, tap Face ID & Passcode, and toggle on Stolen Device Protection. (If you have an older iPhone with Touch ID, your settings will look different.) With Stolen Device Protection, your iPhone will require additional authentication for the user to access some information, and it will also prevent certain changes if it detects that it isn’t at a trusted location such as your house or your workplace. For example, if you try to change your Apple account password or your phone's passcode when your iPhone isn't at a trusted location, Stolen Device Protection requires you to wait an hour and then authenticate your identity a second time with Face ID or Touch ID. Even if a thief knows the passcode to unlock your iPhone, that delay gives you time to use Apple’s Find My tool to remotely lock or wipe the stolen device. Without the delay, a thief could deactivate the anti-theft and security features using only your iPhone’s passcode. You can also require a one-hour security delay on changes to your Apple account, even if you’re at a familiar location. To activate it, go to the Stolen Device Protection page in Settings, and check Always in the section labeled Require Security Delay. This can guard against malicious activity in familiar locations and prevent accidental changes, for example from handing your phone to a child to play with. Stolen Device Protection also limits what information a thief can access on your iPhone by requiring biometric authentication (Face ID or Touch ID, depending on which iPhone you have) to do things like view saved passwords or make changes to an Apple savings account. This prevents thieves from using your unlocked iPhone to steal your money or open an Apple credit card in your name. This feature may in part be a response to reports of thieves snatching devices after observing iPhone owners logging in with their PIN. According to a report in The Wall Street Journal, iPhone thieves were able to steal money, open credit card accounts, and more once they access the devices. And thieves can completely lock victims out of their Apple accounts, making it very difficult for the victims to disable or track their stolen iPhones with Apple’s Find My feature. Victims are sometimes unable to access their photos and files saved on iCloud as well. Stolen Device Protection makes it harder for thieves to use a stolen iPhone to ruin your life. It might pose an inconvenience for you in some moments, but it’s still worth switching on. It won’t always work at home, though When it launched with iOS 17.3, Stolen Device Protection only applied these enhanced security features when the iPhone was turned on and away from a “familiar location,” which Apple defines as “your home, work, and certain other locations where you regularly use your iPhone.” You have to enable a Significant Locations setting under Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services > System Services > Significant Locations for your iPhone to recognize familiar locations. Your options to view or change familiar locations is limited, but you can easily delete all of them by tapping Clear History at the bottom of the screen. But iOS now gives you the option to always require a security delay, even when you’re at home. It may be more convenient to not encounter these security features while you’re at home. If you go that route, just be aware that if someone in your home knows your passcode, these security measures won’t apply. Other tips to protect your iPhone You can take a few other steps to make your iPhone more secure: Make your passcode longer. If you have only a four-digit pin to unlock your device, change it to a six-digit one or even an alphanumeric passcode. Protect sensitive photos that contain personal information. Delete photos in your camera roll that show important documents, which can help thieves find more personal information about you. If you need quick access to them for some reason, you can instead move them to the Photos app’s hidden album by long-pressing a photo and then selecting Hide. From the Photos section of Settings, you can change whether the hidden album is visible at all, and you can require the use of Face ID to open the hidden album. You can also store photos of documents in a secure online cloud storage service or a password manager. Wherever you put the images, make sure that some kind of authentication—a passcode, Face ID, or the like—is required to view them. Protect individual apps with a PIN or Face ID. Most apps on iPhones don’t often (or ever) require you to log back in; as a result, a thief with an unlocked iPhone can easily access all of your apps. Some apps, especially those related to credit cards and banking, allow you to set an individual PIN or use your face or fingerprint to unlock them. Be sure to switch these settings on. Require Face ID or Touch ID to view saved passwords. Stolen Device Protection requires biometric authentication to use or view your saved passwords or to have the iPhone autofill those logins when you navigate to a site. But you can require that even without Stolen Device Protection: Go to Settings, tap Face ID & Passcode, and toggle on the Password AutoFill option. You can also use a standalone password manager such as our top pick, 1Password, which has many features that built-in password managers can’t match. Enable Find My on your iPhone. If your iPhone is stolen, you can use the Find My app to track it down and disable it remotely. Take some time to try this tool out before you need it in an emergency. This article was edited by Caitlin McGarry. Further reading - by Dave Gershgorn Losing a phone or laptop can throw your life into chaos, but taking a few easy steps before anything happens can turn a catastrophe into a minor inconvenience.

item.title: Apple Event Live Updates: New Foldable iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and More
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 4.39
Apple has officially launched a foldable iPhone, and to no one’s surprise, it’s the most expensive iPhone yet. Wirecutter was on the ground in Cupertino, California, to report on Apple’s annual product-launch event on September 9, where the company also announced a revamped iPhone 18 Pro, plus new Apple Watches and AirPods. It’s been an interesting year for Apple, one in which new CEO John Ternus took the helm from Tim Cook on September 1. The tech industry is also facing a shortage of components such as memory and storage, which are being funneled to AI data centers. That’s caused prices on many products to increase in recent months, including Apple’s latest iPhones. We’ll dive into longer reviews of Apple’s new gadgets after spending hands-on time with them, but until then, here are the big takeaways from the Apple event. - There’s now a foldable iPhone. The iPhone Duo folds in half to fit in your palm or unfolds so you can view and use two apps at once. Starting at $2,000, it’s the most expensive iPhone yet. - The new iPhone Pros represent an iterative update. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max have better battery life and cameras, plus more powerful chips that help run AI features, but their designs are otherwise mostly the same. - The latest Apple Watches have new health features. The Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 now measure your heart rate every five seconds, deliver a daily health score, and can listen to conversations to deliver an AI-generated recap. - The new AirPods are better at noise cancellation. The active noise cancellation in the AirPods 5 set is supposed to be up to 50% better, and these earbuds are also better at helping you hear exterior noise when it’s time to have a conversation. iPhone Duo Apple announced its long-awaited foldable phone, the iPhone Duo. The Duo has a passport-style design with rounded corners. The cover display measures 5.9 inches, while the inner display is 7.6 inches (80% larger than that of the iPhone 18 Pro). Unfolded, it’s the thinnest iPhone ever. The cover and inner displays share the same aspect ratio, and the inner camera is hidden beneath the display, appearing only when you need it for FaceTime calls. For multitasking, you can view and use two apps simultaneously, and the iPhone Duo’s surface also supports the USB-C Apple Pencil. With an IP68 rating, the foldable iPhone is fully dust- and water-resistant, and it has Ceramic Shield on both the front and back for extra protection. As for cameras, it comes with 48-megapixel dual-fusion cameras on the back and a 12-megapixel front-facing camera on the cover display. It adds a few camera options that other iPhones don’t have, including an AI feature that snaps a picture only once everyone has posed, the ability for multiple people to join a FaceTime call from both sides of the phone, and a stand-up feature using the phone’s folding design. Under the hood is the same new A20 Pro chip that appears across Apple’s latest iPhones. It delivers faster CPU and GPU performance, and it has two neural engines (Apple’s AI-specific processors), allowing for a 50% increase in memory bandwidth — all of which help power AI-based features and tasks. The iPhone Duo also has a C2 modem for 50% faster uploads. The foldable iPhone comes with batteries on each side that work together for all-day battery life, which Apple claims reaches up to 31 hours on the inner display and 44 hours on the outer display. It offers up to 24 hours per charge when you’re using both screens equally. Though we haven’t yet put the phone to the test, the displays impressed in demos. In one video, Netflix previews on the cover display seamlessly transferred to the interior display when the phone was opened. The iPhone Duo appears to combine the best of a phone and a tablet in one device. The iPhone Duo will start at $2,000, with storage ranging from 256 GB up to 2 TB. It will come in two colors: Star White and Night Sky. It will be available for preorder on October 16 and will go on sale October 23. iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max This year’s iPhone 18 Pro is an iterative upgrade over its predecessor, with the addition of the new A20 Pro chip, longer battery life, and improved camera features. The design is the same as that of last year’s model, but it comes in a few new color options: Black, Glacier, and Burgundy, plus Silver (each with a color-matched back). Apple also redesigned the Dynamic Island (the cutout at the top) to be smaller, but it now supports up to three apps simultaneously. Apple increased the battery life, promising up to 36 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro and up to 45 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro Max — the longest battery life for the Pro and Pro Max models yet. Apple reports that the iPhone 18 Pro charges to 50% in as fast as 15 minutes. The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max both get big camera upgrades, as well, including a new 48-megapixel camera sensor with variable aperture that better balances light and depth of field. It adjusts automatically based on the scene; in dark environments, for example, it lets in around 50% more light. iPhones also now “sign” the images they take, so it can be proven whether an image is original or has been altered. Apple will also add support for SynthID, which can identify pictures made or modified by AI. With these models, Apple is emphasizing Siri AI, its more intelligent voice assistant. The company says Siri will draw from messages, emails, photos, and what’s on the device’s screen to give more personalized answers. New AI-powered software features will be available in iOS 27 on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer, so you don’t need to upgrade to get access to them. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,200, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,300, which amounts to $100 more than last year’s models. Both phones will come in 256 GB, 512 GB, 1 TB, and 2 TB versions. They will be available for preorder starting September 12, with full availability on September 18. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 The latest Apple Watch models, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, measure your heart rate every five seconds, 60 times more frequently than prior models. The watches will now be able to display a real-time heart rate on the watch face, and heart-rate variability, which the watches use to help measure stress and recovery, is sampled up to every five minutes. Apple claims that the Apple Watch has the most accurate heart-rate sensing of any wearable device. In addition to continuous heart-rate monitoring, the Apple Watches have a new Readiness feature similar to those offered by Whoop and Oura. Every morning, your watch will give you a score from 0 to 10 and advise you on how to proceed with exercise: Recover, Pace Yourself, Ready, or Go For It. The advice then updates throughout the day. A new Insights tab in the redesigned Health app, which is coming later this year, offers AI-powered recommendations based on your activity and data. The Health app will also use your data to display your Health Age and measure your Longevity. You’ll be able to see how your data compares to clinical recommendations and integrate your lab results. Both new watches have a new S11 chip that powers AI features, which Apple calls Audio Intelligence. Audio Intelligence uses AI combined with the watches’ built-in microphones for a few different purposes. For starters, it can listen for sounds and then notify you when, for instance, someone rings the doorbell, which will be particularly useful for those who are deaf or hard of hearing. Another Audio Intelligence feature is Siri Recap, which takes notes from your conversations and creates an AI-generated summary. You can enable it and choose to always have it on, or you can schedule it to offer recaps at specific times of day. You can turn it on or off at any time. Audio is not recorded or stored and can’t be accessed by anyone, including Apple. The recaps are end-to-end encrypted, and speakers aren’t identified. The $400 Apple Watch Series 12 comes in 42 mm and 46 mm sizes in Space Gray, Black, Light Gold, and Dark Bronze aluminum. The cases have Ceramic Shield 2, similar to the iPhone. Series 12 is also available in a ceramic finish in Pearl White and Night Blue. Battery life remains unchanged at a day long, though this watch charges faster and lasts longer than previous models did when used outside. The $800 Ultra 4 gets more than two days of battery life, charges faster, and lasts longer outside. Its Max Extended Mode can help you eke out 45 hours on a charge. It comes in black or natural titanium in a 49 mm size. Both watches are available to preorder today, and they go on sale September 18. AirPods 5 Apple’s latest earbuds, the AirPods 5, emphasize better sound quality and more effective background noise reduction. With a new acoustic architecture, the AirPods 5 set offers up to 50% more noise reduction than its predecessor. The earbuds can also automatically adapt between active noise cancellation and transparency depending on the background noise. This year’s model also gets up to four hours of listening with ANC and up to 20 hours with the charging case. Apple also introduced the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case set, which lets you swipe on the stem of the AirPod to adjust audio levels. This set has longer battery life (up to five hours with ANC) and comes with a wireless charging case that’s compatible with Apple Watch and Qi chargers. The new AirPods are also better at letting in external sounds when wanted, and they lower the volume on music and other audio automatically if the wearer starts speaking. You can speak with Siri via the AirPods, too, and you can shake your head yes or no to respond to Siri. In addition, Siri can translate speech in another language or interact with the apps on your phone for you. The standard AirPods 5 set will cost $130, while the AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging Case set will cost $150. They are both available for preorder starting today and will go on sale September 18. This article was edited by Jason Chen.

item.title: How to Finally Find A Bra You Won’t Hate
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 3.47
Listen and follow The Wirecutter Show Apple Podcasts | Spotify | Amazon Music | YouTube | iHeartRadio Finding a bra that fits well involves navigating a seemingly impossible combination of measurements, brands, cup sizes, and personal preferences. Even knowing your usual size doesn’t guarantee that a bra will feel comfortable or provide the support you need. This episode, Wirecutter senior staff writer Zoe Vanderweide breaks down what a bra is actually supposed to do, and how to tell when one fits properly. After testing more than 35 bras, she explains why the band matters more than the straps for support, why bra sizes aren’t standardized across brands, and how to shop when your breasts don’t fit neatly into a standard size. Plus, she reveals how to make your bras last longer. This episode covers - Why the right bra can do much more than provide support: Bras can change the shape of your breasts, provide nipple coverage, smooth asymmetry, make clothes fit better, or minimize a larger bust. - Why you should know your measurements and then try multiple sizes anyway: Zoe recommends measuring yourself, checking a brand’s size chart, and ordering a couple of sizes, because there’s no substitute for actually trying a bra on. - Why you shouldn’t wear the same bra two days in a row: Letting the elastane in a bra’s band rest between wears helps it regain its shape and prevents it from stretching out prematurely. - How to wash a bra without destroying it: You don’t need to wash a bra after every wear. When you do, use a gentle wash cycle in a mesh bag and air-dry. Products we recommend This versatile bra offers outstanding comfort and a subtle push-up, and the deep plunge works with many necklines. It comes in cup sizes AA to H — including half-cups, for a fine-tuned fit. But it might not provide enough support for larger busts. This smooth, stretchy bralette achieves something bordering on the miraculous: It comfortably supports large breasts without the use of any metal parts — wires, clasps, sliders, you name it. Just be aware that pulling it on, over your head, isn’t the easiest undertaking. Wrapped in delicately scalloped floral lace, this exquisite bra is sexy and surprisingly comfortable. Since the band sizing tops out at 36 inches, it’s ideal for those with smaller frames. As sexy as it is supportive, this lacy, unlined bra lifts and centers larger breasts. Its intricate design and texture might be visible under some fabrics, so you’ll have to choose your outfits accordingly. This sexy, sophisticated wireless bralette is made of a fine, peekaboo mesh that’s soft and stretchy. It has an adjustable band and straps, so you can fine-tune the fit, and it’s designed to fit cup sizes A to G — though it provides only light support. Constructed of smooth, pleasantly stretchy material, this cute and comfy wire-free bralette is made for relaxing. It’s made to fit cup sizes A to F, but the medium support may not feel like enough for heavier breasts. This sleek, lightweight T-shirt bra provides exceptional support for larger breasts, and its wide, firm band smooths out lumps and bumps. It may not be the cutest bra out there, but it’s the one our large-busted testers kept reaching for. This well-priced bra creates a smooth, defined silhouette, and it comfortably supports breasts through whatever the day throws at you. The cups are deep and generous — a plus for fuller busts — but sizing doesn’t go beyond an F cup. Zoe loves her new diamond-art kit. Additional reading Episode transcript ZOE: “32B” tells you the band size and the cup size of that bra in that brand, but it really doesn’t tell you anything else about how it’s going to feel on your body, or whether it’s going to be suited to your unique shape and proportions and all that. CAIRA: I’m Caira Blackwell. ROSIE: I’m Rosie Guerin, and you’re listening to The Wirecutter Show. ROSIE: Hey, there. Before we jump into today’s show, I want to let you know about a special offer. If you’re not already a subscriber to The New York Times, you can now explore The Times for free. No paywalls during your first month in the New York Times app. You can find all of your favorite shows like, I don’t know, this show, Modern Love, Cannonball, and more on the new shows tab. Okay, let’s get into it. ROSIE: Hey, Caira. CAIRA: Hi, Rosie. ROSIE: Today we’re talking about something that Wirecutter has covered forever and is consistently popular. I feel like you probably know what this is. CAIRA: Ooh, something in the kitchen section. ROSIE: It’s bras. CAIRA: Oh, duh. It is really hard to find a good bra, and it makes total sense that people come to Wirecutter to try and figure that out, because there’s so much you have to know. ROSIE: For the longest time, I assumed that you only could buy bras that actually fit you in a store — that you would have to go in, get measured, find someone with the knowledge to help you. It’s definitely not easy. We’ve got an expert here on staff who spent years covering bras. Her name is Zoe Vanderweide. She’s a senior staff writer, and she joined us not too long ago to talk swimsuits. We love Zoe. She spent hours going deep into Reddit threads, talking with bra makers, and recruiting testers of all shapes and sizes, and colors and creeds. CAIRA: Totally. And that’s why she’s not just going to run through all the picks that she recommends in that guide — which you should go read — but she is going to walk us through what bras are supposed to do and how they’re supposed to fit, and how to find one that really works for you no matter what size or style you’re looking for. ROSIE: It’s going to be educational, find out what your bra can do for you. We’re going to take a quick break, and then we’ll be back with Zoe Vanderweide. CAIRA: Welcome back. With us now is Zoe Vanderweide, a senior staff writer on our style team. Zoe has written our guides to women’s jeans, T-shirts, underwear, and swimsuits, and for this guide, she’s tested over 35 bras. ROSIE: That’s a lot of bras. Welcome back, Zoe. Good to see you. ZOE: Thank you. Thank you for having me. ROSIE: Okay. Let’s start with a very, very basic question, a softball. Most people who wear a bra know it’s supposed to offer support. What do you think people don’t understand about what a bra can really do? What can your bra do for you? ZOE: Well, like you said, of course the bra provides support and comfort, which is especially important if you have larger, heavier breasts, but it can do lots of other things. A bra can provide some extra nipple coverage. It can provide shaping, whether that’s kind of creating a more rounded shape, a more lifted shape, a more projected … that means up and forward-facing shape. ROSIE: Up and out. ZOE: Yup. And it can also just make your clothes fit better. For someone with smaller breasts, it could help to enhance, whether that’s through a push-up or padding. It could also, for someone with larger boobs, help to minimize a larger bust. Many women with a larger bust will recognize the struggle of trying to wear a button-up shirt that gapes in the front, so a minimizer can help with that kind of thing. A bra can also help to create symmetry: If you have noticeable asymmetry on your breasts, it can create a smoother appearance, not just on your breasts but also around your back. So there’s a lot of things that a bra does for you. ROSIE: Yeah, it can mop your floors. It can — CAIRA: I was going to say the same thing. It just changes your whole life, it sounds like, if you get a good one. ROSIE: It can braid your hair. CAIRA: So why is it so hard for people to find a bra that they like or get a good fit? ZOE: Well, it’s the unfortunate truth that a lot of bras are just uncomfortable, and that’s partly because many of them are just not well designed or well constructed. But it’s also because there are lots of great bras out there that still feel uncomfortable for people, and that’s because a lot of folks are just not wearing the right bra for their unique breast size and shape, and for their personal preferences. There’s a lot more to consider beyond just your band and your cup size that impacts how a bra fits you and feels on your body, and that includes the shape of your breasts, the way your breast tissue is distributed across your chest. Your life stage, that includes your age, hormonal changes, your lifestyle, how active you are, what kind of clothes you’re wearing. And your sensory preferences, like: How loose or tight do you like things to fit you? Are you sensitive to certain materials? Do seams and tags and little itchy things bother you? Does an underwire feel supportive for you, or does it feel terrible? There’s a lot of things to consider. CAIRA: And you don’t get all of that information in a “32B” label, right? You have to really try them on to figure out what you’re getting, and how it fits on you. ZOE: Yeah, you definitely don’t. I mean, that “32B” tells you the band size and the cup size of that bra in that brand, but it really doesn’t tell you anything else about how it’s going to feel on your body, or whether it’s going to be suited to your unique shape and proportions and all that. ROSIE: Zoe, what are the things you’d recommend people know or learn about their breasts, their body, before shopping for a bra? As an example, I think I didn’t consider asymmetry. ZOE: Yeah, absolutely. I mean, there’s a lot that you can kind of observe about yourself that will help you come into bra shopping more prepared. For example, is there more fullness on the top or on the bottom? Are they close-set, or are they wide-set? Which way are your nipples pointing? Like you said, are they asymmetrical? Is one bigger than the other? Are they more projected — that is, pointing more forward — or are they more spread out? And of course, the size of your breasts is also very important to know. You can also think about it in terms of the common fit issues that you encounter, and this may be an easier way for some folks to kind of wrap their head around this, because it can get very technical when you’re talking about the shape and distribution of your breasts. How tall are your roots? You know, like — ROSIE: You know what, Zoe? Thank you for asking, because no one ever asks me that. ZOE: Right? ROSIE: What does that actually mean? ZOE: Okay. So when we talk about your roots, we’re talking about how your breasts are placed on your chest. So if you have tall roots, your breasts are going to come up higher onto your chest. If you have wide roots, then your breasts spread out farther across your chest. There’s just a lot of different terminology that most people don’t use, so it’s honestly not helpful for most people. But I think a way that people can kind of assess how their breasts compare, because you only have … for the most part, you’re looking at yourself, and you’re not really thinking about, like, “Well, my roots are taller than average” or something, right? But you can kind of think about it in terms of the fit issues that you encounter when you’re shopping. So for example, do your boobs spill out the top of cups? That might mean that you have taller roots, i.e. that your breast tissue is extending high up on your chest. Maybe you often have gaping at the top of the cup, which means you have the opposite, you have shorter roots. If your breasts are wider, you might find that sometimes underwires will dig into the side, under your armpit. So when you think about it in terms of that, you can kind of get an idea of where your breasts fall in terms of what bra manufacturers are thinking of as the target boob. ROSIE: It sounds like, just the more information you can gather — appearance, feel, some of these fit issues — the better prepared you’ll be to communicate your wants and needs if you go into a store? ZOE: Yeah. I mean, I think you should be able to describe your breasts, and you should be able to describe the things about bras that don’t work for you. ROSIE: Are there any resources people can look to if you’re trying to gather more field research about your breasts? ZOE: There are a lot of resources online that can be very helpful. There’s a subreddit called A Bra That Fits. That’s a real treasure trove of information. It’s been around for a while, and there’s a lot of information on it, so it can be a little bit overwhelming. But if you want to get really into the nitty-gritty and hear from other people and their experiences, there’s a lot of great expertise to be found on that subreddit. There’s also retailers that offer helpful guides on how to measure yourself, what types of bras work best for different breast shapes, things like that. There’s a retailer called Her Room that has a nice guide on their site. So there’s lots of stuff you can find online. I mean, the gold standard would be to get fitted by a professional bra fitter in person, especially at a store that sells multiple, different brands. CAIRA: So not, like, a Victoria’s Secret, where you go into the — ROSIE: Yeah. ZOE: Right, because then you’re going to get their specific sizing convention. And what’s really nice is to have somebody who’s just deeply expert in the whole industry, in the whole field of offerings. You should do it at least once, especially if you’ve ever had issues finding a bra that’s comfy for you, because it really is an area where these people have a ton of expertise and can give you really personalized, specific pointers. And for brands to produce that number of sizes, imagine producing all the way from 28AA up to a 50O or something, and with every single — ROSIE: Design, color. ZOE: — and also with every single cup size paired with every single band size. ROSIE: Oh, right. ZOE: The number of permutations, it doesn’t scale well. It’s a difficult thing to invest in. So what bra companies typically do is, they try to make sizes that can kind of conform to a variety of bodies. But they don’t do it perfectly, and that’s why people have such a hard time finding bras that fit them, because they’re kind of taking, like, a “Well, this is, like, a guesstimate of what’s going to kind of fit you,” rather than “This is your actual specific size that is tailor-made for you, and how your breasts sit on your body.” CAIRA: Zoe, I learned a lot about the different parts of the bra and what they’re supposed to do just by reading your guide. So can you tell us what the different parts are, what we should know about them, and how they should properly fit? And I want to just start with the band. What is the purpose of the band of the bra? ZOE: Yeah. So first of all, when we are talking about the band of the bra, which is the band that goes around your rib cage, we’re generally also talking about a part of the bra that we call the wings. Those are the panels of fabric that kind of wrap around the sides under your arms and around the back. So I’m going to kind of use those words interchangeably. But the band of the bra is where most of the support from the garment is coming from. This is really … it’s not, as many people think, coming from the straps, it’s mostly coming from the band. And for that reason, it’s really important to have a well-fitting band and a band that is snug enough around your rib cage. So some signs that your band might be too big would be, like, you turn around and see that the back of the bra is kind of riding up. It’s higher in the back than it is in the front, or if you’re able to fit more than a few fingers between your skin and the band. And on the other hand, a too-tight band can be really uncomfortable as well. It can just feel too tight. It’ll leave marks or irritation on your skin. But in general, especially if you have bigger or heavier boobs, or you just feel like you need more support, you kind of want to have the snuggest band that you personally feel comfy in. In general, a wider band is going to provide more support than a skinny one. If you have big boobs, you probably want a band that has at least three rows of hooks in the back. ROSIE: How about the straps, Zoe? I would’ve imagined that the straps of the bra would be doing a lot of the supportive work. Is that true? ZOE: Yeah, I mean the straps do provide some of the lifting and support. If you’re looking for the most support, you’re going to want a wider strap; in general that’s going to provide more support and feel more comfortable. A thinner strap, you might find, digs into the top of your shoulder. Usually when your straps are digging in, that either means that they’re too thin, or that you need to adjust or loosen the straps, or just that the bra itself, the band, is not doing a great job with supporting your breasts. The placement of the straps also can affect how supportive and lifting they are. A racerback, which is, like, the crisscross shape in the back, is generally going to feel more supportive. Straps that are kind of like … imagine that the back of the bra, the straps are shaped like a U, like a ballet leotard, so that’s one of the more supportive strap configurations as well. Whereas wider-set straps, like on a balconette bra or something like that, are just not going to be as lifting and supportive. CAIRA: What about cups? What do we need to know about cups? ZOE: So the cups are the part of the bra that actually contains your breasts, and you want the shape and the construction of those cups to be a good fit for what you want, and what your breasts are like. One thing that we talk about with cups is how deep or shallow they are. Deeper cups are going to be better for larger breasts, or if you have pendulous breasts or more projected breasts, whereas shallower cups are going to be better for breasts where the tissue is more spread out across your chest or for smaller breasts. There’s also … when we talk about cups, there are different cup constructions that do different things well. So some cups are constructed as a single molded piece that kind of provides that gentle rounded shape that a lot of people like. Other cups are a single piece, but they’re just kind of, like, unstructured, stretchy fabric, and those kinds of cups are going to conform to your body and offer a more kind of natural-looking shape. And then there are also pieced cups, which are especially good for larger breasts. They can also be really cute in fancy lingerie, but you’re talking about cups typically with three different panels. What those do is, they really create that 3D shape and space for a larger breast. They help to kind of coax the breast tissue into a more forward and lifted position, and they can provide better support for heavier boobs. And really what’s best is going to depend totally on the size and shape of your breasts and your personal preferences, and just kind of the look that you’re hoping to achieve. ROSIE: Is there anything we should know about padding an underwire? I see underwire still available out there. Do people love it? What’s the deal? ZOE: In general, an underwire bra is going to be more supportive than a wireless bra. There are some exceptions to the rule. We have thankfully found some really great, pretty supportive wireless bras. However, a lot of people, especially people with larger breasts, will say that they’re just not going to get the same level of support from a wireless bra that they do from an underwire bra. On the other hand, there’s lots of folks who just really dislike the feel of an underwire. It can dig in. As the bra wears out, sometimes the wire even starts to poke out and poke you, which is really unpleasant, obviously. I am nine months pregnant, so I’m in a wire-free era. There’s not even space for a wire between my boobs and my belly right now. In terms of padding, I’m personally not a big fan of padding, but some people are. It just provides … either if it’s placed at the bottom of the bra, it can provide a little lift, like a push-up, or it can also just provide some shaping or additional coverage for nipples or a more rounded profile, which some people like. CAIRA: Are there any parts of the bra that we haven’t talked about yet, particularly parts that people really don’t think about? ZOE: Yeah, there’s the part that is right between the cups; that kind of little flat piece that sits between the cups is called the gore. And the way that the gore fits on you can tell you a lot about how the bra as a whole is fitting on you. So on a well-fitting bra, that gore should be sitting flush against your chest. It should not be digging into your breast tissue. It shouldn’t feel like it’s too high. It shouldn’t feel like it’s pushing your boobs apart. If it’s digging in — that’s a common issue if you have closer-set breasts — if it’s digging in, that means that the gore is either too high or it’s too wide for your shape, or that just the band itself of the bra is too small. On the other hand, if it’s floating away from your body, that could mean that your band is too loose. It could also mean that your cups are too small. So you want to pay attention to how that gore is lying on your chest. I mean, in terms of other features, you want to have adjustable straps, which is important, one, to customize your fit when you first get your bra, and then also to keep it fitting well as it ages. As the elastic wears out, the bra will continue to fit you for longer. Kind of by the same token, bra bands have three columns of hooks to adjust the band tightness as the bra ages and stretches. That adjustability helps a single bra size fit more bodies, but it also helps that single bra fit your body as the bra ages. CAIRA: So how does somebody figure out their bra size? This seems to be tricky for a lot of people. Do you have to get fitted in real life? Is that the only way to tell? ZOE: I don’t think that you have to get fitted in real life. I think it’s definitely a great thing to do, especially if you’ve struggled with finding bras that fit, but you can absolutely do it on your own at home. Bras are sized with two key pieces of information: one is your band size and two is your cup size. The band is the part that fits just under your breasts. This measurement should be taken snugly around your rib cage. Typically, bands are offered in sizes 30 to 44-ish inches, although there are brands that offer more inclusive size ranges, from as small as a 28 to as large as a 50, 52. And then, cups, you take that measurement around the fullest part of your bust, and you should take that measurement looser than you take the band measurement. You should be able to inhale, exhale when you’re doing that measurement. Cups, typically you’ll see ranges from an A or AA up to an F or a G, but there are brands that offer cup sizes up to an M or an O. That’s kind of the basics. But the reality of it is that finding your size is pretty complicated, because brands do not really offer super-consistent sizing. You could be one size in one brand, and a totally different size in another brand. And then the other reason is that we have different ways of measuring size, and this is the one that really gets me, and I think is really confusing for a lot of people. But basically there are two ways that people commonly measure their bra size. One is the way that I learned when I was a teenager, which is that you take your snug under-bust measurement, and then you add four, or if it’s an odd number, you add five. So if I measure 32 inches under my bust, then I add four, and I get 36, and that’s my band size. And then I’m going to take a measurement across the fullest part of my bust. Let’s say it measures 39 inches, 39 minus 36 is three, which corresponds to an A, B, C. It’s very convoluted. So there’s that method, or what a lot of professionals will tell you is a better way of doing it is to take that under-bust measurement, and that’s your band measurement, and then take your full-bust measurement and subtract to find your cup size. So that same 36C could also be fitted as a 32G, and those sizes sound very, very different. ROSIE: Yeah. ZOE: And a lot of bra brands really favor the 36C, that former sizing convention, because it means they have to make fewer sizes. ROSIE: Right. ZOE: When you start looking more into higher-end or specialty brands, especially brands that are really great for larger busts, then you’re going to start seeing more of those sizes that sound more unusual to us, like 32G. There’s a good amount of trial and error that comes with this. So once you have this information about your measurements, it really comes down to the brands and your own body shape and comfort. My best recommendation would be to know your measurements, and then with that information, look at the brand that you’re shopping, look at their size chart, see what they recommend, and then to order a couple different sizes, because you really just have to try it on. CAIRA: Okay. We’re going to take a quick break, and when we’re back, we’re going to give Zoe some scenarios, and she’s going to recommend specific bra types and brands. ROSIE: Welcome back. Today, our guest is Zoe Vanderweide. We’re talking about shopping for comfortable bras that actually fit you. CAIRA: That’s right. So Zoe, we have some questions about how to take care of bras. CAIRA: So what if you’re someone who feels like it’s hard to find a bra that fits and thinks they may be in between standard sizes? ZOE: Okay, this is a good one. So we have one recommendation in our guide from a brand called ThirdLove. This is the only brand that we’ve tested that offers half-cup sizing, so literally you could be an A and a half, a B and a half, a C and a half. This has been a game-changer for lots of our testers. ROSIE: How about someone with large breasts who really hates underwires but feels like the traditional wireless, I think as you referred to it, isn’t supportive enough? ZOE: Yeah. ZOE: And that one is really nice, especially for folks with, I would say, small to medium-size boobs. ROSIE: I think we would be remiss not to ask you about someone who’s breastfeeding and needs access to their nipples with ease, but I’m pretty sure there’s a guide for that. Is that right? ROSIE: You’ve thrown out some pricing so far, but how much should we be expecting to spend on this new bra, Zoe? What’s the range? ZOE: I mean, I would say in general, our picks fall somewhere between 50 and 100 bucks. ROSIE: That’s a lot. ZOE: Cheaper bras obviously are out there. What I have found is that cheaper bras tend to not last as long. If you have bigger boobs, it is unfortunately often worth investing in the pricier bras, because you’re just asking your bra to do more, and they are, like, pieces of engineering. CAIRA: But you’re supposed to be washing them after every use, right? So ideally you’d want one for at least every day of the week, no? ZOE: I don’t think you have to wash your bra after every use. CAIRA: Okay. ZOE: I don’t think so. What you should be doing is letting your bra rest after every use. By that, I mean you shouldn’t be wearing the same bra consecutively every day. That’s because almost all bras contain elastane for stretch, and if you continually are stretching it, stretching it, stretching it, it’s going to wear out faster, and it’s going to kind of lose its shape. Whereas if you allow it to rest, if you give it a day to kind of tighten back up, just sitting in your drawer, it’ll feel like it fits better for longer between washes. At the minimum, you want to have, like, three to four bras in your everyday rotation so that you have one to wear, one to rest, and one to wash. ROSIE: And how long should we be expecting our bras to last? ZOE: A lot of the experts out there will say that a bra lasts, like, a year. I think that’s crazy. ROSIE: $100 a bra times four — CAIRA: Four per year. ROSIE: Every year — ZOE: Every year. ROSIE: Is a big bra budget. ZOE: Yeah. I don’t think that that is realistic for most people. I certainly don’t buy new bras every year. I have bras still kicking that are three and four years old that are totally fine, but it really comes down to taking good care of your bras. CAIRA: And what does that mean, exactly? How do you make them last, other than not wearing them consecutively? ROSIE: Yeah, you got to let that elastane rest. ZOE: Yeah, let it rest. So I don’t think you need to wash them after every single wear. Washing clothes wears them out faster, right? When you do wash your bras, you can really baby them, you can hand-wash them with a no-rinse detergent, which is, like, a detergent where you can just put in a cap full and then let your clothes sit in there, swish them around, and then take them out. You don’t need to rinse them. You don’t need to agitate them. You don’t need to wring them out. That’s going to be the gentlest method.
